chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: 1. We are unknown to ourselves, we knowers, and there is good reason for it. We have never searched for ourselves — so how should we ever find ourselves? It has been said rightly: "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Our treasure is where the hives of our knowledge stand. We are always heading for those hives. As born creatures of flight and honey-gatherers of the spirit, we really care in our hearts about one thing only — to bring something "home to the hive!"

As for the rest of life, with its so-called "experiences," which of us takes a serious enough interest in it? Or has enough time? I fear that in dealing with such matters we are never properly present: to be precise, our heart is not in it, and certainly not our ear. We are like a man lost in divine distraction, or sunk in the seas of his own soul, in whose ear the clock has just thundered its twelve strokes of noon with all its force. He suddenly wakes up and asks himself, "What in fact has just struck?" In the same way we sometimes rub our puzzled ears afterwards and ask, in complete astonishment and complete embarrassment, "What have we in fact just lived through?" And further, "Who are we in fact?" Then we count, after they have struck, as I have explained, all twelve throbbing beats of the clock of our experience, of our life, of our being — ah! — and we count wrong in the attempt. Of necessity we remain strangers to ourselves; we do not understand ourselves; we are bound to be mistaken about ourselves. For us the motto holds good for all eternity: "Each one is the farthest away from himself" — as far as ourselves are concerned, we are not "knowers."

2. My thoughts on the genealogy of our moral prejudices — for they are the issue in this polemic — first found their bald and provisional expression in the collection of aphorisms entitled Human, all-too-Human, a Book for Free Minds. I began writing it in Sorrento, during a winter that let me look out over the broad and dangerous territory through which my mind had wandered until then. That was the winter of 1876-77; the thoughts themselves are older. In substance they were already the same thoughts that I take up again in the following treatises — we hope that the long interval has done them good, and that they have grown riper, clearer, stronger, more complete. But I still cling to them even now. In the meantime they have held ever faster to each other; in fact they have grown out of their original shape and into each other. All this strengthens my joyous confidence that they were never originally separate, disconnected, capricious or sporadic phenomena. They must have sprung from a common root, from a fundamental "fiat" of knowledge whose empire reached to the soul's depth, and whose voice and demands grew ever more definite. That is the only proper state of affairs for a philosopher.

We have no right to be "disconnected": we must neither err "disconnectedly" nor strike the truth "disconnectedly." Instead, with the necessity with which a tree bears its fruit, our thoughts, our values, our Yes's and No's and If's and Whether's grow connected and interrelated, mutual witnesses of one will, one health, one kingdom, one sun. Are these fruits of ours to your taste? — But what does that matter to the trees? What does that matter to us, the philosophers?

3. I have a scrupulosity peculiar to myself, which I confess reluctantly — it concerns morality. It showed itself in my life so early, so spontaneously, so persistently, and in such keen opposition to environment, epoch, precedent and ancestry, that I would almost be entitled to call it my "â priori." So my curiosity and my suspicion were early bound to halt at the question of what the origin of our "Good" and our "Evil" actually was. Indeed, at the boyish age of thirteen the problem of the origin of Evil already haunted me. At an age "when games and God divide one's heart," I devoted my first childish attempt at the literary game, my first philosophic essay, to that problem. As for my childish solution, well, I quite properly gave the honor to God and made him the father of evil. Did my own "â priori" demand that solution from me? That new, immoral, or at least "amoral" "â priori," and the "categorical imperative" which was its voice (but oh! how hostile to the Kantian article, and how pregnant with problems!), has had more and more of my attention since then, and indeed more than attention. Fortunately I soon learned to separate theological from moral prejudices, and I gave up looking for a supernatural origin of evil. A certain amount of historical and philological education, to say nothing of an innate faculty of psychological discrimination par excellence, almost immediately transformed my original problem into the following one: Under what conditions did Man invent for himself those judgments of values, "Good" and "Evil"? And what intrinsic value do they have in themselves? Have they so far hindered or advanced human well-being? Are they a symptom of the distress, impoverishment and degeneration of Human Life? Or, conversely, do the fullness, the strength and the will of Life, its courage, its self-confidence, its future, show themselves in them? On this point I found and hazarded in my mind the most diverse answers. I established distinctions among periods, peoples and castes, and I became a specialist in my problem. From my answers grew new questions, new investigations, new conjectures, new probabilities, until at last I had a land of my own and a soil of my own, a whole secret world growing and flowering, like hidden gardens whose existence no one could have an inkling of. Oh, how happy we are, we finders of knowledge, provided that we know how to keep silent long enough.

4. I owe my first impulse to publish some of my hypotheses on the origin of morality to a clear, well-written and even precocious little book. In it a perverse and vicious kind of moral philosophy (your real English kind) was presented to me definitely for the first time. It attracted me with that magnetic attraction which belongs to whatever is diametrically opposed and antithetical to one's own ideas. The title of the book was The Origin of the Moral Emotions; its author was Dr. Paul Rée; the year of its appearance was 1877. I may almost say that I have never read anything in which every single dogma and conclusion called forth from me so emphatic a negation as in that book — though it was a negation tainted by either pique or intolerance. In the works on which I was then working I therefore referred, in season and out of season, to the arguments of that book. I did not mean to refute them — for what have I to do with mere refutations? As is natural to a positive mind, I substituted a more probable theory for an improbable one, and occasionally, no doubt, one philosophic error for another. In that early period I gave, as I have said, the first public expression to the theories of origin to which these essays are devoted. I did it with a clumsiness that I was the last to conceal from myself, for I was still cramped, still without a special language for these special subjects, and still frequently liable to relapse and vacillation. For details, compare what I say in Human, all-too-Human, part i., about the parallel early history of Good and Evil, Aph. 45 (namely, their origin from the castes of the aristocrats and the slaves); similarly, Aph. 136 et seq., on the birth and value of ascetic morality; similarly, Aphs. 96, 99, vol. ii., Aph. 89, on the Morality of Custom, that far older and more original kind of morality which is toto cœlo different from the altruistic ethics (in which Dr. Rée, like all the English moral philosophers, sees the ethical "Thing-in-itself"); finally, Aph. 92. Similarly, Aph. 26 in Human, all-too-Human, part ii., and Aph. 112, the Dawn of Day, on the origin of Justice as a balance between persons of approximately equal power (equilibrium as the hypothesis of all contract, and consequently of all law); similarly, on the origin of Punishment, Human, all-too-Human, part ii., Aphs. 22, 23, on which point the deterrent object is neither essential nor original (as Dr. Rée thinks: rather this object is only imported, under certain definite conditions, and always as something extra and additional).

5. In reality I had set my heart at that time on something much more important than the theories, mine or others', about the origin of morality (or, more precisely, the real function of these theories, from my view, was to point to an end to which they were one means among many). The issue for me was the value of morality, and on that subject I had to place myself in a state of abstraction in which I was almost alone with my great teacher Schopenhauer, to whom that book, with all its passion and inherent contradiction (for that book also was a polemic), turned for present help as though he were still alive. The issue was, strangely enough, the value of the "un-egoistic" instincts, the instincts of pity, self-denial and self-sacrifice, which Schopenhauer had so persistently painted in golden colors, deified and etherealized, that eventually they seemed to him, as it were, high and dry, "intrinsic values in themselves," on the strength of which he uttered his own negation, both to Life and to himself. But against these very instincts a more and more fundamental mistrust voiced itself in my soul, a skepticism that dug ever deeper and deeper. In this very instinct I saw the great danger of mankind, its most sublime temptation and seduction — seduction to what? to nothingness? In these very instincts I saw the beginning of the end, stability, the exhaustion that gazes backwards, the will turning against Life, the last illness announcing itself with its own mincing melancholy. I realized that the morality of pity, which spread wider and wider and whose grip infected even philosophers with its disease, was the most sinister symptom of our modern European civilization. I realized that it was the route along which that civilization slid on its way to — a new Buddhism? — a European Buddhism? — Nihilism? This exaggerated estimation in which modern philosophers have held pity is quite a new phenomenon: up to that time philosophers were absolutely unanimous about the worthlessness of pity. I need only mention Plato, Spinoza, La Rochefoucauld and Kant — four minds as different from each other as is possible, but united on one point: their contempt of pity.

6. This problem of the value of pity and of the pity-morality (I am an opponent of the modern infamous emasculation of our emotions) seems at first blush a mere isolated problem, a note of interrogation standing by itself. But whoever once halts at this problem and learns how to put questions will experience what I experienced. A new and immense vista unfolds before him, a sense of potentiality seizes him like a vertigo, every species of doubt, mistrust and fear springs up, the belief in morality, nay, in all morality, totters — and finally a new demand voices itself. Let us speak out this new demand: we need a critique of moral values, and the value of these values is to be called into question for the first time. For this we need a knowledge of the conditions and circumstances out of which these values grew, under which they evolved and became distorted (morality as a result, as a symptom, as a mask, as Tartuffism, as disease, as a misunderstanding; but also morality as a cause, as a remedy, as a stimulant, as a fetter, as a drug). We need it all the more because such a knowledge has neither existed until now nor is even now generally desired. The value of these "values" was taken for granted as an indisputable fact, beyond all question. No one has shown the faintest doubt or hesitation, until now, in judging the "good man" to be of higher value than the "evil man" — higher value specifically for human progress, utility and prosperity generally, not forgetting the future. What? Suppose the converse were the truth! What? Suppose there lurked in the "good man" a symptom of retrogression, such as a danger, a temptation, a poison, a narcotic, by means of which the present battened on the future! More comfortable and less risky perhaps than its opposite, but also pettier, meaner! So that morality would really be saddled with the guilt, if the maximum potentiality of the power and splendor of the human species were never to be attained? So that really morality would be the danger of dangers?

7. Enough: after this vista had disclosed itself to me, I had reason to search for learned, bold and industrious colleagues (I am doing it even to this very day). It means traversing the immense, distant and completely unexplored land of morality with new clamorous questions and at the same time with new eyes — a morality which has actually existed and been actually lived! And is this not practically equivalent to first discovering that land? If I thought, among others, of the aforesaid Dr. Rée in this context, I did so because I had no doubt that the very nature of his questions would compel him to have recourse to a truer method in order to obtain his answers. Have I deceived myself on that score? At all events I wished to give a better direction of vision to an eye of such keenness and such impartiality. I wished to direct him to the real history of morality, and to warn him, while there was yet time, against a world of English theories that culminated in the blue vacuum of heaven. Other colors, of course, rise immediately to one's mind as being a hundred times more potent than blue for a genealogy of morals: for instance, gray, by which I mean authentic facts capable of definite proof and actually existing — or, to put it shortly, the whole of that long hieroglyphic script (so hard to decipher) of the past history of human morals. This script was unknown to Dr. Rée; but he had read Darwin. And so in his philosophy the Darwinian beast and that pink of modernity, the demure weakling and dilettante who "bites no longer," shake hands politely, in a fashion that is at least instructive. The latter wears a certain facial expression of refined and good-humored indolence, tinged with a touch of pessimism and exhaustion, as if it really did not pay to take all these things — I mean moral problems — so seriously. I, on the other hand, think that there are no subjects which pay better for being taken seriously; part of this payment is that perhaps eventually they admit of being taken gaily. This gaiety, or, to use my own language, this joyful wisdom, is indeed a payment — a payment for a protracted, brave, laborious and burrowing seriousness, which, it goes without saying, is the attribute of but a few. But on the day when we say from the fullness of our hearts, "Forward! our old morality too is fit material for Comedy," we shall have discovered a new plot and a new possibility for the Dionysian drama entitled The Soul's Fate — and he will speedily make use of it, one can safely wager, he, the great ancient eternal dramatist of the comedy of our existence.

8. If this writing is obscure to anyone and jars on his ears, I do not think that I am necessarily to blame. It is clear enough on the hypothesis I presuppose, namely that the reader has first read my previous writings and has not grudged them a certain amount of trouble: it is not, indeed, a simple matter to get at their essence. Take, for instance, my Zarathustra. I allow no one to pass as knowing that book unless every single word in it has at some time wounded him profoundly and at some time enchanted him profoundly. Then, and not till then, can he enjoy the privilege of reverently sharing in the halcyon element from which that work is born, in its sunny brilliance, its distance, its spaciousness, its certainty. In other cases the aphoristic form produces difficulty, but this is only because the form is treated too casually. An aphorism properly coined and cast into its final mold is far from being "deciphered" as soon as it has been read; on the contrary, that is when it first requires to be expounded — and for that an art of exposition is of course necessary. The third essay in this book provides an example of what I call exposition in such cases: an aphorism is prefixed to that essay, and the essay itself is its commentary. One quality is certainly essential in order to practise reading as an art, and it has nowadays been best forgotten — that is why it will take some time yet for my writings to become readable. It is a quality for which one must be a cow, and under no circumstances a modern man! — rumination.
Sils-Maria, Upper Engadine, July 1887.

chapters.title: First Essay — “Good and Evil,” “Good and Bad”
paragraphs: 1. Those English psychologists are the only philosophers so far who deserve thanks for any attempt to reach a history of the origin of morality. These men, I say, are no small problem in their own persons. If I am to be quite frank, they even have an advantage over their books, as living riddles: they themselves are interesting! What do these English psychologists really mean? Whether they intend it or not, we always find them at the same task. They push the partie honteuse of our inner world to the front, and look for the effective, governing and decisive principle in exactly the place where the intellectual self-respect of the race would least like to find it (for example, in the vis inertiæ of habit, or in forgetfulness, or in a blind and chance mechanism and association of ideas, or in some factor that is purely passive, reflex, molecular, or fundamentally stupid). What is the real motive that always drives these psychologists in precisely this direction? Is it an instinct for disparaging man, somewhat sinister, vulgar and malignant, or perhaps incomprehensible even to itself? Or perhaps a touch of pessimistic jealousy, the mistrust of disillusioned idealists who have turned gloomy, poisoned and bitter? Or a petty subconscious enmity and rancor against Christianity (and Plato), that has perhaps never crossed the threshold of consciousness? Or just a vicious taste for those elements of life that are bizarre, painfully paradoxical, mystical and illogical? Or, as a last alternative, a dash of each of these motives: a little vulgarity, a little gloominess, a little anti-Christianity, a little craving for the necessary piquancy?
But I am told that these are simply old, cold, tedious frogs, crawling and hopping around men and inside men, as much at home there as they would be in a swamp.

I object to this; nay, I do not believe it. And if we may wish where knowledge is impossible, I wish from my heart that the opposite picture were true: that these analysts with their psychological microscopes are at bottom brave, proud and magnanimous animals, who know how to bridle both their hearts and their smarts, and who have specifically trained themselves to sacrifice what is desirable to what is true, any truth at all, even the simple, bitter, ugly, repulsive, unchristian and immoral truths — for there are truths of that kind.

2. All honor, then, to the noble spirits who would gladly dominate these historians of morality. But it is certainly a pity that they themselves lack the historical sense, and that all the beneficent spirits of history have deserted them. The whole train of their thought runs, as it always did with old-fashioned philosophers, along thoroughly unhistorical lines; there is no doubt of this. The crass ineptitude of their genealogy of morals shows at once when the question is the origin of the idea and judgment of "good." "Originally," so runs their decree, "man praised altruistic acts and called them 'good' from the standpoint of those on whom they were conferred, that is, those to whom they were useful. Later the origin of this praise was forgotten, and altruistic acts, simply because they were habitually praised as good, also came to be felt as good, as though they contained some intrinsic goodness." The thing is obvious: this first derivation already contains all the typical and peculiar traits of the English psychologists. We have "utility," "forgetting," "habit," and finally "error," the whole assemblage forming the basis of a system of values, of which the higher man has until now been proud, as though it were a privilege of man in general. This pride must be brought low, this system of values must lose its value: is that achieved?

Now the first argument that comes to hand is this: the concept "good" has its real home somewhere other than where it is sought. The judgment "good" did not come from those who received goodness. It came, much rather, from the good themselves, that is, the aristocratic, the powerful, the high-stationed, the high-minded. They felt themselves and their actions to be good, meaning of the first order, and set that against everything low, low-minded, vulgar and plebeian. From this pathos of distance they took for themselves the right to create values for their own profit and to coin names for those values. What did utility have to do with it? Utility is as foreign and as inapplicable a standpoint as can be, when what we face is so volcanic an effervescence of supreme values, which create and mark out a hierarchy among themselves. Here one sees the contrast with that tepid temperature on which every combination of worldly wisdom and every calculation of practical expediency always rests, and rests not once, not as an exception, but chronically. The pathos of nobility and distance, as I have said, is the chronic, despotic esprit de corps and fundamental instinct of a higher dominant race living alongside a meaner race, an "under race." This is the origin of the antithesis of good and bad.

(The masters' right of giving names goes so far that one may look upon language itself as an expression of the power of the masters. They say "this is that, and that"; they finally seal every object and every event with a sound, and thereby take possession of it at the same time.) Because of this origin, the word "good" has no necessary connection with altruistic acts, as the superstitious belief of these moral philosophers holds. On the contrary, it is when aristocratic values decay that the antithesis between "egoistic" and "altruistic" presses more and more heavily on the human conscience. It is, to use my own language, the herd instinct that finds expression in this antithesis in many ways. And even then it takes a considerable time before this instinct becomes dominant enough for the valuation to be inextricably tied to this antithesis (as is the case in contemporary Europe). For today that prejudice prevails which, acting even now with all the intensity of an obsession and brain disease, holds that "moral," "altruistic" and "désintéressé" are concepts of equal value.

3. In the second place, the hypothesis about how the value "good" arose cannot be upheld historically, and apart from that it contains an inherent psychological contradiction. Altruistic conduct was presumably praised at first because it was useful, and this origin was then forgotten. But how could it possibly be forgotten! Did such conduct perhaps stop being useful at some point? The contrary is the case. Its utility was experienced every day, at all times, and so it received a new and regular emphasis with each fresh day. So it could not vanish from consciousness, let alone be forgotten; it must have impressed itself on consciousness more and more distinctly. The contrary theory is much more logical (though no truer for that). Herbert Spencer, for instance, holds it: he sets the concept "good" as essentially similar to "useful" and "purposive," so that in saying "good" and "bad" mankind is simply summarizing its unforgotten and unforgettable experiences of the "useful-purposive" and the "mischievous-non-purposive," and giving them a sanction. On this theory "good" is the attribute of whatever has shown itself useful in the past, and can therefore claim to be considered "valuable in the highest degree," "valuable in itself." This method of explanation is also, as I have said, wrong, but at any rate it is coherent and psychologically tenable.

4. What first put me on the right track was this question: what do the various words for the idea "good," coined in the various languages, really mean etymologically? I found that they all lead back to the same development of the same idea. Everywhere "aristocrat" and "noble" (in the social sense) are the root idea. From it "good" necessarily developed, in the sense of "with an aristocratic soul," "noble," in the sense of "with a soul of high caliber," "with a privileged soul." Alongside this runs, invariably, the other development in which "vulgar," "plebeian" and "low" finally turn into "bad." The most eloquent proof of this last claim is the German word "schlecht" itself. It is the same word as "schlicht" (compare "schlechtweg" and "schlechterdings"), which at first, and without any sinister innuendo, simply meant the plebeian man as opposed to the aristocratic man. The sense changed to the current one only in the fairly late period of the Thirty Years' War. For the Genealogy of Morals this discovery seems to me substantial. That it came so late is due to the retarding influence of democratic prejudice in the modern world on every question of origin. As will shortly be shown, this reaches even into natural science and physiology, which prima facie is the most objective field. Buckle is the notorious case showing how much mischief this prejudice does (once it is free of every trammel but its own malice), particularly to Ethics and History. In Buckle the plebeianism of the modern spirit, which is of English origin, once again erupted from its malignant soil like a slimy volcano, with that salted, rampant and vulgar eloquence in which all volcanoes until now have spoken.

5. Our problem can fairly be called an intimate one, and it chooses to address only a limited number of ears. It is of no small interest, then, to find that the words and roots meaning "good" give us glimpses of the arch-trait by which the aristocrats feel themselves to be beings of a higher order than their fellows. In perhaps the most frequent cases they simply name themselves after their superiority in power ("the powerful," "the lords," "the commanders") or after its most obvious sign, as in "the rich," "the possessors" (that is the meaning of arya, and the Iranian and Slav languages correspond). But they also name themselves after some characteristic peculiarity, and that is the case which concerns us now. They call themselves, for instance, "the truthful." The Greek nobility did this first, and their mouthpiece is the Megarian poet Theognis. The word ἐσθλος, coined for this purpose, means etymologically "one who is": one who has reality, who is real, who is true. Then, with a subjective twist, the "true" becomes the "truthful." At this stage of the idea's development it becomes the motto and party cry of the nobility, and the transition to the meaning "noble" is complete, shutting out the lying, vulgar man as Theognis conceives and portrays him. Finally, once the nobility has decayed, the word is left to describe psychological noblesse, and becomes, as it were, ripe and mellow. In the word κακός, as in δειλός (the plebeian as opposed to the ἀγαθός), cowardice is stressed. This perhaps hints at the lines along which the etymological origin of the very ambiguous ἀγαθός should be investigated. In the Latin malus (which I place beside μέλας) the vulgar man can be recognized as the dark-colored one, and above all the black-haired one ("hic niger est"): he is the pre-Aryan inhabitant of the Italian soil, whose complexion marked him off most clearly from the dominant blonds, the Aryan conquering race. At any rate, Gaelic has given me the exact analogue. There is Fin (for instance in the name Fin-Gal), the distinctive word of the nobility, which finally came to mean good, noble, clean, but originally meant the blond-haired man, as opposed to the dark, black-haired aboriginals. The Celts, if I may say so in parentheses, were throughout a blond race. Virchow, for one, still connects the traces of an essentially dark-haired population, visible on the more detailed ethnographical maps of Germany, with Celtic ancestry or an admixture of Celtic blood; this is wrong. In this context it is rather the pre-Aryan population of Germany that surfaces in those districts. (The same is true, substantially, of the whole of Europe. In fact, the subject race has finally gained the upper hand again, in complexion, in the shortness of the skull, and perhaps in intellectual and social qualities. Who can guarantee that modern democracy, still more modern anarchy, and indeed the tendency to the "Commune," the most primitive form of society, which all the Socialists in Europe now share, does not in its real essence signify a monstrous reversion — and that the conquering and master race, the Aryan race, is not also becoming inferior physiologically?) I believe I can explain the Latin bonus as "warrior." My hypothesis is that I am right to derive bonus from an older duonus (compare bellum = duellum = duen-lum, in which the word duonus appears to me to be contained). Bonus would then be the man of discord, of variance, "entzweiung" (duo), the warrior: one sees what "the good" meant for a man in ancient Rome. Must not our own German word gut mean "the godlike, the man of godlike race"? And be identical with the national name (originally the nobles' name) of the Goths?
The grounds for this supposition do not belong to this work.

6. Above all, this rule has no exception (though there are opportunities for exceptions): the idea of political superiority always resolves itself into the idea of psychological superiority, wherever the highest caste is also the priestly caste and, true to its general character, gives itself a title that specifically alludes to its priestly function. In these cases "clean" and "unclean" first confront each other as badges of class distinction, for instance, and here again a "good" and a "bad" develop in a sense that is no longer merely social. Moreover, one should take care not to take these ideas of "clean" and "unclean" too seriously, too broadly, or too symbolically. All the ideas of ancient man must rather be understood, in their early stages, as crude, coarse, physical and narrow to an almost inconceivable extent, and above all as essentially unsymbolical. The "clean man" is originally only a man who washes himself, who abstains from certain foods that lead to skin diseases, who does not sleep with the unclean women of the lower classes, who has a horror of blood — not more, not much more! On the other hand, the very nature of a priestly aristocracy shows why the opposed values should have been sharpened and intensified, so dangerously, at just such an early stage. It is through these opposed values that gulfs are cleft in the social plane which a veritable Achilles of free thought would shudder to cross. Such sacerdotal aristocracies carry a diseased taint from the outset, and so do the habits that prevail in such societies. Averse to action, these habits are a compound of introspection and explosive emotionalism, and out of them comes the introspective morbidity and neurasthenia that cling almost inevitably to all priests at all times. As for the remedy the priests themselves invented for this disease, the philosopher has no option but to say that its effects have proved a hundred times more dangerous than the disease it was supposed to cure. Humanity itself is still sick from the naïvetés of this priestly cure. Take, for instance, certain kinds of diet (abstention from flesh), fasts, sexual continence, flight into the wilderness (a kind of Weir-Mitchell isolation, though of course without that system of excessive feeding and fattening which is the most efficient antidote to all the hysteria of the ascetic ideal). Consider too the whole metaphysic of the priests, with its war on the senses, its enervation, its hair-splitting. Consider its self-hypnotism on the fakir and Brahman principles (it uses Brahman as a glass disc and obsession), and that climax, which we understand only too well, of an unusual satiety with its panacea of nothingness (or God: the demand for a unio mystica with God is the demand of the Buddhist for nothingness, Nirvana — and nothing else!). In sacerdotal societies everything is more dangerous: not merely cures and remedies, but also pride, revenge, cunning, exaltation, love, ambition, virtue, morbidity. Further, one can fairly say that man first becomes an interesting animal on the soil of this essentially dangerous form of human society, the sacerdotal form. In it the human soul has, in a higher sense, gained depth and become evil. And these are the two fundamental ways in which man has shown himself superior to every other animal until now.

7. The reader will already have guessed how easily the priestly mode of valuation can branch off from the knightly aristocratic mode and then grow into its very antithesis. The opposition gets a special impetus whenever the priestly and warrior castes confront each other in mutual jealousy and cannot agree over the prize. The knightly-aristocratic "values" rest on a careful cult of the physical, on a flowering, rich and even effervescing health that goes well beyond what is needed to maintain life, and on war, adventure, the chase, the dance, the tourney — on everything, in fact, that belongs to strong, free and joyous action. The priestly-aristocratic mode of valuation rests, as we have seen, on other hypotheses: war is bad enough for this class! Yet the priests are, as everyone knows, the worst enemies. Why? Because they are the weakest. Their weakness makes their hate swell into a monstrous and sinister shape, the most crafty and most poisonous shape. The really great haters in the history of the world have always been priests, who are also the cleverest haters; set beside the cleverness of priestly revenge, every other cleverness is practically negligible. Human history would be far too fatuous without the cleverness that the weak have brought into it. Take at once the most important instance. Everything the world has done against the "aristocrats," the "mighty," the "masters," the "holders of power," is negligible beside what the Jews have done against those classes. The Jews, that priestly nation, eventually saw that the one way to get satisfaction from its enemies and tyrants was a radical transvaluation of values, which was at the same time an act of the cleverest revenge. Only a nation of priests could use this method, a nation of the most jealously nursed priestly revengefulness. It was the Jews who dared, with terrifying logic, to set against the aristocratic equation (good = aristocratic = beautiful = happy = loved by the gods) the contrary equation, and to hold on to it with the teeth of the most profound hatred (the hatred of weakness): "the wretched alone are the good; the poor, the weak, the lowly alone are the good; the suffering, the needy, the sick, the loathsome are the only ones who are pious, the only ones who are blessed, for them alone is salvation. But you, on the other hand, you aristocrats, you men of power, you are to all eternity the evil, the horrible, the covetous, the insatiate, the godless; eternally also shall you be the unblessed, the cursed, the damned!" We know who inherited the fruits of this Jewish transvaluation. Faced with the monstrous and inordinately fateful initiative the Jews took in this most fundamental of all declarations of war, I remember the passage I once wrote (Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 195): that the revolt of the slaves in morals begins, in fact, with the Jews; that this revolt has behind it a history of two millennia, and has now only moved out of our sight because it has achieved victory.

8. But you do not understand this? You have no eyes for a force that took two thousand years to win its victory? There is nothing wonderful in that: all lengthy processes are hard to see and to realize. But here is what happened. Out of the trunk of that tree of revenge and hate, Jewish hate, that most profound and sublime hate which creates ideals and turns old values into new creations, the like of which has never been on earth, there grew something equally incomparable: a new love, the most profound and sublime of all kinds of love. And from what other trunk could it have grown? Yet beware of thinking that this love rose up as a real negation of that thirst for revenge, as the antithesis of the Jewish hate! No, the contrary is the truth! This love grew out of that hate, as its crown, its triumphant crown, spreading wider and wider in the clear fullness of the sun. In the very realm of light and height it pursued the same goals as the hate: its victory, its spoil, its strategy. It pursued them with the same intensity with which the roots of that tree of hate sank, ever more firmly and ever more greedily, into everything deep and evil. This Jesus of Nazareth, the gospel of love made flesh, this "Redeemer" who brought salvation and victory to the poor, the sick, the sinful — was he not really temptation in its most sinister and irresistible form, the temptation to take the tortuous path to those very Jewish values and those very Jewish ideals? Has Israel not really reached the final goal of its sublime revenge by the tortuous paths of this "Redeemer," although he might pose as Israel's adversary and destroyer? Is it not the black magic of a really great policy of revenge, a far-seeing, burrowing revenge, acting and calculating slowly, that makes Israel himself repudiate before all the world the very instrument of his revenge, and nail it to the cross, so that all the world — that is, all the enemies of Israel — might nibble without suspicion at this very bait? Moreover, could any human mind, with all its elaborate ingenuity, invent a bait more truly dangerous? Is there anything that even equals, in seductive, intoxicating, defiling and corrupting power, that symbol of the holy cross, that awful paradox of a "god on the cross," that mystery of the unthinkable, supreme and utter horror of a god's self-crucifixion for the salvation of man? This much is certain: sub hoc signo Israel, with its revenge and transvaluation of all values, has until now always triumphed again over all other ideals, over all more aristocratic ideals.

9. "But why do you talk of nobler ideals? Let us submit to the facts: the people have won — or the slaves, or the populace, or the herd, or whatever name you like. If the Jews are the ones through whom this happened, so be it! Then no nation ever had a greater mission in the world's history. The 'masters' have been done away with; the morality of the vulgar man has triumphed. You may call this triumph a blood-poisoning too (it has mixed the races together) — I do not dispute it; but there is no doubt that the intoxication has worked. The 'redemption' of the human race (that is, from the masters) is going along swimmingly. Everything is obviously becoming Judaized, or Christianized, or vulgarized (what is there in the words?). The poisoning of the whole body politic of mankind seems impossible to stop — but from now on its tempo and pace can be slower, more delicate, quieter, more discreet; there is time enough. Given this, has the Church nowadays any necessary purpose? Has it, in fact, a right to live? Or could man do without it? Quæritur. It seems to fetter and retard this tendency rather than speed it up. Well, even that might be its utility. The Church certainly is a crude and boorish institution, repugnant to any intelligence with a pretence at delicacy, to a really modern taste. Should it not at least learn to be somewhat more subtle? Nowadays it alienates more than it allures. Which of us would really be a freethinker if there were no Church? It is the Church that repels us, not its poison; apart from the Church we like the poison." That is the epilogue to my discourse from a freethinker, an honorable animal (as he has abundantly proved), and a democrat to boot. Up to then he had listened to me, and he could not bear my silence; but for me, indeed, there is much on this topic about which to be silent.

10. The revolt of the slaves in morals begins when resentment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values. This is a resentment felt by creatures who, denied the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge. While every aristocratic morality springs from a triumphant affirmation of its own demands, the slave morality says "no" from the very outset to what is "outside itself," "different from itself," and "not itself": and this "no" is its creative deed. This reversal of the valuing standpoint — this inevitable turn toward the objective instead of back toward the subjective — is typical of "resentment." The slave-morality needs an external and objective world as the condition of its existence; to use physiological terms, it needs objective stimuli in order to be capable of action at all. Its action is fundamentally a reaction. The contrary is the case with the aristocrat's system of values: it acts and grows spontaneously, and seeks its antithesis only in order to say a more grateful and exultant "yes" to itself. Its negative conception, "low," "vulgar," "bad," is merely a pale, late-born foil beside its positive and fundamental conception (saturated as it is with life and passion): "we aristocrats, we good ones, we beautiful ones, we happy ones."

When the aristocratic morality goes astray and commits sacrilege against reality, it does so only in the one sphere it does not know well enough — a sphere, in fact, whose real knowledge it disdainfully keeps away from. In some cases it misjudges the sphere it despises, that of the common, vulgar man and the low people. But we should also weigh this: the mood of contempt, of disdain, of superciliousness, even if it falsely portrays the object of its contempt, will always be far from the degree of falsity that marks the attacks — in effigy, of course — which the vindictive hatred and revengefulness of the weak launch against their enemies. In fact, contempt contains too strong a mixture of nonchalance, of casualness, of boredom, of impatience, even of personal exultation, to be able to distort its victim into a real caricature or a real monstrosity. Notice again the almost benevolent shades of meaning which, for instance, the Greek nobility puts into all the words by which it distinguishes the common people from itself. See how a kind of pity, care, and consideration keeps lending them a honeyed flavor, until at last almost all the words applied to the vulgar man survive as expressions for "unhappy," "worthy of pity" (compare δειλο, δείλαιος, πονηρός, μοχθηρός]; the last two really name the vulgar man as labor-slave and beast of burden) — and see how, conversely, "bad," "low," "unhappy" have never stopped ringing in the Greek ear with a tone in which "unhappy" is the dominant note. This is a heritage of the old noble aristocratic morality, which stays true to itself even in contempt (let philologists remember the sense in which ὀιζυρός, ἄνολβος, τλήμων, δυστυχεῑν, ξυμφορά used to be employed). The "well-born" simply felt themselves to be the "happy"; they did not have to manufacture their happiness artificially by looking at their enemies, or, when need arose, talk and lie themselves into happiness (as all resentful men are accustomed to do). And being complete men, exuberant with strength and therefore necessarily energetic, they were too wise to separate happiness from action: for them activity necessarily counts as happiness (that is the etymology of εὖ πρἆττειν). All this stands in sharp contrast to the "happiness" of the weak and the oppressed, with their festering venom and malignity, among whom happiness appears essentially as a narcotic, a deadening, a quietude, a peace, a "Sabbath," a slackening of the mind and a relaxation of the limbs — in short, as a purely passive phenomenon. The aristocratic man lived in confidence and openness with himself (gennaios, "noble-born," stresses the shade of meaning "sincere," and perhaps also "naïf"). The resentful man, on the other hand, is neither sincere nor naïf, nor honest and candid with himself. His soul squints; his mind loves hidden crannies, tortuous paths and back-doors; everything secret appeals to him as his world, his safety, his balm. He is a past master in silence, in not forgetting, in waiting, in provisional self-depreciation and self-abasement. A race of such resentful men will necessarily end up more prudent than any aristocratic race. It will honor prudence on quite a different scale, as a paramount condition of existence. Among aristocratic men, by contrast, prudence tends to carry a delicate flavor of luxury and refinement; so it plays nothing like so essential a part among them as the complete certainty with which the governing unconscious instincts function, or even a certain lack of prudence, such as a vehement and valiant charge against danger or the enemy, or those ecstatic bursts of rage, love, reverence, and gratitude by which noble souls have at all times recognized each other. When the resentment of the aristocratic man shows itself, it fulfills and exhausts itself in an immediate reaction, and so it instills no venom. On the other hand, in countless cases it never shows itself at all, where in the feeble and weak it would be inevitable. An inability to take their enemies, their disasters, their misdeeds seriously for any length of time — that is the sign of the full, strong natures who possess a superfluity of molding, plastic force that heals completely and produces forgetfulness. A good example of this in the modern world is Mirabeau, who had no memory for the insults and meannesses practiced on him, and who could not forgive only because he forgot. Such a man shakes off with a shrug many a worm which would have buried itself in another; only in characters like these do we see the possibility (supposing, of course, that there is such a possibility in the world) of the real "love of one's enemies." How much respect for his enemies, forsooth, is found in an aristocratic man — and such reverence is already a bridge to love! He insists on having his enemy to himself as his distinction. He tolerates no enemy except one in whose character there is nothing to despise and much to honor! Now imagine, on the other hand, the "enemy" as the resentful man conceives him — and it is exactly here that we see his work, his creativeness. He has conceived "the evil enemy," the "evil one," and that is the root idea from which he then derives, as a contrasting and corresponding figure, a "good one": himself — his very self!

11. This man's method is the exact opposite of the aristocrat's. The aristocrat forms the root idea "good" spontaneously, straight out of himself, and only then, from that material, creates for himself a concept of "bad"! This aristocratic "bad" and that "evil" from the cauldron of unsatisfied hatred are two very different things. The first is an imitation, an "extra," an additional nuance; the second is the original, the beginning, the essential act in the making of a slave-morality. Both "bad" and "evil" have the same opposite, "good," yet how great a difference they mark! For the idea "good" is not the same in each. Ask rather: "Who is really evil, according to the morality of resentment?" The answer, in all sternness, is this: just the good man of the other morality, just the aristocrat, the powerful one, the ruler, but seen through the venomous eye of resentfulness and so given a new color, a new meaning, a new look. We would be the last to deny this. A man who got to know those "good" ones only as enemies learned at the same time not to know them only as "evil enemies." Yet these same men are bound so rigorously inter pares by convention, respect, custom, and gratitude, and still more by mutual vigilance and jealousy inter pares. Among themselves they find so many new ways of showing consideration, self-control, delicacy, loyalty, pride, and friendship. But toward whatever lies outside their circle (where the foreign element, a foreign country, begins) they are not much better than beasts of prey let loose. There they are free of all social control. In the wilderness they can vent, with impunity, the tension built up by being fenced in and shut up within the peace of society. They revert to the innocence of the beast-of-prey conscience, like jubilant monsters who may be coming from a ghastly bout of murder, arson, rape, and torture, with bravado and moral equanimity, as if it were merely some wild student's prank, fully convinced that the poets now have plenty to sing and celebrate. At the core of all these aristocratic races we cannot fail to recognize the beast of prey, the magnificent blond brute, greedily prowling for spoil and victory. This hidden core needed an outlet from time to time; the beast had to get loose again and return to the wilderness. The Roman, Arabic, German, and Japanese nobility, the Homeric heroes, the Scandinavian Vikings, all share this need. The aristocratic races left the idea "Barbarian" behind on every path they marched. Nay, a consciousness of this very barbarianism, and even a pride in it, shows itself in their highest civilization (for example, when Pericles tells his Athenians in the celebrated funeral oration, "Our audacity has forced a way over every land and sea, rearing everywhere imperishable memorials of itself for good and for evil"). The audacity of aristocratic races may be mad, absurd, and spasmodic in its expression; their enterprises may be incalculable and fantastic — Pericles sets in special relief and glory the ᾽ραθυμία of the Athenians, their nonchalance and contempt for safety, body, life, and comfort, their awful joy and intense delight in all destruction, in all the ecstasies of victory and cruelty — all these features crystallized, for those who suffered from them, into the picture of the "barbarian," of the "evil enemy," perhaps of the "Goth" and the "Vandal." Even now, the German meets a profound, icy mistrust as soon as he comes to power. That mistrust is still an aftermath of the inextinguishable horror with which Europe, for whole centuries, regarded the wrath of the blond Teuton beast (although there is scarcely a psychological, let alone a physical, relationship between the old Germans and ourselves). I once pointed out Hesiod's embarrassment when he conceived the series of social ages and tried to express them in gold, silver, and bronze. The Homeric world confronted him with a contradiction: an age magnificent indeed, but at the same time so awful and so violent. He could resolve it only by making two ages out of one and setting them one behind the other. First came the age of the heroes and demigods, as that world lived on in the memories of the aristocratic families, who found their own ancestors in it. Then came the bronze age, as that same age looked to the descendants of the oppressed, spoiled, ill-treated, exiled, and enslaved: an age of bronze, as I have said, hard, cold, terrible, without feelings and without conscience, crushing everything and spattering everything with blood. Suppose the now-accepted theory is true, that the whole essence of civilization is to train the beast of prey out of man and make of him a tame and civilized animal, a domesticated animal. Then we must undoubtedly regard as the real tools of civilization all those instincts of reaction and resentment, with whose help the aristocratic races, together with their ideals, were finally degraded and overpowered. That is not yet to say that the bearers of those tools also represented civilization. The opposite is not merely probable — nay, it is palpable today. These bearers of vindictive instincts that have to be bottled up, these descendants of all European and non-European slavery, especially of the pre-Aryan population — these people, I say, represent the decline of humanity! These "tools of civilization" are a disgrace to humanity, and in reality they count more as an argument against civilization, more as a reason to be suspicious of it. One may be quite justified in always fearing the blond beast at the core of every aristocratic race, and in staying on one's guard. But who would not a hundred times rather fear, while admiring, than be free of fear and be forever obsessed with the loathsome sight of the distorted, the dwarfed, the stunted, the envenomed? And is that not our fate? What makes us feel repulsion toward "man" today? — for we suffer from "man," there is no doubt about it. It is not fear. It is rather that we have nothing left to fear from men; that the worm "man" is in the foreground and swarms; that the "tame man," the wretched, mediocre, unedifying creature, has learned to consider himself a goal and a pinnacle, an inner meaning, a historic principle, a "higher man." Yes, and he has a certain right to do so, in so far as he feels that, set against that excess of deformity, disease, exhaustion, and effeteness whose odor is beginning to pollute present-day Europe, he at any rate has achieved a relative success; he at any rate still says "yes" to life.

12. At this point I cannot refrain from a sigh and one last hope. What exactly do I find intolerable? What can I alone not get rid of, what makes me choke and faint? Bad air! Bad air! That something misbegotten comes near me; that I have to breathe the odor of the entrails of a misbegotten soul! — Apart from that, what can one not endure, in need, privation, bad weather, sickness, toil, solitude? In fact, one gets over everything, born as one is to a burrowing and battling existence. One returns again and again to the light; again and again one lives one's golden hour of victory — and then one stands as one was born, unbreakable, tense, ready for something harder and more distant, like a bow drawn tauter by every strain. But from time to time — if "beyond good and evil" there are goddesses who can grant such things — grant me one glimpse, grant me but one glimpse only, of something perfect, fully realized, happy, mighty, triumphant, something that still gives cause for fear! A glimpse of a man who justifies the existence of man, a glimpse of an incarnate human happiness that realizes and redeems, for whose sake one may hold fast to the belief in man! For this is how things stand: our greatest peril lurks in the dwarfing and leveling of the European man, because this very outlook is what fatigues. Today we see nothing that wishes to be greater. We suspect that the process is still going backwards, still backwards, toward something thinner, more inoffensive, more cunning, more comfortable, more mediocre, more indifferent, more Chinese, more Christian — man, there is no doubt about it, grows always "better" — and the destiny of Europe lies in just this: in losing the fear of man we have also lost the hope in man, yea, the will to be man. The sight of man now fatigues. — What is present-day Nihilism, if not that? — We are tired of man.

13. But let us return to the point; the problem of another origin of the good, the good as the resentful man has thought it out, demands a solution. That the lambs bear a grudge against the great birds of prey is not surprising, but it gives no ground for blaming the great birds of prey for carrying off little lambs. And suppose the lambs say among themselves, "These birds of prey are evil; and whoever is as far as possible from being a bird of prey, whoever is rather its opposite, a lamb — is he not good?" There is nothing to cavil at in setting up this ideal, though the birds of prey may look on it a little sneeringly, and perhaps say to themselves, "We bear no grudge against them, these good lambs; we even like them: nothing is tastier than a tender lamb." To demand that strength should not express itself as strength, that it should not be a wish to overpower, a wish to overthrow, a wish to become master, a thirst for enemies and antagonisms and triumphs, is as absurd as to demand that weakness should express itself as strength. A quantum of force is a quantum of movement, will, action — rather, it is nothing but those very phenomena of moving, willing, acting. It can seem otherwise only through the misleading errors of language (and the fundamental fallacies of reason petrified within it), which understands, and understands wrongly, all working as conditioned by a worker, by a "subject." The people separate the lightning from its flash and take the flash for a thing done, the working of a subject called lightning. In the same way, the popular morality separates strength from the expression of strength, as though behind the strong man stood some indifferent, neutral substratum, free to choose whether or not to express strength. But there is no such substratum; there is no "being" behind doing, working, becoming; "the doer" is a mere appendage to the action. The action is everything. In fact, the people double the doing when they make the lightning lighten; that is a "doing-doing": the same phenomenon is made first a cause and then, secondly, the effect of that cause. The scientists do no better when they say, "Force moves, force causes," and so on. For all its coldness and freedom from passion, our whole science is still a dupe of the tricks of language, and has never managed to get rid of that superstitious changeling "the subject" (the atom, to take another instance, is such a changeling, as is the Kantian "Thing-in-itself"). What wonder, then, that the suppressed and stealthily simmering passions of revenge and hatred turn this belief to their own advantage, and indeed hold no belief with a more steadfast enthusiasm than this: "that the strong has the option of being weak, and the bird of prey of being a lamb." Thereby they win the right to make the birds of prey answerable for being birds of prey. The oppressed, down-trodden, and overpowered say to themselves, with the vindictive guile of weakness, "Let us be different from the evil, namely, good! And good is everyone who does not oppress, who hurts no one, who does not attack, who does not pay back, who hands revenge over to God, who keeps himself, as we do, in hiding; who goes out of the way of evil, and demands, in short, little from life; like ourselves the patient, the meek, the just." Yet read coldly and without prejudice, all this means nothing more than "once for all, the weak are weak; it is good to do nothing for which we are not strong enough." But this dismal state of affairs, this prudence of the lowest order, which even insects have (in great danger they are inclined to sham death, so as not to do "too much"), has been dressed up, through the counterfeiting and self-deception of weakness, in the pomp of an ascetic, mute, and expectant virtue. It poses as if the very weakness of the weak — that is, forsooth, its being, its working, its whole unique, inevitable, inseparable reality — were a voluntary result, something wished, chosen, a deed, an act of merit. This kind of man needs the belief in a neutral, free-choosing "subject" out of an instinct of self-preservation, of self-assertion, in which every lie is inclined to sanctify itself. The subject (or, in popular language, the soul) has perhaps been the best dogma in the world simply because it allowed the horde of mortal, weak, and oppressed individuals of every kind to practice that most sublime specimen of self-deception: the interpretation of weakness as freedom, of being this or that as merit.
14. Will anyone look a little into — right into — the mystery of how ideals are manufactured in this world? Who has the courage to do it? Come!

Here we have a vista opened into these grimy workshops. Wait just a moment, dear Mr. Inquisitive and Foolhardy; your eye must first grow accustomed to this false, changing light — Yes! Enough! Now speak! What is happening down there below? Speak out what you see, man of the most dangerous curiosity — for now I am the listener.

"I see nothing, but I hear all the more. It is a cautious, spiteful, gentle whispering and muttering together in all the corners and crannies. It seems to me that they are lying; a sugary softness clings to every sound. Weakness is turned to merit, there is no doubt about it — it is just as you say."
Further!

"And the impotence which does not requite is turned to 'goodness,' craven baseness to meekness, submission to those whom one hates to obedience (namely, obedience to one of whom they say that he ordered this submission — they call him God). The inoffensive character of the weak man, the very cowardice in which he is rich, his standing at the door, his forced necessity of waiting, gain fine names here, such as 'patience,' which is also called 'virtue.' Not being able to avenge oneself is called not wishing to avenge oneself, perhaps even forgiveness (for they know not what they do — we alone know what they do). They also talk of the 'love of their enemies' and sweat as they do so."
Further!

"They are miserable, there is no doubt about it, all these whisperers and counterfeiters in the corners, although they try to get warm by crouching close to each other. But they tell me that their misery is a favor and distinction given to them by God, just as one beats the dogs one likes best; that perhaps this misery is also a preparation, a probation, a training; that perhaps it is still more something which will one day be compensated and paid back with tremendous interest in gold, nay in happiness. This they call 'Blessedness.'"
Further!

"They are now giving me to understand that they are not only better men than the mighty, the lords of the earth, whose spittle they have to lick (not out of fear, not at all out of fear! But because God ordains that one should honor all authority) — not only are they better men, but they also have a 'better time,' or at any rate will one day have a 'better time.' But enough! Enough! I can endure it no longer. Bad air! Bad air! These workshops where ideals are manufactured — verily, they reek with the crassest lies."

Nay. Just one minute! You are saying nothing about the masterpieces of these virtuosos of black magic, who can produce whiteness, milk, and innocence out of any black you like. Have you not noticed what a pitch of refinement is reached by their chef d'œuvre, their most audacious, subtle, ingenious, and lying artist-trick? Take care! These cellar-beasts, full of revenge and hate — what do they make, forsooth, out of their revenge and hate? Do you hear these words? If you trusted only their words, would you suspect that you are among men of resentment and nothing else?

"I understand, I prick up my ears again (ah! ah! ah! and I hold my nose). Now I hear for the first time what they have said so often: 'We good, we are the righteous.' What they demand they call not revenge but 'the triumph of righteousness'; what they hate is not their enemy, no, they hate 'unrighteousness,' 'godlessness'; what they believe in and hope for is not the hope of revenge, the intoxication of sweet revenge (— "sweeter than honey," did Homer call it?), but the victory of God, of the righteous God, over the 'godless'; what is left for them to love in this world is not their brothers in hate, but their 'brothers in love,' as they say, all the good and righteous on the earth."
And what name do they give to that which serves them as a solace against all the troubles of life — their phantasmagoria of their anticipated future blessedness?
"What? Do I hear right? They call it 'the last judgment,' the advent of their kingdom, 'the kingdom of God' — but in the meanwhile they live 'in faith,' 'in love,' 'in hope.'"
Enough! Enough!

15. In the faith in what? In the love for what? In the hope of what? These weaklings! — they also, forsooth, wish to be the strong some time; there is no doubt about it, some time their kingdom also must come — "the kingdom of God" is their name for it, as has been mentioned: they are so meek in everything! Yet to experience that kingdom one has to live long, to live beyond death — yes, eternal life is necessary, so that one can make up forever for that earthly life "in faith," "in love," "in hope." Make up for what? Make up by what? Dante, it seems to me, made a crass mistake when, with awe-inspiring ingenuity, he placed the inscription "Me too made eternal love" over the gate of his hell. At any rate, the inscription "Me too made eternal hate" would have a much better right to stand over the gate of the Christian Paradise and its "eternal blessedness" — granted, of course, that a truth may rightly stand over the gate to a lie! For what is the blessedness of that Paradise? Possibly we could quickly guess it; but it is better to have it explicitly attested by an authority not to be disparaged in such matters, Thomas of Aquinas, the great teacher and saint. "Beati in regno celesti" he says, as gently as a lamb, "videbunt pœnas damnatorum, ut beatitudo illis magis complaceat." Or if we wish to hear a stronger tone, here is a word from the mouth of a triumphant father of the Church, who warned his disciples against the cruel ecstasies of the public spectacles — But why? Faith offers us much more, he says, de Spectac., c. 29 ss., something much stronger. Thanks to the redemption, joys of quite another kind are at our disposal; instead of athletes we have our martyrs; if we wish for blood, well, we have the blood of Christ — but what then awaits us on the day of his return, of his triumph. And then he goes on, this enraptured visionary: "at enim supersunt alia spectacula, ille ultimas et perpetuus judicii dies, ille nationibus insperatus, ille derisus, cum tanta sæculi vetustas et tot ejus nativitates uno igne haurientur. Quæ tunc spectaculi latitudo! Quid admirer! quid rideam! Ubigaudeam! Ubi exultem, spectans tot et tantos reges, qui in cœlum recepti nuntiabantur, cum ipso Jove et ipsis suis testibus in imis tenebris congemescentes! Item præsides" (the provincial governors) "persecutores dominici nominis sævioribus quam ipsi flammis sævierunt insultantibus contra Christianos liquescentes! Quos præterea sapientes illos philosophos coram discipulis suis una conflagrantibus erubescentes, quibus nihil ad deum pertinere suadebant, quibus animas aut nullas aut non in pristina corpora redituras affirmabant! Etiam poetas non ad Rhadamanti nec ad Minois, sed ad inopinati Christi tribunal palpitantes! Tunc magis tragœdi audiendi, magis scilicet vocales" (with louder tones and more violent shrieks) "in sua propria calamitate; tunc histriones cognoscendi, solutiores multo per ignem; tunc spectandus auriga in flammea rota totus rubens, tunc xystici contemplandi non in gymnasiis, sed in igne jaculati, nisi quod ne tunc quidem illos velim vivos, ut qui malim ad eos potius conspectum insatiabilem conferre, qui in dominum scevierunt. Hic est ille, dicam fabri aut quæstuariæ filius" (as the whole of the following shows, and in particular this well-known description of the mother of Jesus from the Talmud, Tertullian is from here on referring to the Jews), "sabbati destructor, Samarites et dæmonium habens. Hic est quem a Juda redemistis, hic est ille arundine et colaphis diverberatus, sputamentis de decoratus, felle et acete potatus. Hic est, quem clam discentes subripuerunt, ut resurrexisse dicatur vel hortulanus detraxit, ne lactucæ suæ frequentia commeantium laderentur. Ut talia species, ut talibus exultes, quis tibi prætor aut consul aut sacerdos de sua liberalitate prastabit? Et tamen hæc jam habemus quodammodo per fidem spiritu imaginante repræsentata. Ceterum qualia illa sunt, quæ nec oculus vidit nec auris audivit nec in cor hominis ascenderunt?" (I Cor. ii. 9.) "Credo circo et utraque cavea" (the first and fourth row, or, according to others, the comic and the tragic stage) "et omni studio gratiora." Per fidem: so it stands written.

16. Let us come to a conclusion. The two opposing values, "good and bad" and "good and evil," have fought a dreadful fight in the world for a thousand years. The second value has undoubtedly had the upper hand for a long time, yet there are still places where the outcome of the fight is undecided. One can almost say that the fight has meanwhile risen to a higher and higher level, becoming more and more intense and always more psychological. So today there is perhaps no more decisive mark of the higher, more psychological nature than to be self-contradictory in that sense: to be still, in fact, a battleground for those two opposites. The symbol of this fight, written in a script that has stayed worth reading throughout history up to now, is "Rome against Judæa, Judæa against Rome." Until now there has been no greater event than that fight, that question, that deadly antagonism. Rome saw in the Jew the incarnation of the unnatural, as if he were its own diametrically opposed monstrosity; and in Rome the Jew was held guilty of hatred of the whole human race. Rightly so, in so far as it is right to tie the well-being and future of the human race to the unconditional mastery of the aristocratic values, the Roman values. What, conversely, did the Jews feel toward Rome? We can guess it from a thousand symptoms, but it is enough to recall the Johannine Apocalypse, the most obscene of all written outbursts, which has revenge on its conscience. (One should also appreciate at its full value the profound logic of the Christian instinct, which wrote the name of the Disciple of Love over this very book of hate — that same disciple to whom it ascribed that impassioned and ecstatic Gospel. A portion of truth lurks in this, however much literary forgery may have been needed for it.) The Romans were the strong and aristocratic; no stronger or more aristocratic nation has ever existed in the world, or has even been dreamed of. Every relic of them, every inscription, enraptures, provided one can divine what it is that writes the inscription. The Jews, on the other hand, were that priestly nation of resentment par excellence, with a unique genius for popular morals. Just compare the nations with analogous gifts, such as the Chinese or the Germans, with the Jews, and you will afterwards realize what is first rate and what is fifth rate.

Which of them has been victorious for the time being, Rome or Judæa? There is not a shadow of doubt. Just consider whom you bow down to even in Rome itself today, as though to the quintessence of all the highest values — and not only in Rome, but over almost half the world, wherever man has been tamed or is about to be tamed. You bow to three Jews, as we know, and one Jewess (Jesus of Nazareth, Peter the fisher, Paul the tent-maker, and the mother of the aforesaid Jesus, named Mary). This is very remarkable: Rome is undoubtedly defeated. At any rate, in the Renaissance there was a brilliantly sinister revival of the classical ideal, of the aristocratic valuation of all things. Rome herself, like a man waking from a trance, stirred under the weight of the new Judaized Rome built over her, which looked like an œcumenical synagogue and was called the "Church." But Judæa immediately triumphed again, thanks to that fundamentally popular (German and English) movement of revenge called the Reformation, and thanks also to its inevitable corollary, the restoration of the Church — which also restored the ancient graveyard peace of classical Rome. In the French Revolution Judæa again proved victorious over the classical ideal, in a sense even more crucial and more profound. The last political aristocracy in Europe, that of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century France, broke into pieces under the instincts of a resentful populace. The world had never heard a greater jubilation, a more uproarious enthusiasm. Yet in the midst of it the most monstrous and unexpected thing happened: the ancient ideal itself rose before the eyes and conscience of humanity with all its life and with unheard-of splendor. Against resentment's lying war-cry of the prerogative of the most, against the will to lowliness, abasement, and equalization, the will to a retrogression and twilight of humanity, there rang out once more, stronger, simpler, and more penetrating than ever, the terrible and enchanting counter-warcry of the prerogative of the few! Then, like a final signpost to other ways, Napoleon appeared, the most unique and violent anachronism that ever existed, and in him the incarnate problem of the aristocratic ideal in itself. Consider well what a problem it is: Napoleon, that synthesis of Monster and Superman.

17. Was that the end of it? Was that greatest of all antitheses of ideals thereby put ad acta for all time? Or only postponed, postponed for a long time? May there not come a day when the old conflagration flares up again, far more awful and far more carefully prepared? Further! Should one not wish for that outcome with all one's strength? — will it oneself? demand it oneself? Whoever begins at this point, like my readers, to reflect and think further will find it hard to reach a quick conclusion. That is reason enough for me to conclude myself, taking it for granted that by now it has been sufficiently clear what I mean, exactly what I mean by that dangerous motto inscribed on the body of my last book: Beyond Good and Evil — which at any rate is not the same as "Beyond Good and Bad."

Note. — This treatise gives me the opportunity to express, openly and formally, a wish I have so far voiced only in occasional conversations with scholars. I wish that some Faculty of philosophy would earn the glory of promoting further study of the history of morals through a series of prize essays; perhaps this book may give a forceful impetus in that direction. For such a possibility, the following question deserves consideration. It deserves the attention of philologists and historians quite as much as that of actual professional philosophers.
"What indication of the history of the evolution of the moral ideas is afforded by philology, and especially by etymological investigation?"

On the other hand, it is of course equally necessary to interest physiologists and doctors in these problems (the value of the valuations that have prevailed until now). Here the professional philosophers may be trusted to act as spokesmen and intermediaries, once they have fully managed to turn the relationship between philosophy and physiology and medicine, originally one of coldness and suspicion, into the friendliest and most fruitful reciprocity. In fact, every table of values, every "thou shalt" known to history and ethnology, first needs a physiological elucidation and interpretation, at any rate in preference to a psychological one; all of them equally call for a critique from medical science. The question "What is the value of this or that table of 'values' and morality?" will be asked from the most varied standpoints. The question "valuable for what?", for instance, can never be analyzed with enough nicety. Something that would obviously be valuable for giving a race the greatest possible powers of endurance (or for increasing its adaptability to a specific climate, or for preserving the greatest number) would be nowhere near as valuable if the aim were to develop a stronger species. In gauging values, the good of the majority and the good of the minority are opposed standpoints. We leave it to the naïveté of English biologists to regard the first as intrinsically superior. All the sciences must now pave the way for the future task of the philosopher, understood as this: he must solve the problem of value, he has to fix the hierarchy of values.

chapters.title: Second Essay — “Guilt,” “Bad Conscience,” and the Like
paragraphs: 1. Breeding an animal that can make promises — is this not the very paradox of a task that nature has set itself with regard to man? Is it not the real problem of man? Anyone who can fully appreciate the force of forgetfulness, which works against it, will find it all the more remarkable that the problem has been largely solved. Forgetfulness is not simply a vis inertiæ, as the superficial believe. It is rather an active power of obstruction, positive in the strictest sense of the word. It is the reason why nothing we live through, experience or take into ourselves enters consciousness while we digest it (we might call this psychic absorption), any more than the whole manifold process of our physical nutrition, the so-called "incorporation," does. The doors and windows of consciousness are shut for a time. We are relieved of the clamor of alarms and skirmishes with which our subconscious world of servant organs works in mutual co-operation and antagonism. There is a little quiet, a little tabula rasa of consciousness, to make room again for the new, and above all for the nobler functions and functionaries: room for government, foresight, predetermination (for our organism is built on an oligarchic model). This, as I have said, is the use of active forgetfulness. It is a very sentinel and nurse of psychic order, repose and etiquette; and it shows at once why there can be no happiness, no gladness, no hope, no pride, no real present, without forgetfulness. If this preventive apparatus is damaged and broken in a man, he is like a dyspeptic, and more than like one — he can "get rid of" nothing. But this very animal, who must be forgetful, and in whom forgetfulness is a force and a form of robust health, has bred for himself an opposing power, a memory, with whose help forgetfulness is in certain cases held in check — namely in the cases where promises have to be made. So this memory is by no means a merely passive inability to get rid of an impression once made, nor merely the indigestion caused by a pledged word that one cannot dispose of. It is an active refusal to get rid of it, a continuing and a wish to continue what was once willed: an actual memory of the will. Between the original "I will," "I shall do," and the actual discharge of the will, its act, we can therefore easily interpose a world of new and strange circumstances, events and even acts of will, without snapping this long chain of the will. But what does all this presuppose? In order to regulate the future in this way, man must first have learnt, and learnt thoroughly, to distinguish necessitated from accidental events, to think causally, to see the distant as present and anticipate it, to fix with certainty what is the end and what the means to that end, and above all to reckon, to be able to calculate. Man must first have become thoroughly calculable, disciplined, necessitated, even in his own eyes and his own conception of himself, so that, like a man making a promise, he could guarantee himself as a future.

2. All this is simply the long history of the origin of responsibility. The task of breeding an animal that can make promises includes, as we have already seen, a more immediate task as its condition and preliminary: first to make man to a certain extent necessitated, uniform, like among his like, regular and therefore calculable. What I have called the "morality of custom" (cp. Dawn of Day, Aphs. 9, 14, and 16) was an immense work: man's actual work on himself during the longest period of the human race, his whole prehistoric work.
