This work finds its meaning and its great justification (in spite of all its innate hardness, despotism, stupidity and idiocy) in this: with the help of the morality of customs and of social strait-waistcoats, man was made genuinely calculable. But suppose we stand at the end of this colossal process, at the point where the tree finally ripens its fruit and society and its morality of custom at last bring to light what they were only the means to. There we find, as the ripest fruit on its tree, the sovereign individual, who resembles only himself, who has got loose from the morality of custom: the autonomous "super-moral" individual (for "autonomous" and "moral" exclude each other) — in short, the man of the personal, long and independent will, who is able to promise. In him we find a proud consciousness, vibrating in every fibre, of what has at last been achieved and has come alive in him, a genuine consciousness of power and freedom, a feeling of human perfection in general. And this man who has grown to freedom, who is really able to promise, this lord of the free will, this sovereign — how can he fail to know how great his superiority is over everything that cannot bind itself by promises or be its own security, how great a trust, awe and reverence he awakens (he "deserves" all three), and that with this mastery over himself he is necessarily also given mastery over circumstances, over nature, over all creatures with shorter wills and less reliable characters? The "free" man, the owner of a long, unbreakable will, finds in this possession his standard of value. Looking out from himself upon others, he honors or he despises. Just as necessarily as he honors his peers, the strong and the reliable (those who can bind themselves by promises) — that is, everyone who promises like a sovereign, with difficulty, rarely and slowly, who is sparing with his trust but confers honor by the very act of trusting, who gives his word as something that can be relied on because he knows himself strong enough to keep it even in the teeth of disasters, even in the "teeth of fate" — so with equal necessity will he have the heel of his foot ready for the lean and empty jackasses who promise when they have no business to, and his rod of chastisement ready for the liar who already breaks his word at the very moment it is on his lips. The proud knowledge of the extraordinary privilege of responsibility, the consciousness of this rare freedom, of this power over himself and over fate, has sunk right down to his innermost depths and has become an instinct, a dominating instinct. What name will he give to it, to this dominating instinct, if he needs a word for it? There is no doubt about it: the sovereign man calls it his conscience.

3. His conscience? — One sees at once that the idea "conscience," which appears here in its supreme form, supreme almost to the point of strangeness, must already have a long history and evolution behind it. To be able to guarantee oneself with all due pride, and at the same time to say yes to oneself — that is, as has been said, a ripe fruit, but also a late fruit. How long this fruit had to hang sour and bitter on the tree! And for a still longer period there was not a glimpse of such a fruit to be had. No one had taken it on himself to promise it, although everything on the tree was quite ready for it and everything was maturing toward that very consummation. "How is a memory to be made for the man-animal? How is an impression to be fixed so deeply upon this ephemeral understanding, half dense and half silly, upon this incarnate forgetfulness, that it will stay permanently present?" One may imagine that this primeval problem was not solved with exactly gentle answers and gentle means. Perhaps there is nothing more awful and more sinister in the early history of man than his system of mnemonics. "Something is burnt in so that it stays in his memory: only what never stops hurting stays in his memory." This is an axiom of the oldest (unfortunately also the longest) psychology in the world. It might even be said that wherever solemnity, seriousness, mystery and gloomy colors are now found in the life of men and nations, there is some survival of that horror which was once the universal companion of all promises, pledges and obligations. The past, the past with all its length, depth and hardness, breathes on us and wells up in us again when we become "serious." Whenever man has thought it necessary to make a memory for himself, it has never happened without blood, tortures and sacrifice. The most dreadful sacrifices and forfeitures belong here (among them the sacrifice of the first-born), the most loathsome mutilations (for instance, castration), the most cruel rituals of all the religious cults (for all religions are really at bottom systems of cruelty) — all these things originate in that instinct which found in pain its most potent mnemonic. In a certain sense the whole of asceticism is to be ascribed to this. Certain ideas have to be made inextinguishable, omnipresent, "fixed," with the aim of hypnotizing the whole nervous and intellectual system through these "fixed ideas" — and the ascetic methods and modes of life are the means of freeing those ideas from competition with all other ideas, so as to make them "unforgettable." The worse man's memory was, the ghastlier the signs presented by his customs. The severity of the penal laws in particular gives a gauge of how hard man found it to conquer forgetfulness, and to keep a few primal postulates of social life present in the minds of those who were slaves of every momentary emotion and every momentary desire. We Germans certainly do not regard ourselves as an especially cruel and hard-hearted nation, still less as an especially casual and happy-go-lucky one. But one has only to look at our old penal ordinances to realize how much trouble it takes in the world to develop a "nation of thinkers" (I mean: the European nation that today shows the maximum of reliability, seriousness, bad taste and positiveness, and that on the strength of these qualities has a right to train every kind of European mandarin). These Germans used terrible means to make a memory for themselves, to master their rooted plebeian instincts and the brutal crudity of those instincts. Think of the old German punishments: stoning (as far back as the legend, the millstone falls on the head of the guilty man); breaking on the wheel (the most original invention and speciality of the German genius in the sphere of punishment); dart-throwing; tearing or trampling by horses ("quartering"); boiling the criminal in oil or wine (still practiced in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries); the highly popular flaying ("slicing into strips"); cutting the flesh out of the breast. Think also of the evil-doer smeared with honey and then exposed to the flies in a blazing sun. With the help of such images and precedents man finally kept in his memory five or six "I will nots," about which he had already given his promise so as to enjoy the advantages of society — and truly, with the help of this kind of memory man finally arrived at "reason"! Alas! Reason, seriousness, mastery over the emotions, all these gloomy, dismal things called reflection, all these privileges and pageantries of humanity: how dear is the price they have exacted! How much blood and cruelty lies at the foundation of all "good things"!

4. But how did that other melancholy thing come into the world, the consciousness of sin, the whole "bad conscience"? Here we turn back to our genealogists of morals. For the second time I say — or have I not said it yet? — that they are worth nothing. They have only their own five-spans-long, limited, modern experience; no knowledge of the past and no wish for it; still less a historic instinct, a power of "second sight" (which is just what is required here) — and despite this they go in for the history of morals. Naturally, such work must yield results that stand at more than a respectful distance from the truth.

Have these current genealogists of morals ever allowed themselves even the vaguest notion, for instance, that the cardinal moral idea of "ought" originates in the very material idea of "owe"? Or that punishment developed as a retaliation absolutely independently of any prior assumption about the freedom or determination of the will? — And this to such an extent that a high degree of civilization was always necessary first, before the animal man could begin to make those much more primitive distinctions of "intentional," "negligent," "accidental," "responsible," and their contraries, and apply them in assessing punishment. That idea — "the wrong-doer deserves punishment because he might have acted otherwise" — is nowadays so cheap, obvious, natural and inevitable, and has had to serve as an illustration of how the sentiment of justice appeared on earth; yet in fact it is an exceedingly late, even refined, form of human judgment and inference, and to project it back to the beginning of the world is simply a clumsy violation of the principles of primitive psychology. Throughout the longest period of human history punishment was never based on the evil-doer's responsibility for his action, and was therefore not based on the assumption that only the guilty should be punished. On the contrary, punishment was inflicted for the same reason that parents punish their children even nowadays: out of anger at an injury suffered, an anger that vents itself mechanically on the author of the injury. But this anger is kept in bounds and modified by the idea that every injury has somewhere its equivalent price and can really be paid off, even if by means of pain to the author. Where has this ancient, deep-rooted and now perhaps ineradicable idea, the idea of an equivalence between injury and pain, drawn its strength? I have already revealed its origin: it lies in the contractual relationship between creditor and debtor, which is as old as the existence of legal rights at all, and which in its turn points back to the primary forms of purchase, sale, barter and trade.

5. The realization of these contractual relations naturally arouses (as our previous remarks would lead us to expect) a great deal of suspicion and opposition toward the primitive society that made or sanctioned them. In this society promises will be made; in this society the aim is to give the promiser a memory; in this society, as we may suspect, there will be full scope for hardness, cruelty and pain. The "debtor," in order to inspire credit in his promise of repayment, in order to guarantee the earnestness and sanctity of his promise, in order to drill into his own conscience the duty, the solemn duty, of repayment, will pledge something he still possesses, something still in his power, under a contract with his creditor to cover the case of his not paying. He may pledge his life or his wife, or his freedom or his body (or, under certain religious conditions, even his salvation, his soul's welfare, even his peace in the grave; so in Egypt, where the corpse of the debtor found no rest from the creditor even in the grave — and from the Egyptian standpoint this peace was of particular importance). But above all the creditor has the power to inflict on the body of the debtor all kinds of pain and torture, for instance to cut off as much as seemed proportionate to the size of the debt. From this point of view precise schemes of valuation arose early and everywhere, often horrible in the minuteness and meticulousness with which they were applied: legally sanctioned valuations for individual limbs and parts of the body. I consider it already a progress, a proof of a freer, less petty and more Roman conception of law, when the Roman Code of the Twelve Tables decreed that it did not matter how much or how little the creditors cut off in such a case: "si plus minusve secuerunt, ne fraude esto." Let us make the logic of this whole process of equalization clear; it is strange enough. The equivalence is this: instead of an advantage that directly compensates for his injury (that is, instead of an equalization in money, lands or some kind of chattel), the creditor is granted, by way of repayment and compensation, a certain sensation of satisfaction. It is the satisfaction of being able to vent his power without any trouble on one who is powerless, the delight "de faire le mal pour le plaisir de le faire," the joy in sheer violence. This joy will be relished in proportion to the lowness and humbleness of the creditor's place in society, and it is quite apt to have the effect of the most delicious dainty, and even to seem a foretaste of a higher social position. Thanks to the punishment of the "debtor," the creditor shares in the rights of the masters. At last he too, for once, attains the edifying consciousness of being able to despise and ill-treat a creature as an "inferior" — or at any rate of seeing him despised and ill-treated, in case the actual power of punishing, the administration of punishment, has already been transferred to the "authorities." So the compensation consists in a claim on cruelty and a right to draw on it.

6. It is, then, in this sphere of the law of contract that we find the cradle of the whole moral world of the ideas "guilt," "conscience," "duty," the "sacredness of duty." Like the beginning of all great things on earth, their beginning was soaked through and through with blood. And should we not add that this world has never entirely lost a certain savor of blood and torture (not even in old Kant; the categorical imperative reeks of cruelty)? It was likewise in this sphere that there first formed that sinister and perhaps now indissoluble association of the ideas "guilt" and "suffering." To put the question once more: why can suffering be a compensation for "owing"? — Because inflicting suffering produces the highest degree of happiness; because the injured party gets in exchange for his loss (including his vexation at his loss) an extraordinary counter-pleasure: the infliction of suffering — a real feast, something that, as I have said, was prized all the more the greater the paradox presented by the creditor's rank and social status. These observations are purely conjectural, for the task is painful, and it is hard to plumb such depths. The clumsy introduction of the idea of "revenge" as a connecting link simply hides and obscures the view instead of making it clearer (revenge itself leads back to the identical problem: "How can the infliction of suffering be a satisfaction?"). In my opinion it offends the delicacy, and still more the hypocrisy, of tame domestic animals (that is, modern men; that is, ourselves) to realize with full energy the extent to which cruelty was the great joy and delight of ancient man, an ingredient that seasoned nearly all his pleasures. It offends them equally to realize how naively and innocently he showed his need for cruelty, when he made "disinterested malice" (or, to use Spinoza's expression, the sympathia malevolens) a matter of principle and a normal characteristic of man — and therefore something to which the conscience says a hearty yes. The more profound observer has perhaps already had enough occasion to notice this most ancient and radical joy and delight of mankind. In Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 188 (and even earlier, in The Dawn of Day, Aphs. 18, 77, 113), I have cautiously pointed to the ever-growing spiritualization and "deification" of cruelty, which runs through the whole history of higher civilization (and in the larger sense even constitutes it). At any rate the time is not long past when it was impossible to conceive of royal weddings and national festivals on a grand scale without executions, tortures or perhaps an auto-da-fé, or to conceive of an aristocratic household without a creature to serve as a butt for the cruel and malicious baiting of the inmates. (The reader will perhaps remember Don Quixote at the court of the Duchess: today we read the whole of Don Quixote with a bitter taste in the mouth, almost with a sensation of torture, which would seem very strange and incomprehensible to its author and his contemporaries — they read it with the best conscience in the world as the gayest of books; they almost died laughing at it.) The sight of suffering does one good, the infliction of suffering does one more good — this is a hard maxim, but a fundamental maxim none the less, old, powerful and "human, all-too-human"; one, moreover, to which perhaps even the apes would subscribe, for it is said that in inventing bizarre cruelties they give abundant proof of their future humanity, to which they are, as it were, playing the prelude. Without cruelty, no feast: so teaches the oldest and longest history of man — and in punishment too there is so much that is festive.

7. Since I hold these thoughts, I am, let me say in parenthesis, fundamentally opposed to supplying our pessimists with fresh water for the discordant, groaning mills of their disgust with life. On the contrary, it should be shown specifically that at the time when mankind was not yet ashamed of its cruelty, life on earth was brighter than it is nowadays, when there are pessimists. The darkening of the heavens over man has always grown in proportion to the growth of man's shame before man. The tired pessimistic outlook, the mistrust of the riddle of life, the icy negation of disgusted ennui — none of these is a sign of the most evil age of the human race. Much rather do they first come to light, as the swamp-flowers they are, when the swamp they belong to comes into existence. I mean the diseased refinement and moralization thanks to which the "animal man" has at last learnt to be ashamed of all his instincts. On the road to angelhood (not to use a harder word in this context) man has developed that dyspeptic stomach and coated tongue which have made not only the joy and innocence of the animal repulsive to him, but life itself — so that sometimes he stands before his own self with stopped nostrils and, like Pope Innocent the Third, draws up a black list of his own horrors ("unclean generation, loathsome nutrition when in the maternal body, badness of the matter out of which man develops, awful stench, secretion of saliva, urine, and excrement"). Nowadays suffering is always trotted out as the first argument against existence, as its most sinister question. It is well, then, to remember the times when men judged on the opposite principle because they could not do without inflicting suffering, and saw in it a magic of the first order, a veritable bait of seduction to life.

Perhaps in those days (this is to comfort the weaklings) pain did not hurt as much as it does nowadays. A physician who has treated negroes (granting that these are taken as representative of prehistoric man) for severe internal inflammations, which would bring a European, even one with the soundest constitution, almost to despair, could draw this conclusion. Pain does not have the same effect on negroes. (The curve of human sensitivity to pain seems indeed to sink in an extraordinary and almost sudden fashion once one has passed the upper ten thousand or ten million of over-civilized humanity. I personally have no doubt that, compared with one painful night endured by a single hysterical chit of a cultured woman, the suffering of all the animals taken together who have been put to the question of the knife to get scientific answers is simply negligible.) We may perhaps be allowed to admit that the craving for cruelty need not really have died out. Since pain hurts more nowadays, it only requires a certain sublimation and subtilization. It must above all be translated to the imaginative and psychic plane and adorned with such smug euphemisms that even the most fastidious and hypocritical conscience could never grow suspicious of their real nature ("Tragic pity" is one of these euphemisms; another is "les nostalgies de la croix"). What really raises one's indignation against suffering is not suffering in itself but the senselessness of suffering. Such senselessness existed neither in Christianity, which interpreted suffering into a whole mysterious apparatus of salvation, nor in the beliefs of naive ancient man, who knew how to find a meaning in suffering only from the standpoint of the spectator or the inflictor of suffering. To get the secret, undiscovered, unwitnessed suffering out of the world it was almost compulsory to invent gods and a hierarchy of intermediate beings: in short, something that roams even in secret places, sees even in the dark, and makes a point of never missing an interesting and painful spectacle. With the help of such inventions life learnt the tour de force, which has become part of its stock-in-trade, the tour de force of self-justification, of the justification of evil. Nowadays this would perhaps require other auxiliary devices (for instance, life as a riddle, life as a problem of knowledge). "Every evil is justified in the sight of which a god finds edification" — so ran the logic of primitive sentiment. And indeed, was it only of primitive sentiment? The gods conceived as friends of spectacles of cruelty — oh, how far this primeval conception extends even nowadays into our European civilization! One would perhaps like to consult Luther and Calvin here. At any rate it is certain that even the Greeks knew no more piquant seasoning for the happiness of their gods than the joys of cruelty. What, do you think, was the mood in which Homer's gods looked down on the fates of men? What final meaning do the Trojan War and similar tragic horrors really have? There can be no doubt about it: they were meant as festival games for the gods, and, insofar as the poet is of a more godlike breed than other men, as festival games for the poets as well. In just this spirit and no other, the moral philosophers of Greece at a later date conceived the eyes of God as still looking down on the moral struggle, the heroism and the self-torture of the virtuous. The Heracles of duty was on a stage and knew it; virtue without witnesses was something quite unthinkable for this nation of actors. Must not that philosophic invention, so audacious and so fatal, which was then absolutely new to Europe, the invention of "free will," of man's absolute spontaneity in good and evil, simply have been made for the specific purpose of justifying the idea that the gods' interest in humanity and human virtue was inexhaustible?

On the stage of this free-will world there would never be a shortage of really new, really novel and exciting situations, plots and catastrophes. A world thought out on completely deterministic lines would be easily guessed by the gods and would therefore soon bore them. That is sufficient reason for these friends of the gods, the philosophers, not to ascribe such a deterministic world to their gods. The whole of ancient humanity is full of delicate consideration for the spectator, being a world of thorough publicity and theatricality, which could not conceive of happiness without spectacles and festivals. — And, as has already been said, even in great punishment there is so much that is festive.

8. The feeling of "ought" and of personal obligation (to pick up the thread of our inquiry again) began, as we saw, in the oldest and most original personal relationship there is: the relationship between buyer and seller, creditor and debtor. Here for the first time one individual confronted another and measured himself against him. No level of civilization has been found so low that it shows no trace of this relationship. Setting prices, assessing values, working out equivalents, exchanging: all this so filled the earliest thinking of man that in a certain sense it was thinking itself. Here the oldest form of shrewdness was trained, and here, perhaps, we can trace the first beginning of man's pride, of his feeling of superiority over other animals. Perhaps our word "Mensch" (manas) still expresses something of this self-pride: man named himself the being who measures values, who values and measures, the "assessing" animal par excellence. Buying and selling, with their psychological accompaniments, are older than any form of social organization or union. The budding consciousness of exchange, commerce, debt, right, obligation and compensation grew out of the most rudimentary form of individual right. From there it was first carried over to the rudest and most elementary of the social complexes (in their dealings with similar complexes), together with the habit of comparing force with force, and of measuring and calculating. His eye was now trained on this perspective. With the ponderous consistency of ancient thought, which is hard to set in motion but then follows inflexibly the line it has started on, man soon reached the great generalization, "everything has its price, all can be paid for." This is the oldest and most naive moral canon of justice, and the beginning of all "kindness," all "equity," all "goodwill," all "objectivity" in the world. In this first phase, justice is the goodwill among people of roughly equal power to come to terms with each other, to reach an understanding again by means of a settlement; and, toward those of less power, it is the goodwill that compels them to agree among themselves to a settlement.

9. Measured always by the standard of antiquity (and this antiquity is present, or possible again, in every period), the community stands toward its members in that important and radical relationship of creditor to his "debtors." Man lives in a community and enjoys its advantages (and what advantages! we sometimes underestimate them nowadays). He lives protected and spared, in peace and trust, safe from certain injuries and enmities to which the man outside the community, the "peaceless" man, is exposed (a German understands the original meaning of "Elend" (êlend)). He is safe because he has bound himself by pledges and obligations to the community with regard to those very injuries and enmities. What happens when this is not the case? The community, the defrauded creditor, will get itself paid as well as it can; one can count on that. In this case the direct damage done by the offender is quite secondary. Quite apart from it, the criminal is above all a breaker, a breaker of his word and covenant to the whole, with regard to all the advantages and amenities of communal life in which up to then he had shared. The criminal is a "debtor" who not only fails to repay the advances and advantages given to him, but even sets out to attack his creditor. So in the future he is not only deprived, as is fair, of all these advantages and amenities; he is also reminded how important those advantages were. The wrath of the injured creditor, the community, throws him back into the wild and outlawed state from which he was protected until then. The community repudiates him, and now every kind of enmity can vent itself on him. At this stage of civilization, punishment is simply the copy, the mimicry, of the normal treatment of the hated, despised and conquered enemy, who is deprived not only of every right and protection but of every mercy. So we have the martial law and the triumphant festival of the væ victis! in all its mercilessness and cruelty. This shows why war itself (counting the sacrificial cult of war) has produced all the forms in which punishment has appeared in history.

10. As the community grows more powerful, it tends to take the offences of the individual less seriously, because they now seem much less revolutionary and less dangerous to the existence of the whole. The evil-doer is no longer outlawed and put outside the pale, and the common wrath can no longer vent itself on him with its old license. On the contrary, from this time on the community carefully shields and protects the evil-doer against this wrath, and particularly against the wrath of those directly injured. As penal law develops, the following characteristics become more and more marked: a compromise with the wrath of those directly affected by the misdeed; a consequent effort to confine the matter locally and to prevent any further, let alone general, spread of the disturbance; attempts to find equivalents and to settle the whole affair (compositio); and above all the will, showing itself with increasing definiteness, to treat every offence as to some degree capable of being paid off, and so, at least up to a point, to separate the offender from his act. As a community's power and self-confidence increase, its penal law becomes milder in proportion; and conversely, every weakening or endangering of the community revives the harshest forms of that law. The creditor has always grown more humane as he has grown richer; in the end, the amount of injury he can bear without really suffering becomes the measure of his wealth. One can imagine a society so conscious of its own power that it could indulge in the most aristocratic luxury it has: letting its wrong-doers go scot-free. "What do my parasites matter to me?" such a society might say. "Let them live and flourish! I am strong enough for it." The justice that began with the maxim, "Everything can be paid off, everything must be paid off," ends by winking at those who cannot pay and letting them escape. It ends, like every good thing on earth, by destroying itself. The self-destruction of Justice! We know the pretty name it gives itself: Grace! And, as is obvious, Grace remains the privilege of the strongest, or better still, their super-law.

11. I must say a discouraging word here about the recent attempts to base the origin of justice on something quite different, namely resentment. Let me whisper in the psychologists' ear, if they want to study revenge itself up close: this plant flourishes loveliest today among Anarchists and anti-Semites. It is a hidden flower, as it has always been, like the violet, though, to be sure, with another perfume. Like must come from like, so we should not be surprised to find in just such circles the birth of efforts (it is their old birthplace; compare above, First Essay, paragraph 14) to sanctify revenge under the name of justice, as though Justice were at bottom only a development of the consciousness of injury. By rehabilitating revenge in this way, they hope to reinstate all the reactive emotions generally and collectively. That last point is the one I object to least. Seen from the standpoint of the whole problem of biology (from which the value of these emotions has until now been underestimated), it even seems meritorious. What I alone want to point out is that this new nuance of scientific equity (which works for the benefit of hate, envy, mistrust, jealousy, suspicion, rancor, revenge) grows out of the spirit of revenge itself. This scientific "equity" breaks off at once, and makes way for the accents of deadly enmity and prejudice, whenever another group of emotions appears. In my opinion these emotions have a much higher biological value than the reactions, and so have a paramount claim to the valuation and appreciation of science: I mean the really active emotions, such as personal and material ambition, and so forth. (E. Dühring, Value of Life; Course of Philosophy, and passim.) That is enough against this tendency in general. As for Dühring's particular maxim, that the home of Justice lies in the sphere of the reactive feelings, our love of truth forces us to turn his own proposition sharply around and set against it this other: the last sphere conquered by the spirit of justice is the sphere of the feeling of reaction! Suppose the just man really stays just even toward the person who injures him (and is not merely cold, moderate, reserved, indifferent: being just is always a positive state). Suppose that, despite the strong provocation of personal insult, contempt and calumny, the lofty, clear objectivity of the just and judging eye (whose glance is as profound as it is gentle) remains untroubled. Why, then we have a piece of perfection, a past master of the world; but it would not be wise to expect such a thing, and at any rate it should not be too easily believed. Speaking generally, there is no doubt that even the justest individual needs only a small dose of hostility, malice or innuendo to send the blood to his head and drive the fairness out. The active, attacking, aggressive man is always a hundred degrees nearer to justice than the man who merely reacts. He certainly has no need to use the tactics the reacting man must use, of falsifying and biasing his valuation of his object. For this very reason the aggressive man has at all times had the stronger, bolder, more aristocratic and also freer outlook, and the better conscience. On the other hand, we already suspect who has the invention of the "bad conscience" on his own conscience: the resentful man! Finally, let man look at himself in history. Where has the whole administration of law, the real need of law, had its earthly home until now? Perhaps with the reacting man? Not for a minute. Rather with the active, strong, spontaneous, aggressive man? I deliberately defy the agitator I mentioned (who himself makes this self-confession, "the creed of revenge has run through all my works and endeavors like the red thread of Justice"), and I say that, judged historically, law on earth is the very war against the reactive feelings. It is a war waged on them by the powers of activity and aggression, which spend part of their strength on damming and holding within bounds this effervescence of hysterical reactivity, and on forcing it into some compromise. Wherever justice is practiced and maintained, we can see the stronger power looking for weapons to end the senseless fury of resentment among the weaker powers beneath it (whether groups or individuals). It does this partly by pulling the victim of resentment out of the clutches of revenge, partly by putting a campaign of its own against the enemies of peace and order in the place of revenge, partly by finding, suggesting and sometimes enforcing settlements, and partly by fixing standard equivalents for injuries, to which resentment is from then on finally referred. The most drastic step the supreme power takes against the preponderance of spite and vindictiveness, and it takes it as soon as it is strong enough, is to found law: it declares imperatively what in its eyes counts as just and lawful and what as unjust and unlawful. Once law is founded, the supreme power treats the aggressive and arbitrary acts of individuals, or of whole groups, as violations of law and as revolt against itself. That draws its subjects' feelings away from the immediate injury such a violation causes, and so in the end it achieves the very opposite of what revenge always wants, since revenge sees and recognizes only the standpoint of the injured party. From then on the eye is trained toward an ever more impersonal valuation of the deed, even the eye of the injured party himself (though that comes last of all, as I remarked before). On this principle "right" and "wrong" first arise after the foundation of law (and not, as Dühring maintains, only after the act of violation). To speak of intrinsic right and intrinsic wrong is absolute nonsense. An injury, an oppression, an exploitation, an annihilation cannot be intrinsically wrong, because life is essentially (that is, in its cardinal functions) something that works by injuring, oppressing, exploiting and annihilating, and cannot be conceived at all without this character. I must make a still more serious confession. From the most advanced biological standpoint, conditions of legality can only be exceptional conditions. They are partial restrictions of the real life-will, which aims at power, and they are subordinate to that life-will's general end as particular means, that is, as means of creating larger units of strength. Imagine a legal organization conceived as sovereign and universal, not as a weapon in the fight between complexes of power but as a weapon against fighting, something in the style of Dühring's communistic model in which every will is treated as equal to every other will. It would be a principle hostile to life, a destroyer and dissolver of man, an outrage on the future of man, a symptom of fatigue, a secret path to Nothingness. —

12. Let me say a little more on the origin and the end of punishment. These are two problems that are, or ought to be, kept separate, but unfortunately they are usually thrown together. And how have our moral genealogists gone about it until now? With their inveterate naïveté. They discover some "end" in punishment, such as revenge or deterrence, and then in all their innocence place this end at the beginning, as the causa fiendi of the punishment, and they have done the trick. But the last use that the "End in Law" should be put to is patching together a history of the origin of law. For any kind of history, perhaps no principle is more pregnant than this one. It is hard to master, yet it should be mastered down to the last detail: the origin of a thing's existence and its final utility, its practical application and its place in a system of ends, are toto cœlo opposed to each other. Whatever exists and prevails anywhere will always be given new purposes by a force superior to it, will be taken over afresh, and will be turned and transformed to new uses. All "happening" in the organic world consists of overpowering and dominating, and all overpowering and domination is a new interpretation and adjustment, which must obscure, or even wholly extinguish, the "meaning" and "end" that existed before. You may understand perfectly the utility of some physiological organ (or of a legal institution, a social custom, a political habit, a form in art or religious worship), and that does not in the least mean you understand its origin. Older men may find this uncomfortable and unpalatable, for people have always believed that to understand the final cause or the utility of a thing, a form, an institution, was to understand why it came into being. By this logic the eye was made to see and the hand was made to grasp, and so punishment too was supposed to have been invented in order to punish. But all ends and all utilities are only signs that a Will to Power has mastered some less powerful force and has stamped on it, out of its own self, the meaning of a function. By the same principle, the whole history of a "Thing," an organ, a custom, can be seen as a continuous "sign-chain" of ever new interpretations and adjustments. Their causes need not be connected with one another at all; sometimes they simply follow and alternate by chance. In the same way, the evolution of a "thing," of a custom, is anything but a progressus toward an end, and even less a logical, direct progressus achieved with the least expense of energy and cost. It is rather a succession of processes of subjugation, more or less profound, more or less independent of one another, that act on the thing. It also includes the resistance offered against each subjugation, the Protean wriggles of defense and reaction, and the results of successful counter-efforts. The form is fluid, but the meaning is more fluid still. Even inside every individual organism it is the same: whenever the whole genuinely grows, the "function" of the single organs shifts. In certain cases the partial perishing of these organs, a reduction in their number (for instance, by the annihilation of the connecting members), can be a symptom of growing strength and perfection. What I mean is this: even partial loss of utility, decay and degeneration, loss of function and purpose, in a word death, belong among the conditions of genuine progressus. Genuine progressus always takes the shape of a will and way to greater power, and is always won at the expense of innumerable smaller powers. A "progress" is measured by the greatness of the sacrifice it demands: humanity as a mass sacrificed to the prosperity of the one stronger species of Man, that would be a progress. I stress this cardinal feature of the historical method all the more because in its essence it runs against the predominant instincts and the prevailing taste. They would much rather put up with absolute casualness, even with the mechanical senselessness of all phenomena, than with the theory of a power-will playing through all phenomena without exception. The democratic idiosyncrasy against everything that rules and wishes to rule, the modern misarchism (to coin a bad word for a bad thing), has gradually dressed itself so thoroughly in the guise of intellectualism, the most abstract intellectualism, that today it penetrates step by step, and has the right to penetrate, even the most exact and apparently most objective sciences. In my view it has already come to dominate the whole of physiology and biology, to their detriment, as is obvious, because it has spirited away a radical idea, the idea of true activity. Under the tyranny of this idiosyncrasy the theory of "adaptation" is pushed to the front of the argument and exploited. Adaptation means a second-class activity, a mere capacity for "reacting"; in fact, life itself has been defined (by Herbert Spencer) as an ever more effective internal adaptation to external circumstances. This definition, however, fails to grasp the real essence of life, its will to power. It fails to see the paramount superiority of those plastic forces of spontaneity, aggression and encroachment, with their new interpretations and tendencies, for which adaptation is only a natural corollary. As a result, the sovereign office of the highest functionaries in the organism itself (among which the life-will appears as an active and formative principle) is repudiated. One remembers Huxley's reproach to Spencer of his "administrative Nihilism": but it is a case of something much more than "administration."

13. Back to our subject, punishment. We must draw a double distinction. On one side is the relatively permanent element: the custom, the act, the "drama," a certain rigid sequence of procedures. On the other is the fluid element: the meaning, the end, the expectation that goes with carrying out such procedures. Here we at once assume, per analogiam (following the theory of the historical method developed above), that the procedure itself is older and earlier than its use for punishment. That use was introduced and read into the procedure (which had existed for a long time but was employed with another meaning). In short, the case is different from what our naïf genealogists of morals and of law have supposed until now. They thought the procedure was invented for the purpose of punishment, just as they had earlier thought the hand was invented for the purpose of grasping. Now the other element in punishment, the fluid one, its meaning. At a very late stage of civilization (for instance in contemporary Europe), the idea of punishment no longer shows just one meaning but a whole synthesis "of meanings." The past history of punishment in general, the history of its use for the most diverse ends, finally crystallizes into a kind of unity that is hard to break down into its parts, and that, it must be stressed, absolutely defies definition. (Today it is impossible to say definitely why people punish at all. Every idea in which a whole process is promiscuously summed up eludes definition; only what has no history can be defined.) At an earlier stage, on the contrary, that synthesis of meanings looks much less rigid and much more elastic. We can see how, in each individual case, the elements of the synthesis change their value and their position, so that now one element stands out and dominates the rest, now another; nay, in certain cases one element (perhaps the end of deterrence) seems to wipe out all the others. At any rate, to give some idea of how uncertain, supplementary and accidental the meaning of punishment is, and of how one identical procedure can be used and adapted for the most diametrically opposed objects, I will set down here a scheme that has suggested itself to me, itself based on comparatively small and accidental material. — Punishment as making the criminal harmless and unable to do further injury. — Punishment as compensation to the injured party for the injury sustained, in any form whatsoever (including the form of sentimental compensation). — Punishment as the isolation of whatever disturbs the equilibrium, in order to stop the disturbance from spreading further. — Punishment as a means of inspiring fear of those who determine and carry out the punishment. — Punishment as a kind of compensation for advantages the wrong-doer has enjoyed until then (for example, when he is put to work as a slave in the mines). — Punishment as the elimination of an element of decay (sometimes of a whole branch, as under the Chinese laws, and so as a means of purifying the race or preserving a social type). — Punishment as a festival, as the violent oppression and humiliation of an enemy who has at last been subdued. — Punishment as a mnemonic, whether for the man who suffers it (the so-called "correction") or for those who witness it being carried out. Punishment as the payment of a fee stipulated by the power that protects the evil-doer from the excesses of revenge. — Punishment as a compromise with the natural phenomenon of revenge, in so far as the stronger races still maintain revenge and claim it as a privilege. — Punishment as a declaration and measure of war against an enemy of peace, of law, of order, of authority. Society fights him with the weapons war provides, as a spirit dangerous to the community, as a breaker of the contract on which the community is based, as a rebel, a traitor and a breaker of the peace.

14. This list is certainly not complete; punishment, obviously, is overloaded with utilities of every kind. That makes it all the more permissible to remove one supposed utility, which passes, at any rate in the popular mind, for the most essential of all. It is just this utility that still gives the strongest support to the faith in punishment, a faith that is tottering today for many reasons. Punishment is supposed to be valuable because it awakens in the guilty the consciousness of guilt. In punishment people look for the proper instrumentum of that psychic reaction known as the "bad conscience," "remorse." But this theory violates reality and psychology even as applied to the present; how much worse when it is applied to the longest period of man's history, his primitive history! Genuine remorse is certainly extremely rare among wrong-doers and the victims of punishment. Prisons and houses of correction are not the soil in which this worm of remorse likes best to breed. All conscientious observers agree on this, and in many cases they reach such a judgment only reluctantly and against their own wishes. Generally speaking, punishment hardens and numbs, it concentrates, it sharpens the consciousness of alienation, it strengthens the power of resistance. Sometimes it breaks a man's energy and brings about a piteous prostration and abjectness. That result is certainly even less salutary than the average effect of punishment, which is a harsh and sinister doggedness. Thinking of those prehistoric millennia, we must conclude without hesitation that punishment, more than anything, held back the development of the consciousness of guilt, at any rate in the victims of the punishing power. In particular, let us not underestimate how far the sight of the judicial and executive procedure itself keeps the wrong-doer from feeling that his deed, the character of his act, is intrinsically reprehensible. He sees the same kind of acts clearly practiced in the service of justice, then called good, and practiced with a good conscience: espionage, trickery, bribery, trapping, the whole intriguing and insidious art of the policeman and the informer. He sees the whole system, in fact, that appears in the various kinds of punishment (a system excused not by passion but based on principle), of robbing, oppressing, insulting, imprisoning, racking, murdering. And he sees his judges treat all this not as acts deserving censure and condemnation in themselves, but only in a particular context and application. The "bad conscience," that most sinister and interesting plant of our earthly vegetation, did not grow in this soil. In fact, for a very long period, the man who judged and punished had no idea at all that he was dealing with a "guilty man." He was dealing merely with the author of an injury, an irresponsible piece of fate. And the man on whom the punishment then fell like a piece of fate felt no more "inner pain" than he would feel at the sudden approach of some unforeseen event, some terrible natural catastrophe, a rushing, crushing avalanche against which there is no resistance.

15. This truth dawned insidiously on Spinoza (to the disgust of his commentators, who, like Kuno Fischer, for instance, go to endless trouble to misunderstand him on this point). One afternoon, as he sat raking up who knows what memory, he asked himself what was really left for him personally of the celebrated morsus conscientiæ. Here was a man who had relegated "good and evil" to the sphere of human imagination, and who indignantly defended the honor of his "free" God against the blasphemers who claimed that God did everything sub ratione boni ("but this was tantamount to subordinating God to fate, and would really be the greatest of all absurdities"). For Spinoza the world had gone back to that innocence in which it lay before the bad conscience was discovered. So what had become of the morsus conscientiæ? "The antithesis of gaudium," he said at last to himself: "A sadness accompanied by the recollection of a past event which has turned out contrary to all expectation" (Eth. III., Propos. XVIII. Schol. i. ii.). For thousands of years, evil-doers overtaken by punishment have felt about their "offence" exactly as Spinoza did: "here is something which went wrong contrary to my anticipation," not "I ought not to have done this." They submitted to punishment as one submits to a disease, a misfortune or death, with that stubborn, resigned fatalism that even now gives the Russians, for instance, an advantage over us Westerners in managing life. If actions were criticized at that period, the criterion was prudence. What punishment unquestionably achieves is chiefly a sharper sense of prudence, a longer memory, a will to be more cautious, suspicious and secretive from now on, a recognition that many things are unquestionably beyond one's capacity, and a kind of improvement in self-criticism. In man and beast alike, the broad results that punishment can obtain are increased fear, a sharper sense of cunning, and mastery of the desires. So punishment tames man, but does not make him "better"; it would be more correct even to go so far as to assert the contrary ("Injury makes a man cunning," says a popular proverb: so far as it makes him cunning, it makes him also bad. Fortunately, it often enough makes him stupid).

16. At this point I cannot avoid giving a tentative, provisional statement of my own hypothesis about the origin of the bad conscience. It is hard to make it fully understood, and it takes continuous meditation, attention and digestion. I regard the bad conscience as the serious illness that man was bound to catch under the pressure of the most radical change he has ever gone through — the change that came when he found himself locked at last within the walls of society and of peace.

The plight of these half-animals, perfectly adapted as they were to the savage life of war, prowling and adventure, was like that of the water-animals when they were forced either to become land-animals or to perish. Suddenly all their instincts were rendered worthless and "switched off." From now on they had to walk on their own feet and "carry themselves," where until then the water had carried them: a terrible heaviness weighed on them. They found themselves clumsy at the simplest tasks. In this new and unknown world they no longer had their old guides, the regulative instincts that had led them unconsciously to safety. These unhappy creatures were reduced to thinking, inferring, calculating, putting causes and results together; they were reduced to their poorest and most error-prone organ, their "consciousness." I do not believe there was ever such a feeling of misery on earth, such a leaden discomfort. And what is more, the old instincts had not suddenly stopped making their demands! It was only that gratifying them was difficult and rarely possible; speaking broadly, they had to satisfy themselves by new and, as it were, hole-and-corner methods. All instincts that find no outlet outwards turn inwards. This is what I mean by the growing "internalization" of man, and with it we get the first growth in man of what was later called his soul. The whole inner world, originally as thin as if it were stretched between two layers of skin, burst apart and expanded, and gained depth, breadth and height, in proportion as man's outward discharge was obstructed. The social organization protected itself against the old instincts of freedom with terrible bulwarks (punishments belong pre-eminently among these bulwarks), and the result was that all the instincts of wild, free, prowling man were turned backwards against man himself. Enmity, cruelty, delight in persecution, in surprise attacks, in change, in destruction: all these instincts turned against their own possessors. This is the origin of the "bad conscience." It was man who, lacking external enemies and obstacles and imprisoned in the oppressive narrowness and monotony of custom, lost patience and lacerated, persecuted, gnawed, frightened and ill-treated himself. It was this animal in the hands of the tamer, beating itself against the bars of its cage. It was this creature, pining and yearning for the desert home it had been deprived of, who was forced to create out of its own self an adventure, a torture-chamber, a hazardous and perilous desert. It was this fool, this homesick and desperate prisoner, who invented the "bad conscience." But in doing so he introduced the gravest and most sinister illness, one from which mankind has not yet recovered: the suffering of man from the disease called man. It came as the result of a violent break with his animal past, a spasmodic plunge, as it were, into new surroundings and new conditions of existence, a declaration of war against the old instincts that had until then been the staple of his power, his joy and his formidableness. Let us add at once that this fact of an animal ego turning against itself and taking sides against itself produced something so novel, profound, unheard-of, problematic, inconsistent and pregnant with the future that the face of the world was radically altered. In truth, only divine spectators could have appreciated the drama that then began, and whose end still baffles conjecture. It was a drama too subtle, too wonderful, too paradoxical to be played out senselessly and unnoticed on some random, grotesque planet! From now on man must be counted among the most unexpected and sensational lucky throws in the game of Heracleitus' "big baby," whether he is called Zeus or Chance. He awakens on his own behalf an interest, an excitement, a hope, almost a confidence, that he is the harbinger and forerunner of something: that man is no end, but only a stage, an interlude, a bridge, a great promise.

17. This hypothesis about the origin of the bad conscience involves, first, that the change was neither gradual nor voluntary, and that it did not appear as an organic adaptation to new conditions. It came as a break, a leap, a necessity, an inevitable fate, against which there was no resistance and never a spark of resentment. It involves, second, that fitting an unchecked and shapeless population into a fixed form, a process that began with an act of violence, could only be completed by acts of violence and nothing else. The oldest "State" therefore appeared as a ghastly tyranny, a grinding, ruthless piece of machinery, and it kept working until the raw material of this semi-animal populace was not only thoroughly kneaded and pliable, but also molded. I used the word "State," and my meaning is self-evident: a herd of blond beasts of prey, a race of conquerors and masters, which with all its warlike organization and all its organizing power pounces with its terrible claws on a population that may be tremendously superior in numbers, but is still formless and still nomad. Such is the origin of the "State." The fantastic theory that makes it begin with a contract is, I think, disposed of. What has he to do with contracts, the man who can command, who is a master by "nature," who comes on the scene forceful in deed and gesture? Such beings defy calculation. They come like fate, without cause, reason, notice or excuse; they are there as the lightning is there, too terrible, too sudden, too convincing, too "different," even to be hated personally. Their work is an instinctive creating and impressing of forms; they are the most involuntary, unconscious artists there are. Their appearance instantly produces a living scheme of sovereignty, in which the functions are divided and apportioned, and in which above all no part is admitted or finds a place until it is pregnant with a "meaning" in relation to the whole. These born organizers do not know the meaning of guilt, responsibility or consideration. In them that terrible artist-egoism predominates, which gleams like brass and knows itself justified for all eternity in its work, as a mother is in her child. It is not in them that the bad conscience grew; that much is elementary. But it would not have grown without them, this repulsive growth; it would be missing, had a tremendous quantity of freedom not been expelled from the world by the force of their hammer-strokes, their artist violence, or at any rate made invisible and, as it were, latent. This instinct of freedom forced into latency — it is already clear — this instinct of freedom forced back, trodden back, imprisoned within itself, and finally able to find vent and relief only in itself: this, only this, is the beginning of the "bad conscience."

18. Beware of thinking lightly of this phenomenon because of its initial painful ugliness. At bottom the same active force is at work. On a grander scale it works in those potent artists and organizers and builds states. Here, inwardly, on a smaller and pettier scale and with a backward tendency, it makes itself a bad conscience in the "labyrinth of the breast," to use Goethe's phrase, and builds negative ideals. It is, I repeat, that identical instinct of freedom (to use my own language, the will to power). Only the material on which this force, with all its constructive and tyrannous nature, is let loose is here man himself, his whole old animal self — and not, as in the case of that more grandiose and sensational phenomenon, the other man, other men. This secret self-tyranny, this cruelty of the artist, this delight in giving form to oneself as a piece of difficult, refractory and suffering material, in burning into it a will, a critique, a contradiction, a contempt, a negation; this sinister and ghastly labor of love on the part of a soul whose will is split in two within itself, which makes itself suffer out of delight in inflicting suffering; this wholly active bad conscience has finally (as one already anticipates) produced an abundance of novel and amazing beauty and affirmation, true fountainhead as it is of idealism and imagination, and perhaps it was really the first to give birth to beauty at all. What would beauty be, indeed, if its contradiction had not first been presented to consciousness, if the ugly had not first said to itself, "I am ugly"? At any rate, after this hint the problem of how far idealism and beauty can be traced in such opposite ideas as "selflessness," self-denial and self-sacrifice becomes less problematic. And in future we shall undoubtedly know the real and original character of the delight felt by the selfless, the self-denying, the self-sacrificing: this delight is a form of cruelty. — So much for now on the origin of "altruism" as a moral value, and on marking out the ground from which this value has grown. It is only the bad conscience, only the will to self-abuse, that provides the necessary conditions for the existence of altruism as a value.

19. Undoubtedly the bad conscience is an illness, but an illness in the way pregnancy is an illness. If we search out the conditions under which this illness reaches its most terrible and sublime peak, we shall see what first brought it into the world. But to do this we must take a long breath, and first go back once again to an earlier point of view. The civil-law relation of the ower to his creditor (which has already been discussed in detail) has been reinterpreted once again, in a way that is historically very remarkable and suspicious, as a relationship that is perhaps more incomprehensible to us moderns than to any other era. I mean the relationship of the existing generation to its ancestors. In the original tribal association (we are speaking of primitive times) each living generation recognizes a legal obligation towards the earlier generation, and particularly towards the earliest, which founded the family. (This is something much more than a mere sentimental obligation, the existence of which during the longest period of man's history is by no means indisputable.) The living are convinced that the race persists at all only thanks to the sacrifices and efforts of their ancestors, and that they have to pay this back to them with sacrifices and services. Thus a debt is recognized as owing, and it keeps accumulating, because these ancestors never cease, in their later life as potent spirits, to secure new privileges and advantages for the race by their power. For nothing, perhaps? But there is no "for nothing" in that raw and "mean-souled" age. What return can be made? Sacrifice (at first, nourishment in its crudest sense), festivals, temples, tributes of veneration, above all obedience, since all customs, as works of the ancestors, are equally their precepts and commands. Are the ancestors ever given enough? This suspicion remains and grows. From time to time it extorts a great wholesale ransom, something monstrous in the way of repayment to the creditor (the notorious sacrifice of the first-born, for example, blood, human blood in any case). According to this kind of logic, the fear of the ancestors and their power, and the consciousness of owing them debts, increase in exact proportion as the race itself increases, as the race itself becomes more victorious, more independent, more honored, more feared. This, and not the contrary, is the fact. Each step towards the decay of the race, all disastrous events, all symptoms of degeneration and approaching disintegration, always diminish the fear of the founder's spirit, and whittle away the idea of his sagacity, providence and potent presence. Imagine this crude logic carried to its climax. It follows that the ancestors of the most powerful races must, through the growing fear they exercise on the imagination, swell to monstrous dimensions and be relegated to the gloom of a divine mystery that transcends imagination. The ancestor becomes at last necessarily transfigured into a god. Perhaps this is the very origin of the gods, an origin from fear! And those who feel bound to add, "but from piety also," will have difficulty maintaining this theory for the primeval and longest period of the human race. This is of course even more true of the middle period, the formative period of the aristocratic races, which gave back with interest to their founders, the ancestors (heroes, gods), all the qualities that had meanwhile appeared in themselves, that is, the aristocratic qualities. We shall glance again later at the ennobling and promotion of the gods (which is of course totally distinct from their "sanctification"). For now, let us follow to its end the course of this whole development of the consciousness of "owing."

20. According to the teaching of history, the consciousness of owing debts to the deity by no means came to an end with the decay of the clan organization of society. Mankind inherited the ideas of "good" and "bad" from the race-nobility (together with its fundamental tendency to establish social distinctions). In the same way, along with the heritage of the racial and tribal gods, it also inherited the incubus of debts as yet unpaid and the desire to discharge them. The transition is made by those large populations of slaves and bondsmen who, whether through compulsion or through submission and "mimicry," have accommodated themselves to the religion of their masters. Through this channel these inherited tendencies flood the world. The feeling of owing a debt to the deity has grown continuously for several centuries, always in the same proportion in which the idea of God and the consciousness of God have grown and been exalted among mankind. (The whole history of ethnic fights, victories, reconciliations and amalgamations, in fact everything that precedes the eventual ranking of all the social elements in each great race-synthesis, is mirrored in the hotch-potch genealogy of their gods, in the legends of their fights, victories and reconciliations. Progress towards universal empires always means progress towards universal deities; despotism, with its subjugation of the independent nobility, always paves the way for some system or other of monotheism.) The appearance of the Christian god, as the greatest god so far, has for that very reason brought into the world the greatest amount of guilt consciousness. Suppose we have gradually started on the reverse movement. Then there is no little probability, deduced from the continuous decay in the belief in the Christian god, that a considerable decay in the human consciousness of owing (ought) already exists. In fact, we cannot shut our eyes to the prospect of the complete and final triumph of atheism, which would free mankind from all this feeling of obligation to its origin, its causa prima. Atheism and a kind of second innocence complement and supplement each other.

21. So much for my rough, preliminary sketch of how the ideas "ought" (owe) and "duty" are interrelated with the postulates of religion. Until now I have intentionally held back the actual moralization of these ideas (their being pushed back into the conscience, or more precisely the interweaving of the bad conscience with the idea of God). At the end of the last paragraph I spoke as if this moralization did not exist, and as if these ideas had therefore necessarily come to an end, since their hypothesis, the belief in our "creditor," in God, had collapsed. The actual facts differ terribly from this theory. With the moralization of the ideas "ought" and "duty," and their being pushed back into the bad conscience, comes the first actual attempt to reverse the direction of the development we have just described, or at any rate to arrest its progress. It is just at this juncture that the very hope of an eventual redemption has to shut itself once for all in the prison of pessimism; it is at this juncture that the eye has to recoil and rebound in despair from an adamantine impossibility; it is at this juncture that the ideas "guilt" and "duty" have to turn backwards. Turn backwards against whom? There is no doubt about it: primarily against the "ower." In him the bad conscience now establishes itself, eats, spreads and grows like a polypus throughout his length and breadth, and with such virulence that at last, with the impossibility of paying the debt, there is conceived the impossibility of paying the penalty, the thought of its inexpiability (the idea of "eternal punishment"). Finally it also turns against the "creditor." It may find him in the causa prima of man, the origin of the human race, its sire, who from then on is burdened with a curse ("Adam," "original sin," "determination of the will"). Or it may find him in Nature, from whose womb man springs, and on whom the responsibility for the principle of evil is now cast ("Diabolization of Nature"). Or it may find him in existence generally, which on this logic is an absolute white elephant, with which mankind is landed (the Nihilistic flight from life, the demand for Nothingness, or for the opposite of existence, for some other existence, Buddhism and the like). Then suddenly we stand before that paradoxical and awful expedient through which a tortured humanity found a temporary alleviation, that stroke of genius called Christianity: God personally sacrificing himself for the debt of man, God paying himself personally out of a pound of his own flesh, God as the one being who can deliver man from what man had become unable to deliver himself from — the creditor playing scapegoat for his debtor, from love (can you believe it?), from love of his debtor!...

22. The reader will already have guessed what took place on the stage and behind the scenes of this drama. It was the will to self-torture, the inverted cruelty of the animal man. Turned subjective and scared into introspection (he was encaged in "the State" as part of his taming process), he invented the bad conscience in order to hurt himself, once the natural outlet for his will to hurt was blocked. This man of the bad conscience, in other words, seized on the religious hypothesis to drive his martyrdom to the ghastliest pitch of agonized intensity. Owing something to God: this thought becomes his instrument of torture. In God he grasps the most extreme opposites he can find to his own characteristic, ineradicable animal instincts. And he reinterprets those instincts as directed against what he "owes" to God (as enmity, rebellion and revolt against the "Lord," the "Father," the "Sire," the "Beginning of the world"). He places himself between the horns of the dilemma, "God" and "Devil." Every negation that he is inclined to utter against himself, against the nature, naturalness and reality of his being, he whips into a "yes," uttering it as something existing, living and effective, as being God, as the holiness of God, the judgment of God, the hangmanship of God, as transcendence, as eternity, as unending torment, as hell, as infinity of punishment and guilt. Here is a madness of the will, in the sphere of psychological cruelty, that has absolutely no parallel: man's will to find himself guilty and blameworthy to the point of inexpiability; his will to think of himself as punished, without the punishment ever being able to balance the guilt; his will to infect and poison the fundamental basis of the universe with the problem of punishment and guilt, in order to cut off once and for all any escape from this labyrinth of "fixed ideas"; his will to rear an ideal, that of the "holy God," face to face with which he can have tangible proof of his own unworthiness. Alas for this mad, melancholy beast, man! What fantasies invade it, what paroxysms of perversity, hysterical senselessness and mental bestiality break out the moment it is even slightly checked from being the beast of action. All this is excessively interesting, yet it is tainted with a black, gloomy, enervating melancholy, and we must forbid ourselves, firmly, to look too long into these abysses. Here is disease, undoubtedly, the most ghastly disease that has yet played havoc among men. And whoever can still hear (but man now turns a deaf ear to such sounds) how in this night of torment and nonsense there has rung out the cry of love, the cry of the most passionate ecstasy, of redemption in love, turns away gripped by an invincible horror. In man there is so much that is ghastly. Too long has the world been a mad-house.

23. That is enough, once for all, about the origin of the "holy God." The conception of gods is not in itself bound to lead to this degradation of the imagination (we felt bound to give a temporary picture of its vagaries). There exist nobler ways of using the invention of gods than this self-crucifixion and self-degradation of man, in which the last two thousand years of Europe have been past masters. Fortunately we can still see this whenever we look at the Grecian gods, those mirrors of noble and grandiose men, in whom the animal in man felt itself deified instead of devouring itself in subjective frenzy. For a long time these Greeks used their gods simply as buffers against the "bad conscience," so that they could go on enjoying their freedom of soul. This is of course diametrically opposed to Christianity's use of its god. They went very far on this principle, these splendid, lion-hearted children, and no less an authority than the Homeric Zeus occasionally makes them realize that they are taking life too casually. "Wonderful," says he on one occasion (it has to do with the case of Ægistheus, a very bad case indeed) —
"Wonderful how they grumble, the mortals against the immortals, Only from us, they presume, comes evil, but in their folly, Fashion they, spite of fate, the doom of their own disaster."

Yet note that this Olympian spectator and judge is not at all angry with them, and does not think ill of them for it. "How foolish they are," he thinks of the misdeeds of mortals. And "folly," "imprudence," "a little brain disturbance," and nothing more, are what the Greeks, even of the strongest, bravest period, have admitted to be the ground of much that is evil and fatal. — Folly, not sin, do you understand?... But even this brain disturbance was a problem. "Come, how is it even possible? How could it really have got into brains like ours, the brains of men of aristocratic ancestry, of men of fortune, of men of good natural endowments, of men of the best society, of men of nobility and virtue?" This was the question the aristocratic Greek asked himself for century after century, whenever he was confronted with every (to him incomprehensible) outrage and sacrilege with which one of his peers had polluted himself. "It must be that a god had infatuated him," he would say at last, nodding his head. — This solution is typical of the Greeks, ... and accordingly the gods in those times served to justify man to a certain extent even in evil. In those days they took upon themselves not the punishment but, what is more noble, the guilt.

24. I conclude with three queries, as you will see. "Is an ideal actually set up here, or is one pulled down?" I am perhaps asked.... But have you asked yourselves sufficiently how dear a payment the setting up of every ideal in the world has exacted? To achieve that, how much truth must always be slandered and misunderstood, how many lies must be sanctified, how much conscience must be disturbed, how many pounds of "God" must be sacrificed every time? For a sanctuary to be set up, a sanctuary has got to be destroyed: that is a law. Show me an instance where it has not been fulfilled!... We modern men inherit the immemorial tradition of vivisecting the conscience and practicing cruelty on our animal selves. That is the sphere of our most protracted training, perhaps of our artistic prowess, at any rate of our dilettantism and our perverted taste. Man has for too long regarded his natural proclivities with an "evil eye," so that eventually they have become affiliated in his system to a bad conscience. The converse endeavor would in itself be feasible, but who is strong enough to attempt it? It would be to affiliate to the "bad conscience" all those unnatural proclivities, all those transcendental aspirations contrary to sense, instinct, nature and animalism: in short, all past and present ideals, which are all ideals opposed to life and slandering the world. To whom is one to turn nowadays with such hopes and pretensions? It is just the good men that we should thus bring down about our ears. And in addition, as stands to reason, the indolent, the hedgers, the vain, the hysterical, the tired.... What is more offensive, or more thoroughly calculated to alienate, than giving any hint of the exalted severity with which we treat ourselves? And again, how conciliatory and full of love the whole world shows itself towards us as soon as we do as all the world does, and "let ourselves go" like all the world. For such an achievement we need spirits of a different caliber from what seems really feasible in this age: spirits made potent through wars and victories, to whom conquest, adventure, danger, even pain, have become a need. For it we need to be used to sharp, rare air, to winter wanderings, to ice and mountains literal and metaphorical. We even need a kind of sublime malice, a supreme and most self-conscious insolence of knowledge, which is the appanage of great health. We need (to sum up the awful truth) just this great health!

Is this even feasible today?... But some day, in an age stronger than this rotting, introspective present, he must come to us indeed, the redeemer of great love and scorn, the creative spirit, driven by his own force back away from every transcendental plane and dimension. The people misunderstand (sic) his solitude, as though it were a flight from reality; — while actually it is only his diving, burrowing and penetrating into reality, so that when he returns to the light he can at once redeem this reality by these means, redeem it from the curse the old ideal has laid upon it. This man of the future will redeem us in this way from the old ideal, and also from what that ideal necessarily brings with it: the great nausea, the will to nothingness, and Nihilism. He is the tocsin of noon and of the great verdict, which makes the will free again; he gives back to the world its goal and to man his hope; he is this Antichrist and Antinihilist, this conqueror of God and of Nothingness — he must one day come.

25. But what am I talking of? Enough! Enough? At this juncture I have only one proper course, silence. Otherwise I trespass on a domain open only to one who is younger than I, one stronger, more "future" than I — open only to Zarathustra, Zarathustra the godless.

chapters.title: Third Essay — What is the Meaning of Ascetic Ideals?
paragraphs: "Careless, mocking, forceful — so does wisdom wish us: she is a woman, and never loves anyone but a warrior." Thus Spake Zarathustra.

1. What do ascetic ideals mean? In artists, nothing, or too much. In philosophers and scholars, they mean a kind of "flair," an instinct for the conditions that best suit advanced intellectualism. In women, at best, they mean one more seductive charm: a little morbidezza on a fine piece of flesh, the angelhood of a fat, pretty animal. In physiological failures and whiners (which is to say, most mortals), they mean an attempt to pose as "too good" for this world, a holy form of debauchery, their chief weapon against lingering pain and ennui. In priests, they mean the true priestly faith, their best engine of power and the supreme authority that licenses it. In saints, finally, they mean a pretext for hibernation, their novissima gloriæ cupido, their peace in nothingness ("God"), their form of madness.

Yet the very fact that the ascetic ideal has meant so much to man shows the basic feature of man's will, his horror vacui.
