He needs a goal; and he will sooner will nothingness than not will at all. — Am I not understood? — Have I not been understood? — "Certainly not, sir?" — Well, then, let us begin at the beginning.

2. What do ascetic ideals mean? Or, to take one case on which I have often been consulted: what does it mean when an artist like Richard Wagner pays homage to chastity in his old age? In a certain sense he had always done so, of course. But only at the very end did he do it in an ascetic sense. What does this "change of attitude" mean, this radical revolution (for that is what it was)? Wagner swung right round into his own opposite. And what does it mean when an artist swings round into his own opposite? Here, if we are willing to dwell a little on the question, we think at once of the best, strongest, gayest and boldest period that Wagner's life perhaps ever had. It was the time when he was deeply and genuinely absorbed in the idea of "Luther's Wedding." Who knows by what chance we now have the Meistersingers in place of that wedding music? And how much of the one may be an echo of the other? Still, there is no doubt that the theme would have praised chastity. It would certainly have praised sensuality as well; and even so it would have seemed quite in order, and just as Wagnerian. For chastity and sensuality are not necessarily opposed: every good marriage, every authentic, heart-felt love, rises above that opposition. It seems to me that Wagner would have done well to bring this pleasing reality home to his Germans once more, with a bold and graceful "Luther Comedy." There were and are many revilers of sensuality among the Germans, and perhaps Luther's greatest merit is just that he had the courage of his sensuality (it used to be called, prettily enough, "evangelistic freedom "). Even where the opposition between chastity and sensuality really does exist, fortunately it has not needed to be a tragic one for some time now. That should hold for all beings sound in mind and body. They are far from counting their delicate balance between "animal" and "angel" as, on the face of it, one of the principles opposed to existence. The most subtle and brilliant spirits, Goethe and Hafiz for example, have even found in it a further charm of life. Such "conflicts" actually tempt one to live. On the other hand, it is only too clear what happens when these ruined swine are reduced to worshipping chastity (and there are such swine): all they see and worship in it is the opposite of themselves, the opposite of ruined swine. Oh, what tragic grunting and eagerness! Just imagine it. They worship that painful and superfluous contrast which Richard Wagner in his last years undoubtedly wanted to set to music and put on the stage! "For what purpose, forsooth?" we may fairly ask. What did the swine matter to him; what do they matter to us?

3. Here we cannot help asking what he really had to do with that manly (ah, so unmanly) country bumpkin, that poor devil and natural, Parsifal, whom he finally made a Catholic by such fraudulent devices. What? Was this Parsifal really meant seriously? One might be tempted to suppose the opposite, even to wish it: that the Wagnerian Parsifal was meant joyously, as the closing play of a trilogy or satyric drama, in which Wagner the tragedian wanted to take his leave of us, of himself, and above all of tragedy, in a fitting and worthy way. He would do it with an excess of the most extreme and flippant parody of the tragic itself, of the ghastly earthly seriousness and earthly woe of old; a parody of the crudest phase in the unnaturalness of the ascetic ideal, a phase long since overcome. As I have said, that would have been quite worthy of a great tragedian. Like every artist, he reaches the supreme peak of his greatness only when he can look down on himself and his art, when he can laugh at himself. Is Wagner's Parsifal his secret laugh of superiority at himself, the triumph of the supreme artistic freedom and artistic transcendency he has at last attained? We might, I repeat, wish it were so; for what can Parsifal amount to, taken seriously? Must we really see in it (in an expression once used against me) the product of an insane hate of knowledge, mind and flesh? A curse on flesh and spirit in one breath of hate? An apostasy and a relapse into the morbid Christian and obscurantist ideals? And, in the end, a self-negation and self-elimination by an artist who until then had put all the strength of his will into the opposite, the highest artistic expression of soul and body? Not only of his art, but of his life too. Remember how enthusiastically Wagner once followed in Feuerbach's footsteps. Feuerbach's motto of "healthy sensuality" rang in Wagner's ears in the thirties and forties of the century, as it did in the ears of many Germans (they called themselves "Young Germans"), like a word of redemption. Did he change his mind on this in the end? For at any rate it seems that in the end he wished to change his teaching on it ... and not only in the Parsifal trumpets on the stage. In the melancholy, cramped and embarrassed lucubrations of his later years, a hundred passages show a secret wish and will: a despondent, uncertain, unavowed will to preach actual retrogression, conversion, Christianity, mediævalism, and to tell his disciples, "All is vanity! Seek salvation elsewhere!" Even the "blood of the Redeemer" is invoked once.

4. Let me say frankly what I think in a case like this. It has many painful elements, and it is a typical case. It is certainly best to separate an artist from his work so completely that he is not taken as seriously as the work. He is, after all, only the presupposition of his work: the womb, the soil, in some cases the dung and manure, in which and out of which it grows. So in most cases he is something to be forgotten if one is to enjoy the work itself. Insight into how a work originates belongs to psychologists and vivisectors, never, now or in the future, to the æsthetes, the artists. The author and creator of Parsifal could no more be spared the need to live and sink himself into the terrible depths and foundations of mediæval soul-contrasts than a pregnant woman can be spared the horrors and marvels of pregnancy, which, as I have said, must be forgotten if the child is to be enjoyed. He could not be spared the need for a malignant abstraction from all intellectual elevation, severity and discipline, or the need for a kind of mental perversity (if the reader will pardon the word). We must be on guard against a confusion into which an artist himself falls only too easily (to use the English term), out of psychological "contiguity." He thinks he himself is the very thing he is able to represent, imagine and express. In fact, even if he believed he were such a thing, he would certainly not represent, conceive or express it. Homer would not have created an Achilles, nor Goethe a Faust, if Homer had been an Achilles or Goethe a Faust. A complete and perfect artist is cut off for all eternity from the "real," from the actual. On the other hand, it will be understood that he can at times grow tired, to the point of despair, of this eternal "unreality" and falseness of his innermost being. Then he sometimes tries to trespass on the most forbidden ground, on reality, and to have real existence. With what success? One can guess. It is the typical velleity of the artist, the same velleity to which Wagner fell victim in his old age, and for which he had to pay so dearly and so fatally (it cost him his most valuable friends). But quite apart from this velleity, who would not wish emphatically, for Wagner's own sake, that he had said farewell to us and to his art differently? Not with a Parsifal, but in a more victorious, more self-confident, more Wagnerian style; one less misleading, less ambiguous about his whole meaning, less Schopenhauerian, less Nihilistic?...

5. What, then, do ascetic ideals mean? In the case of an artist we are beginning to see: nothing at all ... or so much that it is as good as nothing at all. Indeed, what use are they? For a long time our artists have not taken a position independent enough, in the world or against it, to make their valuations, or any changes in them, interesting. At all times they have been the valets of some morality, philosophy or religion. Unfortunately they have also often been the inordinately supple courtiers of their clients and patrons, and the inquisitive toadies of the powers that be, or even of the powers still to come. At the very least, they always need a rampart, a support, some authority already in place. Artists never stand by themselves; standing alone goes against their deepest instincts. Thus Richard Wagner, "when the time had come," took the philosopher Schopenhauer as his covering man in front, as his rampart. Who would think it even possible that he could have had the courage for an ascetic ideal without the support of Schopenhauer's philosophy, without the authority of Schopenhauer, which dominated Europe in the seventies? (Here I set aside the question whether an artist without the milk of an orthodoxy could have existed at all.) This brings us to the more serious question: what does it mean when a real philosopher pays homage to the ascetic ideal? I mean a really self-dependent intellect like Schopenhauer, a man and knight with a glance of bronze, who has the courage to be himself, who knows how to stand alone without first waiting for men to cover him in front and for nods from his superiors. Let us look at once at Schopenhauer's remarkable attitude to art, an attitude that even fascinates certain types. For that, obviously, is why Richard Wagner suddenly went over to Schopenhauer (persuaded to it, as is well known, by a poet, Herwegh). He went over so completely that a rift opened, a total theoretical contradiction, between his earlier and his later æsthetic faiths. The earlier was set out, for example, in Opera and Drama; the later in the writings he published from 1870 onwards. Above all, from then on Wagner had no scruples about changing his judgment of the value and position of music itself (and this volte-face is what alienates us most). Until then he had made music a means, a medium, a "woman," who needed an end in order to thrive, a man, that is, the drama. What did he care? He suddenly saw that the novelty of the Schopenhauerian theory could achieve more in majorem musicæ gloriam, that is, through the sovereignty of music as Schopenhauer understood it. Music was abstracted from all the other arts and set against them, as the independent art-in-itself. It did not reflect the phenomenal world as the other arts do. It was rather the language of the will itself, speaking straight out of the "abyss" as the will's most personal, original and direct manifestation. This extraordinary rise in the value of music (a rise that seemed to grow out of the Schopenhauerian philosophy) came at once with an unprecedented rise in the esteem given to the musician himself. Now he became an oracle, a priest, nay, more than a priest: a kind of mouthpiece for the "intrinsic essence of things," a telephone from the other world. From then on he spoke not only music, this ventriloquist of God; he spoke metaphysic. Is it any wonder that one day he spoke ascetic ideals?

6. Schopenhauer took over the Kantian treatment of the æsthetic problem, though he certainly did not look at it through Kantian eyes. Kant believed he was honoring art when he put in the foreground those predicates of the beautiful that make up the honor of knowledge: impersonality and universality. I will not discuss here whether this was a complete mistake. I only want to stress that Kant, like other philosophers, did not approach the æsthetic problem from the experiences of the artist (the creator). He considered art and beauty only from the spectator's standpoint, and so imperceptibly brought the spectator himself into the idea of the "beautiful"! If only the philosophers of the beautiful knew this "spectator" well enough! I mean knew him as a great fact of personality, as a great experience, as a wealth of strong and highly individual events, desires, surprises and raptures in the sphere of beauty! But, as I feared, the opposite was always the case. So from the very beginning our philosophers hand us definitions in which the lack of subtler personal experience squats like a fat worm of crass error. It does so in Kant's famous definition of the beautiful. "That is beautiful," says Kant, "which pleases without interesting." Without interesting! Set this definition beside another, made by a real "spectator" and "artist," Stendhal, who once called the beautiful une promesse de bonheur. Here the one point Kant stresses in the æsthetic position is rejected and struck out: le désintéressement. Who is right, Kant or Stendhal? Our æsthetes never tire of putting into the scales on Kant's side the fact that under the magic of beauty men can look at even naked female statues "without interest." Forsooth, we may laugh a little at their expense. On this ticklish point the experiences of artists are more "interesting," and at any rate Pygmalion was not necessarily an "unæsthetic man." Let us think all the better of the innocence of our æsthetes, mirrored in such arguments. Let us even count it to Kant's honor that he taught with such country-parson naïveté about the peculiar character of the sense of touch! And here we come back to Schopenhauer. He stood much closer to the arts than Kant did, and yet he never got outside the pale of the Kantian definition. How was that? The circumstance is marvelous enough. He reads the phrase "without interest" in the most personal way, out of an experience that in his case must have been part and parcel of his regular routine. On few subjects does Schopenhauer speak with such certainty as on the working of æsthetic contemplation. He says it simply counteracts sexual interest, like lupulin and camphor, and he never tires of praising this escape from the "Life-will" as the great advantage and utility of the æsthetic state. One is in fact tempted to ask whether his basic conception of Will and Idea, the thought that freedom from the "will" is possible only by means of "idea," did not originate in a generalization from this sexual experience. (In every question about the Schopenhauerian philosophy, one should, by the way, keep in mind that it is the conception of a youth of twenty-six. It shares, therefore, not only in what is peculiar to Schopenhauer's life but in what is peculiar to that special period of it.) Let us listen, for instance, to one of the most expressive of the countless passages he wrote in honor of the æsthetic state (World as Will and Idea, i. 231). Let us listen to the tone, the suffering, the happiness, the gratitude, in which such words are spoken: "This is the painless state which Epicurus praised as the highest good and as the state of the gods; we are during that moment freed from the vile pressure of the will, we celebrate the Sabbath of the will's hard labor, the wheel of Ixion stands still." What vehemence of language! What images of anguish and long-drawn revulsion! How nearly pathological is that temporal antithesis between "that moment" and everything else: the "wheel of Ixion," "the hard labor of the will," "the vile pressure of the will." But grant that Schopenhauer was a hundred times right for himself personally. How does that help our insight into the nature of the beautiful? Schopenhauer has described one effect of the beautiful, the calming of the will; but is this effect really normal? As was mentioned, Stendhal, a nature just as sensual but more happily made than Schopenhauer, points to another effect of the "beautiful." "The beautiful promises happiness." For him the essential fact seems to be precisely that beauty excites the "will" (the "interest"). And does Schopenhauer not finally expose himself to the objection that he is quite wrong to regard himself as a Kantian here? That he has altogether failed to understand the Kantian definition of the beautiful in a Kantian sense? That the beautiful pleased him too through an interest, in fact the strongest and most personal interest of all, that of the victim of torture who escapes from his torture? — And to return to our first question, "What does it mean when a philosopher pays homage to ascetic ideals?" Now we have, at any rate, a first hint: he wishes to escape from a torture.

7. Let us beware of pulling dismal faces at the word "torture." In this case there is certainly plenty to deduct and plenty to discount; there is even something to laugh at. For we must not underestimate the fact that Schopenhauer treated sexuality in practice as a personal enemy (including its tool, woman, that "instrumentum diaboli"), and that he needed enemies to keep him in good humor. He loved grim, bitter, blackish-green words. He raged for the sake of raging, out of passion. Without his enemies, without Hegel, woman, sensuality and the whole "will for existence," "keeping on," he would have fallen ill and become a pessimist (for he was not a pessimist, however much he wished to be). Without them Schopenhauer would not have "kept on"; that is a safe wager. He would have run away. But his enemies held him fast, and his enemies always lured him back to existence. His wrath was, as it was for the ancient Cynics, his balm, his recreation, his recompense, his remedium against disgust, his happiness. So much for what is most personal in Schopenhauer's case. On the other hand, much in him is also typical, and only now do we come back to our problem. It is an accepted and indisputable fact that, as long as there have been philosophers in the world, and wherever they have existed (from India to England, to take the opposite poles of philosophic ability), they have felt a real irritation and rancor towards sensuality. Schopenhauer is merely its most eloquent outburst and, for anyone with an ear for it, also the most fascinating and enchanting. Philosophers likewise have a real bias and affection for the whole ascetic ideal; let there be no illusions on this score. Both feelings, as has been said, belong to the type. A philosopher who lacks both is, you may be certain, never anything but a "pseudo." What does this mean? For this state of affairs must first be interpreted: in itself it stands there stupid, for all eternity, like any "Thing-in-itself." Every animal, la bête philosophe included, strives instinctively for an optimum of favorable conditions, in which it can let its whole strength play and attain its maximum feeling of power. With equal instinctiveness, and with a fine perceptive flair superior to any reason, every animal shudders mortally at every kind of disturbance and hindrance that blocks, or could block, its way to that optimum. (I am not talking about his way to happiness, but about his way to power, to action, to the most powerful action, and in fact in many cases his way to unhappiness.) In the same way the philosopher shudders mortally at marriage and at all that could persuade him to it, since marriage is a fatal hindrance on the way to the optimum. Which great philosophers have been married, up to now? Heracleitus, Plato, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Kant, Schopenhauer: none was married, and, what is more, one cannot imagine them married. A married philosopher belongs to comedy. That is my rule. As for the exception, Socrates, the malicious Socrates seems to have married ironice, just to prove this very rule. Every philosopher would say what Buddha said when the birth of a son was announced to him: "Râhoula has been born to me, a fetter has been forged for me" (Râhoula means here "a little demon"). An hour of reflection must come to every "free spirit" (granted that an hour of thoughtlessness came first), just as it once came to that same Buddha: "Narrowly cramped," he reflected, "is life in the house; it is a place of uncleanness; freedom is found in leaving the house." Thinking so, he left the house. The ascetic ideal shows so many bridges to independence that the philosopher cannot help exulting and clapping his hands when he hears the story of all those resolute men who one day said nay to all servitude and went into some desert, even granting that they were only strong asses and the absolute opposite of strong minds. What, then, does the ascetic ideal mean in a philosopher? This is my answer, which will have been guessed long ago: when he sees this ideal, the philosopher smiles, because he sees in it an optimum of the conditions for the highest and boldest intellectuality. He does not thereby deny "existence." Rather he affirms his existence, and only his existence, and this perhaps to the point of being not far from the blasphemous wish, pereat mundus, fiat philosophia, fiat philosophus, fiam!

8. You see, these philosophers are far from being uncorrupted witnesses or judges of what the ascetic ideal is worth. They are thinking of themselves — what is the "saint" to them? What they have in mind is whatever they personally cannot do without: release from compulsion, disturbance and noise; release from business, duties and cares; a clear head; thoughts that dance, spring and fly; and good air — rare, clear, free and dry, the air of the heights, in which every animal creature grows more intellectual and sprouts wings. They have in mind peace in every cellar; every hound neatly chained; no baying of enmity, no uncouth rancor; no remorse from wounded ambition; internal organs that are quiet and submissive, busy as mills yet unnoticed; a heart that is alien, transcendent, future, posthumous. In short, what they mean by the ascetic ideal is the joyous asceticism of an animal that has been deified and newly fledged, and that sweeps over life instead of resting on it. The three great catch-words of the ascetic ideal are familiar to us: poverty, humility, chastity. Now look closely at the lives of all the great, fruitful, inventive spirits. Again and again you will find these three qualities in them, to a certain degree. This is, of course, not for a minute as though, perhaps, they belonged among such men's virtues — what has this type of man to do with virtues? — but because they are the most essential and natural conditions of such a man's best existence and finest fruitfulness. It is quite possible, in this connection, that their dominant intellectualism first had to rein in an unruly, irritable pride, or an insolent sensualism, or that it had its work cut out defending its wish for the "desert" against perhaps a leaning toward luxury and dilettantism, or against an extravagant generosity of heart and hand. Their intellect managed all this for one simple reason: it was the dominant instinct, and it imposed its orders on all the other instincts. It still does so; if it ceased, it would no longer be dominant. But in all this there is not one iota of "virtue." Further, take the desert I just mentioned, where the strong, independent and well-equipped spirits withdraw into their hermitage — oh, how unlike the desert the cultured classes dream of! In certain cases the cultured classes themselves are the desert. And it is certain that none of the actors of the intellect could endure that desert for even a minute. It is not romantic or Syrian enough for them; it is nowhere near enough of a stage desert! There are plenty of asses here too, but the resemblance stops there. A desert today looks more like this — perhaps a deliberate obscurity; stepping out of one's own way; a dread of noise, admiration, newspapers, influence; a little office, a daily task, something that conceals rather than reveals; at times the company of harmless, cheerful beasts and fowls whose sight refreshes; a mountain for company, though not a dead one, one with eyes (that is, with lakes); in some cases even a room in a crowded hotel, where one can count on going unrecognized and on talking with anyone without risk. That is the desert — oh, it is lonely enough, believe me! I admit that when Heracleitus withdrew to the courts and cloisters of the colossal temple of Artemis, his "wilderness" was worthier. Why do we lack such temples? (Perhaps we do not; I am thinking just now of my splendid study in the Piazza di San Marco, in spring, of course, and in the morning, between ten and twelve.) But what Heracleitus fled, we too avoid today: the noise and democratic babble of the Ephesians, their politics, their news from the "empire" (Persia, I mean, of course), their market-trade in "the things of today." For there is one thing above all that we philosophers need a rest from: the things of "today." We honor whatever is silent, cold, noble, far and past — in fact, anything the sight of which does not force the soul to brace and defend itself; something one can speak with without speaking aloud. Now listen to the tone of a spirit when it speaks; every spirit has a tone of its own and loves it. That one over there, for instance, is bound to be an agitator, that is, a hollow head, a hollow mug: whatever goes in comes back out of him dull and thick, heavy with the echo of the great void. That other spirit nearly always speaks hoarsely. Has he, perhaps, thought himself hoarse? It may be so — ask the physiologists. But someone who thinks in words thinks as a speaker and not as a thinker (this shows that he does not think about objects, or think objectively, but only about his relations to objects; in fact, that he thinks only of himself and his audience). A third speaks aggressively; he comes too near our body and his breath blows on us — we involuntarily shut our mouths, though he speaks to us through a book. The tone of his style supplies the reason: he has no time, he has little faith in himself, he finds expression now or never. A spirit who is sure of himself, however, speaks softly; he seeks secrecy and lets himself be waited for. A philosopher is recognized by his shunning three brilliant and noisy things, fame, princes and women — which is not to say that they do not come to him. He shuns every glaring light, and so he shuns his own time and its "daylight." In this he is like a shadow: the lower the sun sinks, the larger the shadow grows. As for his humility, he puts up with a certain dependence and obscurity just as he puts up with darkness. Further, he is afraid of the shock of lightning; he shudders at the insecurity of a tree that stands too isolated and exposed, on which every storm vents its temper and every temper its storm. His "maternal" instinct, his secret love for what is growing in him, leads him into states in which he is relieved of the need to look after himself, just as the "mother" instinct in woman has thoroughly preserved her dependent position down to the present. After all, they ask little enough, these philosophers; their favorite motto is, "He who possesses is possessed." As I must say again and again, none of this is to be put down to a virtue or to a meritorious wish for moderation and simplicity. It happens because their supreme lord demands it of them, wisely and inexorably — a lord who is eager for one thing only, and for that alone gathers and hoards everything: time, strength, love, interest. This kind of man does not like being disturbed by enmity, nor by friendship; it is a type that forgets or despises easily. He finds it bad form to play the martyr, to "suffer for truth"; he leaves that to the ambitious and the stage-heroes of the intellect, and to all those who have time for such luxuries (the philosophers themselves have something to do for truth). They use big words sparingly; they are said to dislike the very word "truth," which has a "high falutin'" ring. Finally, as for the chastity of philosophers: the fruitfulness of this type of mind lies plainly in another sphere than children; perhaps it is in some other sphere, too, that they have the survival of their name, their little immortality (philosophers in ancient India would say it with still greater boldness: "Of what use is posterity to him whose soul is the world?"). In this attitude there is no trace of chastity out of any ascetic scruple or hatred of the flesh, any more than it is chastity when an athlete or a jockey stays away from women. It is rather the will of the dominant instinct, at any rate during the time of their advanced philosophic pregnancy. Every artist knows how harmful sexual intercourse is in times of great mental strain and preparation. For the strongest artists, those with the surest instincts, this is not necessarily a matter of experience — hard experience; it is simply their "maternal" instinct, which, for the benefit of the growing work, recklessly spends the vigor of its animal life (beyond all its normal stocks and supplies). The greater power then absorbs the lesser. Now let us use this interpretation to judge correctly the case of Schopenhauer, already mentioned. In his case the sight of the beautiful evidently worked like a resolving irritant on the chief power of his nature (the power of contemplation and intense penetration), so that this strength exploded and suddenly became master of his consciousness. But that does not at all rule out the possibility that the particular sweetness and fullness peculiar to the æsthetic state springs directly from an ingredient of sensuality (just as the "idealism" peculiar to girls at puberty has the same source). It may be, then, that sensuality is not removed when the æsthetic state approaches, as Schopenhauer believed, but only transfigured, so that it no longer enters consciousness as sexual excitement. (I shall come back to this point in connection with the more delicate problems of the physiology of the æsthetic, a subject that has so far been singularly untouched and unelucidated.)

9. A certain asceticism, a grimly gay and wholehearted renunciation, is, as we have seen, among the most favorable conditions for the highest intellectualism, and so also for its most natural consequences. It should therefore not surprise us that philosophers in particular have always had a certain fondness for the ascetic ideal. A serious historical investigation shows that the bond between the ascetic ideal and philosophy is tighter and stronger still. One may say that philosophy learned to take its first steps and baby paces only in the leading strings of this ideal — alas, how clumsy, alas, how cross, alas, how ready to tumble and lie on its belly was this shy little darling of a brat on its bandy legs! The early history of philosophy is like that of all good things: for a long time they lacked the courage to be themselves, kept looking around to see whether anyone would come to help them, and were afraid of everyone who looked at them. Just list the particular tendencies and virtues of the philosopher in order: his tendency to doubt, to deny, to wait (to be "ephectic"), to analyze, search, explore and dare, to compare and to equalize; his will to be neutral and objective, his will for everything that is "sine ira et studio". Has anyone yet realized that for quite a long period these tendencies ran against the first claims of morality and conscience? (To say nothing of Reason, which even Luther chose to call Frau Klüglin, the sly whore.) Has anyone yet appreciated that a philosopher who arrives at self-consciousness must feel himself an incarnate "nitimur in vetitum" — and must therefore guard himself against "his own sensations," against self-consciousness? I repeat: it is the same with all the good things we now pride ourselves on. Judged even by the standard of the ancient Greeks, our whole modern life, in so far as it is not weakness but power and the consciousness of power, looks like pure "Hybris" and godlessness. For the very opposites of the things we honor today had conscience on their side for a long time, and God as their guardian. "Hybris" is our whole attitude to nature nowadays, our violation of nature with the aid of machinery and the unscrupulous ingenuity of our scientists and engineers. "Hybris" is our attitude to God — that is, to some alleged teleological and ethical spider behind the meshes of the great trap of the causal web. Like Charles the Bold in his war with Louis the Eleventh, we may say, "je combats l'universelle araignée." "Hybris" is our attitude to ourselves, for we experiment on ourselves in a way we would not permit with any animal, and gladly and curiously we cut open our soul while the body lives. What does the "salvation" of the soul matter to us now? Afterwards we heal ourselves; being ill is instructive, we do not doubt it, even more instructive than being well — inoculators of disease seem to us today even more necessary than any medicine-men and "saviors." There is no doubt that we do violence to ourselves nowadays, we crackers of the soul's kernel, we incarnate riddles who are forever asking riddles, as though life were nothing but the cracking of a nut. And precisely by this we must become, day by day, more and more worthy to be questioned and to question. Perhaps by this we also become worthier to — live?

... All good things were once bad things; every original sin has turned into an original virtue. Marriage, for instance, long seemed a sin against the rights of the community; a man once paid a fine for having the insolence to claim one woman for himself (the jus primæ noctis belongs to this phase; in Cambodia it is still today the privilege of the priest, that guardian of the "good old customs").

The soft, benevolent, yielding, sympathetic feelings were eventually valued so highly that they almost became "intrinsic values"; yet for a very long time their own possessors despised them. Gentleness was then a matter of shame, just as hardness is now (compare Beyond Good and Evil, Aph. 260). Submission to law: oh, with what qualms of conscience the noble races everywhere renounced the vendetta and gave the law power over themselves! For a long time law was a vetitum, a blasphemy, an innovation. It was introduced by force, as a force, and men submitted to it only with a sense of personal shame. In the past, every tiny step forward in the world was made at the cost of mental and physical torture. Today this whole point of view — "that not only stepping forward, nay, stepping at all, movement, change, all needed their countless martyrs" — sounds quite strange to us. I have set it out in the Dawn of Day, Aph. 18. "Nothing is purchased more dearly," the same book says a little later, "than the modicum of human reason and freedom that is now our pride. But this very pride makes it almost impossible for us now to feel sympathy with those immense periods of the 'Morality of Custom,' which lie at the beginning of the 'world's history' and which, as the real decisive historical principle, fixed the character of humanity. In those periods, I repeat, suffering passed for virtue, cruelty for virtue, deceit for virtue, revenge for virtue, repudiation of the reason for virtue throughout the world; and conversely, well-being passed for danger, the desire for knowledge for danger, pity for danger, peace for danger, being pitied for shame, work for shame, madness for divinity, and change for immorality and incarnate corruption!"

10. In the same book, Aph. 12, there is an explanation of the burden of unpopularity borne by the earliest race of contemplative men — who were despised almost as widely as they were first feared! There is no doubt about it: contemplation first appeared on earth in disguise, in an ambiguous form, with an evil heart and often with an uneasy head. The inactive, brooding, unwarlike element in the instincts of contemplative men long surrounded them with a cloud of suspicion, and the only way to counter this was to arouse a definite fear. The old Brahmans, for example, knew exactly how to do it! The oldest philosophers knew well how to give their very existence and appearance a meaning, a firmness and a background, which taught men to fear them. Looked at more closely, they did so from an even more fundamental need: the need to inspire fear and self-reverence in themselves. For they found all the valuations in their own souls turned against themselves; they had to fight down every kind of suspicion and antagonism toward "the philosophic element in themselves." They were men of a terrible age, and they used terrible means: cruelty to themselves, ingenious self-mortification. This was the chief method of these ambitious hermits and intellectual revolutionaries, who had to force down the gods and traditions of their own souls so as to be able to believe in their own revolution. I remember the famous story of King Vicvamitra, who, after a thousand years of self-martyrdom, reached such a consciousness of power and such confidence in himself that he undertook to build a new heaven: the sinister symbol of the oldest and newest history of philosophy in the whole world. Everyone who has ever built a "new heaven" anywhere first found the power to do so in his own hell... Let us compress the facts into a short formula. For the philosophic spirit to be possible at all, it had to masquerade and disguise itself as one of the previously established types of contemplative man: as priest, wizard, soothsayer, as a religious man generally. For a long time the ascetic ideal served the philosopher as a superficial form, as a condition that allowed him to exist... To be a philosopher, he had to exemplify the ideal; to exemplify it, he was bound to believe in it. The peculiarly etherealized abstraction of philosophers, with their negation of the world, their enmity to life, their disbelief in the senses, has been kept up until very recently, and has almost come to be accepted as the ideal philosophic attitude. This abstraction is the result of the enforced conditions under which philosophy came into existence and continued to exist; for a very long time philosophy would have been absolutely impossible in the world without an ascetic cloak and dress, without an ascetic self-misunderstanding. Put plainly and palpably: the ascetic priest has taken the repulsive and sinister form of the caterpillar, beneath and behind which alone philosophy could live and slink about...

Has all that really changed? That flamboyant and dangerous winged creature, the "spirit" that the caterpillar hid inside itself: has it, thanks to a sunnier, warmer, lighter world, really and finally flung off its hood and escaped into the light? Is there enough pride, daring, courage, self-confidence, mental will, will for responsibility and freedom of the will to be found today, to make the philosopher really possible in the world now?

11. And now that we have caught sight of the ascetic priest, let us take up our problem. What is the meaning of the ascetic ideal? Now it first becomes serious — vitally serious. We now face the real representatives of seriousness. "What is the meaning of all seriousness?" This still more radical question is perhaps already on the tip of our tongue: a question, fairly, for physiologists, which we skip for now. In that ideal the ascetic priest finds not only his faith but also his will, his power, his interest. His right to exist stands or falls with that ideal. No wonder that we run into a terrible opponent here (supposing, of course, that we are opponents of that ideal) — an opponent fighting for his life against those who repudiate it!... On the other hand, it is improbable from the start that so biased an attitude toward our problem will do him much good. The ascetic priest will hardly prove the happiest champion of his own ideal (on the same principle by which a woman usually fails when she wants to champion "woman"), still less the most objective critic and judge of the controversy we have raised. So much is already clear: we shall have to help him defend himself properly against us, rather than fear being too well beaten by him. The idea in dispute is the value our life has from the standpoint of the ascetic priests. They set this life (together with the whole of which it is a part, "Nature," "the world," the whole sphere of becoming and passing away) in relation to an existence of quite another kind, which it excludes and to which it is opposed, unless it denies itself. In that case, the case of an ascetic life, life is taken as a bridge to that other existence. The ascetic treats life as a maze in which one must walk backwards until one reaches the place where it starts; or he treats it as an error which one may, nay must, refute by action, for he demands that he be followed and enforces his valuation of existence wherever he can. What does this mean? Such a monstrous valuation is no exceptional case or curiosity in human history; it is one of the most general and persistent facts there are. Someone who read the capital letters of our earthly life from the vantage of a distant star might perhaps conclude that the earth was the especially ascetic planet, a den of discontented, arrogant and repulsive creatures who never got rid of a deep disgust with themselves, with the world, with all life, and who hurt themselves as much as possible out of pleasure in hurting — presumably their one and only pleasure. Consider how regularly, how universally, how practically at every period the ascetic priest appears: he belongs to no particular race; he thrives everywhere; he comes out of all classes. It is not that he perhaps bred this valuation by heredity and propagated it — the contrary is the case. A necessity of the first order must be what makes this species, hostile as it is to life, grow again and thrive again. Life itself must certainly have an interest in the continuance of such a type of self-contradiction. For an ascetic life is a self-contradiction. Here rules a resentment without parallel, the resentment of an insatiate instinct and ambition that wants to be master, not over some element in life, but over life itself, over its deepest, strongest, innermost conditions. Here an attempt is made to use power to dam the sources of power. Here the green eye of jealousy turns even against physiological well-being, especially against its expression, beauty and joy; while pleasure is felt and sought in abortion, decay, pain, misfortune, ugliness, voluntary punishment, in the exercising, flagellation and sacrifice of the self. All this is in the highest degree paradoxical: we face a rift that wills itself to be a rift, that enjoys itself in this very suffering and grows more and more certain of itself, more and more triumphant, in proportion as its own presupposition, physiological vitality, declines. "The triumph just in the supreme agony": under this extravagant emblem the ascetic ideal has fought from of old. In this mystery of seduction, in this picture of rapture and torture, it recognized its brightest light, its salvation, its final victory. Crux, nux, lux — it has all three in one.

12. Suppose such an incarnate will for contradiction and unnaturalness is induced to philosophize. On what will it vent its pet caprice? On whatever has been felt with the greatest certainty to be true and real; it will look for error exactly where the life instinct fixes truth most positively. For instance, following the ascetics of the Vedanta Philosophy, it will reduce matter to an illusion, and treat pain, multiplicity and the whole logical contrast of "Subject" and "Object" the same way: errors, nothing but errors! To renounce belief in one's own ego, to deny oneself one's own "reality" — what a triumph! And here we already have a much higher kind of triumph, not merely over the senses, over the palpable, but an infliction of violence and cruelty on reason. This ecstasy culminates in ascetic self-contempt, in the ascetic scorn of one's own reason, which issues this decree: there is a domain of truth and of life, but reason is specially excluded from it... By the way, even in the Kantian idea of "the intelligible character of things" a trace remains of that schism so dear to the ascetic's heart, the schism that likes to turn reason against reason. For "intelligible character" means, in Kant, a kind of quality in things of which the intellect comprehends only this: that for the intellect it is absolutely incomprehensible. After all, as knowers, let us not be ungrateful for such determined reversals of the usual perspectives and values, with which the mind for too long raged against itself in an apparently futile sacrilege! In the same way, merely to see another vista, merely to wish to see another vista, is no small training and preparation of the intellect for its eternal "Objectivity." By objectivity I mean not "contemplation without interest" (for that is inconceivable and nonsensical), but the ability to have one's pros and cons in one's power and to switch them on and off, so as to learn to use the difference in perspectives and emotional interpretations in the service of knowledge. But from now on, my philosophic colleagues, let us indeed guard ourselves more carefully against this mythology of dangerous ancient ideas, which has set up a "pure, will-less, painless, timeless subject of knowledge"; let us guard ourselves against the tentacles of such contradictory ideas as "pure reason," "absolute spirituality," "knowledge-in-itself." These theories require us to think an eye that cannot be thought, an eye which ex hypothesi has no direction at all, an eye in which the active and interpreting functions are cramped, are absent — the very functions by means of which "abstract" seeing first became seeing something. So these theories always demand of the eye something absurd and nonsensical. There is only a seeing from a perspective, only a "knowing" from a perspective, and the more emotions we express over a thing, the more eyes, different eyes, we train on the same thing, the more complete our "idea" of that thing, our "objectivity," will be. But to eliminate the will altogether, to switch off the emotions all and sundry, supposing we could — what! would that not be called intellectual castration?

13. But let us turn back. The self-contradiction that seems to show itself among the ascetics, "Life turned against Life," is simply nonsense — this much is absolutely obvious — when judged from the physiological standpoint and not, now, the psychological one. It can only be an apparent contradiction. It has to be a kind of provisional expression, an explanation, a formula, an adjustment: a psychological misunderstanding of something whose real nature could not be grasped for a long time, and whose real essence could not be described. It is a mere word jammed into an old gap in human knowledge. Put briefly, the facts that count against its being real are these. The ascetic ideal comes out of the protective, self-preserving instincts of a decadent life, a life that tries by every means it has to hold its position and fight for its existence. It points to a partial physiological depression and exhaustion, and the deepest, still intact life-instincts keep fighting this ceaselessly with new weapons and new discoveries. The ascetic ideal is one such weapon. So its position is exactly the reverse of what its worshippers imagine: life is struggling in it and through it with death and against death, and the ascetic ideal is a dodge to keep life going. History teaches something important about how far this ideal could rule over man and exercise power over him, especially in every place where the civilization and taming of man was completed. What it shows is the diseased state of man up to now, at any rate of the tamed man: his physiological struggle with death (more precisely, with disgust with life, with exhaustion, with the wish for the "end"). The ascetic priest is the incarnate wish for an existence of another kind, on another plane. He is, in fact, the highest point of this wish, its official ecstasy and passion. Yet the very strength of this wish is the fetter that ties him down here. It is just this that turns him into a tool, one who has to labor to create more favorable conditions for earthly existence, for existence on the human plane. With this very strength he holds the whole herd of failures, distortions, abortions, unfortunates and sufferers from themselves of every kind fast to existence, while he walks instinctively ahead of them as their herdsman. You understand me already: this ascetic priest, this apparent enemy of life, this denier — he actually belongs among the really great conservative and affirmative forces of life.... Where does this diseased state come from? For man is more diseased, more uncertain, more changeable and more unstable than any other animal, there is no doubt of it — he is the diseased animal. So where does it spring from? Certainly he has also dared more, innovated more, braved more and challenged fate more than all the other animals put together. He is the great experimenter with himself, the unsatisfied, the insatiate, who fights for supreme mastery against beast, Nature and gods. He is the as yet ever uncompelled, the ever future, who can no longer find any rest from his own aggressive strength, driven mercilessly on by the spur of the future dug into the flesh of the present. How could so brave and rich an animal fail to be also the most endangered, the animal with the longest and deepest sickness among all sick animals?... Man grows sick of it, and often enough whole epidemics of this satiety break out (as around 1348, the time of the Dance of Death). Yet even this very nausea, this tiredness, this disgust with himself, is thrown off by him with such force that it is at once made into a new fetter. His "nay" to life brings forth, as though by magic, an abundance of graceful "yeas"; and even when he wounds himself, this master of destruction and of self-destruction, it is the wound itself afterward that forces him to live.

14. The more normal this sickliness in man is — and we cannot deny that it is normal — the more honor is owed to the rare cases of psychical and physical powerfulness, the windfalls of humanity, and the more strictly the sound must be protected from that worst of airs, the air of the sick-room. Is that being done? The sick are the greatest danger to the healthy; the strong are harmed not by the strongest but by the weakest. Is that known? Looked at broadly, it is not the fear of man that we should wish to see diminished, not for a minute. This fear forces the strong to be strong and at times terrible, and so keeps the sound type of man intact. What we must fear, what works with a fatality found in no other fate, is not the great fear of man but the great nausea with man, and equally the great pity for man. Suppose these two were one day to be joined in marriage. The maximum of monstrousness would inevitably come into the world at once: the "last will" of man, his will for nothingness, Nihilism. And indeed the road to it is well paved. Anyone who has not only a nose to smell with but also eyes and ears will sniff, almost wherever he goes today, an air something like that of a mad-house or a hospital. I am speaking, as stands to reason, of the cultured areas of mankind, of every kind of "Europe" that there is in fact in the world. The sick are the great danger to man, not the evil, not the "beasts of prey." The ones who are botched, oppressed and broken from the start, the weakest, are the ones who most undermine life under the feet of man, and who instil the most dangerous venom and skepticism into our trust in life, in man, in ourselves. Where shall we escape it, that covert look (which leaves us carrying away a deep sadness), that averted look of the man who was misborn from the beginning, the look that betrays what such a man says to himself — the look that is a groan? "Would that I were something else," this look groans, "but there is no hope. I am what I am: how could I get away from myself? And, verily — I am sick of myself!" Out of such a soil of self-contempt, a veritable swamp soil, grows that weed, that poisonous growth, so tiny, so hidden, so ignoble, so sugary. Here the worms of revenge and vindictiveness swarm; here the air reeks of things secret and unmentionable; here the net of the most malignant conspiracy is forever being spun — the conspiracy of the sufferers against the sound and the victorious; here the sight of the victorious is hated. And what lying, so as never to admit this hate as hate! What a show of big words and attitudes, what an art of "righteous" calumniation! These abortions! What noble eloquence pours from their lips! What a quantity of sugary, slimy, humble submission oozes in their eyes! What do they really want? At any rate to represent righteousness, love, wisdom, superiority: that is the ambition of these "lowest ones," these sick ones! And how clever such an ambition makes them! In fact you cannot help admiring the counterfeiter's skill with which the stamp of virtue, even the ring, the golden ring of virtue, is copied here. They have taken out a lease on virtue absolutely for themselves, these weaklings and wretched invalids, there is no doubt of it. "We alone are the good, the righteous," they say, "we alone are the homines bonæ voluntatis." They stalk about among us as living reproaches, as warnings to us — as though health, fitness, strength, pride, the sensation of power were vicious things in themselves, for which one would someday have to do penance, bitter penance. Oh, how ready they themselves are in their hearts to make others do penance, how they thirst to be hangmen!

Among them are plenty of revengeful ones disguised as judges, who forever mouth the word righteousness like a venomous spittle — with mouth, I say, always pursed, always ready to spit at anything that does not wear a discontented look but goes its way in good cheer. Among them, too, is that most loathsome species of the vain, the lying abortions, who make a point of playing "beautiful souls," and perhaps bring to market, as "purity of heart," their distorted sensualism wrapped up in verses and other bandages: the species of "self-comforters" and masturbators of their own souls. The sick man wants to represent some form of superiority, and has an instinct for crooked paths leading to a tyranny over the healthy — where can this will to power of the very weakest not be found? The sick woman especially: no one surpasses her in refinements of ruling, oppressing, tyrannizing. The sick woman, moreover, spares nothing living and nothing dead; she digs up again the most deeply buried things (the Bogos say, "Woman is a hyena"). Look into the background of every family, every body, every community: everywhere you will find the fight of the sick against the healthy. It is mostly a silent fight, waged with minute poisoned powders, with pin-pricks, with spiteful grimaces of patience, but at times also with that diseased pharisaism of pure pantomime which likes best to play the role of "righteous indignation." It can make itself heard right into the hallowed chambers of knowledge, this hoarse yelping of sick hounds, this rabid lying and frenzy of such "noble" Pharisees (I remind readers who have ears once more of that Berlin apostle of revenge, Eugen Dühring, who makes the most disreputable and revolting use of moral refuse anywhere in present-day Germany; Dühring, the paramount moral blusterer there is today, even among his own kidney, the Anti-Semites). They are all men of resentment, these physiological distortions and worm-riddled objects, a whole quivering kingdom of burrowing revenge, indefatigable and insatiable in its outbursts against the happy, and equally so in its disguises for revenge, its pretexts for revenge. When will they really reach their final, fondest, most sublime triumph of revenge? Doubtless when they succeed in pushing their own misery, in fact all misery, into the consciousness of the happy, so that the happy begin one day to be ashamed of their happiness and perhaps say to themselves when they meet, "It is a shame to be happy! there is too much misery!" ... But there could not possibly be a greater and more fatal misunderstanding than for the happy, the fit, the strong in body and soul to begin in this way to doubt their right to happiness. Away with this "perverse world"! Away with this shameful soddenness of sentiment! To stop the sick from making the healthy sick — for that is what such soddenness comes to — ought to be our supreme object in the world. For this it is above all essential that the healthy stay separated from the sick, that they even guard themselves from the look of the sick, that they not even associate with the sick. Or is it perhaps their mission to be nurses or doctors? They could not mistake and disown their mission more grossly. The higher must not degrade itself into the tool of the lower, and the pathos of distance must keep their missions separate to all eternity. The right of the happy to exist, the right of bells with a full tone over the discordant cracked bells, is verily a thousand times greater: they alone are the sureties of the future, they alone are bound to man's future. What they can do and must do, the sick can never do and should never do! But if they are to be enabled to do what only they must do, how can they possibly be free to play the doctor, the comforter, the "Saviour" of the sick?... And therefore good air! good air! and away, at any rate, from the neighborhood of all the madhouses and hospitals of civilization! And therefore good company, our own company, or solitude if it must be so! But away, at any rate, from the evil fumes of internal corruption and the secret worm-eaten state of the sick! So that, indeed, my friends, we may defend ourselves, at least for a while longer, against the two worst plagues that could have been kept in store for us — against the great nausea with man! against the great pity for man!

15. Suppose you have understood in all their depths why it cannot be the business of the healthy to nurse the sick and make them healthy — and I demand that you grasp these reasons profoundly and understand them profoundly. Then it follows that you have grasped a further necessity: the necessity of doctors and nurses who are themselves sick. And now we have and hold, with both hands, the essence of the ascetic priest. We have to accept him as the predestined savior, herdsman and champion of the sick herd; only then do we first understand his awful historic mission. His kingdom is lordship over sufferers; his instinct points him toward it, and in it he finds his own special art, his master-skill, his kind of happiness. He must himself be sick, he must be kith and kin to the sick and the abortions, so as to understand them and come to an understanding with them. But he must also be strong, even more master of himself than of others, impregnable, indeed, in his will for power, so that he can win the trust and the awe of the weak and be their hold, bulwark, prop, compulsion, overseer, tyrant, god. He has to protect them, protect his herds — against whom? Against the healthy, doubtless, and also against envy of the healthy. He must be the natural adversary and scorner of every rough, stormy, unbridled, hard, violently predatory health and power. The priest is the first form of the more delicate animal, which scorns more easily than it hates. He will not be spared a war with the beasts of prey, a war of guile (of "spirit") rather than of force, as is self-evident. In certain cases he will find it necessary to conjure up out of himself, or at any rate to represent in practice, a new type of the beast of prey — a new animal monstrosity in which the polar bear, the supple, cold, crouching panther and, not least important, the fox are joined together in a trinity as fascinating as it is fearsome. If necessity demands it, he will step onto the scene with bearish seriousness, venerable, wise, cold, full of treacherous superiority, as the herald and mouthpiece of mysterious powers. Sometimes he will go even among the other kind of beasts of prey, determined to sow suffering, discord and self-contradiction on their soil wherever he can, and only too sure of his art of being, at all times, lord of sufferers. He brings with him, doubtless, salve and balsam; but before he can play the physician he must first wound. So while he soothes the pain the wound makes, he at the same time poisons the wound. He is well versed in this above all, this wizard and wild beast tamer, in whose presence everything healthy must needs fall ill and everything ill must needs grow tame. He protects his sick herd well enough, indeed, this strange herdsman. He also protects them against themselves, against the sparks of wickedness, knavery, malice and all the other ills that the plaguey and the sick are heir to (sparks that fly even in the center of the herd). With cunning, hardness and stealth he fights anarchy and the ever imminent break-up inside the herd, where resentment, that most dangerous blasting-stuff and explosive, accumulates and accumulates. His real feat, his supreme usefulness, is to get rid of this blasting-stuff in such a way that it does not blow up the herd and the herdsman. If you want the value of the priestly life in the shortest formula, it would be correct to say that the priest is the diverter of the course of resentment. For every sufferer instinctively looks for a cause of his suffering; to put it more exactly, for a doer — to put it still more precisely, for a sentient responsible doer — in brief, for something living on which he can vent his emotions, actually or in effigie, on any pretext. For the venting of emotions is the sufferer's greatest attempt at alleviation, that is to say, at stupefaction: his mechanically desired narcotic against pain of any kind. In this phenomenon alone, according to my judgment, lies the real physiological cause of resentment, revenge and their family — that is, in a demand for the deadening of pain through emotion. This cause is generally sought, but in my view very erroneously, in the defensive parry of a bare protective principle of reaction, of a "reflex movement" at any sudden hurt and danger, just as a decapitated frog still moves in order to get away from a corrosive acid. But the difference is fundamental. In one case the aim is to prevent being hurt any further; in the other the aim is to deaden a racking, insidious, nearly unbearable pain with a more violent emotion of any kind whatsoever, and at any rate for the time being to drive it out of the consciousness. For this an emotion is needed, as wild an emotion as possible, and to excite that emotion some excuse or other is needed. "It must be somebody's fault that I feel bad" — this kind of reasoning is peculiar to all invalids, and the more pronounced the more ignorant they remain of the real cause of their feeling bad, the physiological cause (the cause may lie in a disease of the nervus sympathicus, or in an excessive secretion of bile, or in a lack of sulphate and phosphate of potash in the blood, or in pressure in the bowels that stops the circulation of the blood, or in degeneration of the ovaries, and so forth). All sufferers are awfully resourceful and ingenious at finding excuses for painful emotions. They even enjoy their jealousy and their broodings over base actions and apparent injuries. They burrow through the intestines of their past and present in search of obscure mysteries, where they are free to wallow in a torturing suspicion and get drunk on the venom of their own malice. They tear open the oldest wounds, they make themselves bleed from scars long since healed, and they turn friend, wife, child and everything nearest to them into evil-doers. "I suffer: it must be somebody's fault" — so thinks every sick sheep. But his herdsman, the ascetic priest, tells him, "Quite so, my sheep, it must be the fault of someone; but you yourself are that someone, it is all the fault of yourself alone — it is the fault of yourself alone against yourself." That is bold enough, false enough, but one thing at least is achieved; thereby, as I have said, the course of resentment is — diverted.

16. You can see now what the remedial instinct of life has at least tried to bring about, according to my conception, through the ascetic priest, and for what purpose he had to use a temporary tyranny of such paradoxical and anomalous ideas as "guilt," "sin," "sinfulness," "corruption," "damnation." The sick were to be made harmless up to a certain point; the incurable were to be destroyed by means of themselves; the milder cases were to be turned severely back on themselves, and their resentment given a backward direction ("man needs but one thing"). In the same way the bad instincts of all sufferers were to be exploited for self-discipline, self-surveillance and self-mastery. It is obvious that with a "medication" of this kind, a mere emotional medication, there can be no question at all of any real healing of the sick in the physiological sense. It cannot even be claimed for a moment that in this connection the instinct of life has set healing as its goal and purpose. On the one hand there was a kind of congestion and organization of the sick (the word "Church" is the most popular name for it); on the other, a kind of provisional safeguarding of the comparatively healthy, the more perfect specimens, and a rift driven between healthy and sick. For a long time that was all! and it was much! it was very much!

I start in this essay, as you see, from a hypothesis that does not need proof, as far as the readers I want are concerned: the hypothesis that "sinfulness" in man is not an actual fact but only the interpretation of a fact, of a physiological discomfort — a discomfort seen through a moral and religious perspective that no longer binds us. So the fact that anyone feels "guilty" or "sinful" is certainly no proof yet that he is right to feel so, any more than anyone is healthy just because he feels healthy. Remember the celebrated witch-ordeals. In those days the most acute and humane judges had no doubt that they were confronted with guilt in these cases, and the "witches" themselves had no doubt on the point — and yet the guilt was lacking. Let me elaborate this hypothesis. I do not for a minute accept the very "pain in the soul" as a real fact; I accept it only as an explanation (a causal explanation) of facts that until now could not be precisely formulated. I regard it therefore as something as yet absolutely in the air and devoid of scientific cogency — just a nice fat word standing where a lean question mark belongs. When anyone fails to get rid of his "pain in the soul," the cause lies, speaking crudely, not in his "soul" but more probably in his stomach (speaking crudely, I repeat, but by no means wishing that you should therefore listen to me or understand me in a crude spirit). A strong and well-constituted man digests his experiences (deeds and misdeeds all included) just as he digests his meals, even when he has some tough morsels to swallow. If he fails to "relieve himself" of an experience, this kind of indigestion is quite as physiological as the other kind — and indeed, in more ways than one, merely one of its results. You can adopt such a theory and yet, entre nous, be nevertheless the strongest opponent of all materialism.

17. But is he really a physician, this ascetic priest? We already understand why we are scarcely allowed to call him one, however much he likes to feel like a "saviour" and to be worshipped as one. He combats only the actual suffering, the sufferer's discomfort, not its cause, not the actual state of sickness. This must be our most radical objection to priestly medication. Yet put yourself just once into that point of view, which the priests have a monopoly on, and you will find it hard to exhaust your amazement at all he has seen, sought and found from that standpoint. The mitigation of suffering, every kind of "consoling" — all this shows itself as his very genius. With what ingenuity has he interpreted his mission as consoler, with what aplomb and audacity has he chosen the weapons the part requires! Christianity in particular should be called a great treasure-chamber of ingenious consolations, so great a store of refreshing, soothing, deadening drugs has it piled up within itself. It has hazarded so many of the most dangerous and daring expedients; with such subtlety and refinement, Oriental refinement, it has divined which emotional stimulants can conquer, at least for a time, the deep depression, the leaden fatigue and the black melancholy of physiological cripples. For, speaking generally, all religions are mainly concerned with fighting a certain fatigue and heaviness that has infected everything. You can take it as prima facie probable that in certain places in the world there was almost bound to prevail from time to time, among large masses of the population, a sense of physiological depression. Owing to their lack of physiological knowledge, this did not appear to their consciousness as such, and so its "cause" and its cure could only be sought and tried in the science of moral psychology (this, in fact, is my most general formula for what is generally called a "religion"). Such a feeling of depression can have the most diverse origins. It may result from the crossing of too heterogeneous races (or of classes — genealogical and racial differences also show themselves in the classes: the European "Weltschmerz," the "Pessimism" of the nineteenth century, is really the result of an absurd and sudden class-mixture). It may be brought about by a mistaken emigration, a race falling into a climate for which its power of adaptation is insufficient (the case of the Indians in India). It may be the effect of old age and fatigue (the Parisian pessimism from 1850 onwards). It may come from a wrong diet (the alcoholism of the Middle Ages, the nonsense of vegetarianism — though these have in their favor the authority of Sir Christopher in Shakespeare). It may come from blood-deterioration, malaria, syphilis and the like (German depression after the Thirty Years' War, which infected half of Germany with evil diseases and thereby paved the way for German servility, for German pusillanimity). In such a case a war on a grand scale against the feeling of depression is invariably attempted. Let us inform ourselves briefly about its most important practices and phases (I leave aside, as stands to reason, the actual philosophic war against the feeling of depression, which is usually simultaneous — it is interesting enough, but too absurd, too practically negligible, too full of cobwebs, too much of a hole-and-corner affair, especially when pain is proved to be a mistake, on the naïf hypothesis that pain must needs vanish once the mistake underlying it is recognized — but behold! it does anything but vanish ...). That dominant depression is fought primarily by weapons that reduce the consciousness of life itself to the lowest degree. Wherever possible, no more wishes, no more wants; avoid everything that produces emotion, that produces "blood" (eating no salt, the fakir hygiene); no love; no hate; equanimity; no revenge; no getting rich; no work; begging; as far as possible, no woman, or as little woman as possible; as far as the intellect is concerned, Pascal's principle, "il faut s'abêtir." In ethical and psychological language, the result is "self-annihilation," "sanctification"; in physiological language, "hypnotism." It is the attempt to find some approximate human equivalent for what hibernation is for certain animals and æstivation for many tropical plants: a minimum of assimilation and metabolism in which life just manages to subsist without really entering the consciousness. An amazing amount of human energy has been devoted to this object — perhaps uselessly? There cannot be the slightest doubt that these sportsmen of "saintliness," of whom nearly every nation has at times had an abundance, really found a genuine relief from what they fought with such rigorous training. In countless cases they really did escape deep physiological depression with the help of their system of hypnotism, and their method is consequently counted among the most universal ethnological facts. Similarly it is improper to treat such a plan of starving the physical element and the desires as itself a symptom of insanity (as a clumsy species of roast-beef-eating "freethinkers" and Sir Christophers are fain to do). All the more certain is it that their method can and does pave the way to all kinds of mental disturbances, for instance "inner lights" (as with the Hesychasts of Mount Athos), auditory and visual hallucinations, voluptuous ecstasies and effervescences of sensualism (the history of St. Theresa). The explanation the victims give of such events is always the acme of fanatical falsehood; this is self-evident. Note well, however, the tone of implicit gratitude that rings in the very will to an explanation of such a character. They always regard the supreme state, salvation itself, that final goal of universal hypnosis and peace, as the mystery of mysteries, which even the most supreme symbols are inadequate to express. They regard it as an entry and homecoming to the essence of things, a liberation from all illusions, "knowledge," "truth," "being," an escape from every end, every wish, every action, something even beyond Good and Evil.
"Good and Evil," the Buddhists say, "both are fetters. The perfect man has mastered both of them."

"The done and the undone," says the disciple of the Vedanta, "do him no harm; the good and the evil he shakes off, wise man that he is; his kingdom suffers no more from any act; good and evil, he goes beyond them both." — An entirely Indian conception, as Brahmanist as it is Buddhist. In neither the Indian nor the Christian doctrine is this "Redemption" thought to be reachable through virtue and moral improvement, however highly they rate the hypnotic efficiency of virtue. Keep clear on this point; it simply corresponds with the facts. That they stayed true on it is perhaps to be counted the best example of realism in the three great religions, which with this one exception are absolutely soaked in morality. "For those who know, there is no duty." "Redemption is not gained by acquiring virtues; for redemption consists in being one with Brahman, who cannot acquire any perfection; and it consists just as little in giving up faults, for the Brahman, unity with whom is what constitutes redemption, is eternally pure" (these passages are from the Commentaries of the Cankara, as quoted by the first real European expert on Indian philosophy, my friend Paul Deussen). So we wish to honor the idea of "redemption" in the great religions. But it is rather hard to stay serious when we see how highly these exhausted pessimists, too tired even to dream, esteem deep sleep — deep sleep taken, that is, as already a fusing into Brahman, as the attainment of the unio mystica with God. "When he has fallen completely asleep," says the oldest and most venerable "script" on this point, "and come to perfect rest, so that he sees no more any vision, then, oh dear one, he is united with Being, he has entered into his own self — encircled by the Self with its absolute knowledge, he has no more any consciousness of what is outside or of what is inside. Day and night do not cross these bridges, nor do age, death, suffering, good deeds or evil deeds." "In deep sleep," say likewise the believers in this deepest of the three great religions, "the soul lifts itself out of this body of ours, enters the supreme light and stands out in it in its true shape: there it is the supreme spirit itself, which travels about, jesting and playing and enjoying itself, whether with women, or chariots, or friends; there its thoughts turn no more back to this appanage of a body, to which the 'prana' (the vital breath) is harnessed like a beast of burden to the cart." None the less we will take care to realize (as we did when discussing "redemption") that, for all its pomp of Oriental extravagance, this simply expresses the same criticism of life as the clear, cold, Greekly cold, but still suffering Epicurus made. The hypnotic sensation of nothingness, the peace of deepest sleep, anæsthesia in short — that is what the sufferers and the utterly depressed take for their supreme good, their value of values, if you please; that is what must be treasured by them as something positive, and felt by them as the essence of the Positive (by the same logic of the feelings, nothingness is called God in all pessimistic religions).

18. Such a hypnotic deadening of sensibility and of susceptibility to pain presupposes rather rare powers, above all courage, contempt of opinion and intellectual stoicism. It is less common than another training against states of depression, which is certainly easier. I mean mechanical activity. It is beyond dispute that a suffering existence can be considerably eased in this way. Today this fact goes by the rather ignoble name of the "Blessing of work." The relief consists in turning the sufferer's attention completely away from suffering, in the constant monopoly of consciousness by action, so that little room is left for suffering — for narrow it is, this chamber of human consciousness! Mechanical activity and what goes with it, such as absolute regularity, punctilious unreasoning obedience, the chronic routine of life, the complete filling of time, a certain freedom to be impersonal, nay, a training in "impersonality," self-forgetfulness, "incuria sui" — with what thoroughness and expert subtlety the ascetic priest has exploited all these methods in his war with pain!

When he has to deal with sufferers of the lower orders, slaves or prisoners (or women, who for the most part are a mixture of labor-slave and prisoner), all he has to do is juggle a little with names and rechristen things, so that they henceforth see a benefit, a comparative happiness, in what they used to hate — the slave's discontent with his lot was in any case not invented by the priests. An even more popular means of fighting depression is the prescribing of a little joy that is easy to reach and can be made into a rule; this medicine is often used together with the earlier ones. The commonest form in which joy is prescribed as a cure is joy in giving joy (such as doing good, giving presents, relieving, helping, exhorting, comforting, praising, treating with distinction), together with the prescription of "love your neighbour." In the most cautious doses, the ascetic priest prescribes what is in practice a stimulation of the strongest and most life-assertive impulse, the Will for Power. The happiness of the "smallest superiority" that goes with all benefiting, helping, extolling and making oneself useful is the fullest consolation, and physiological distortions, if they are well advised, make use of it; in other cases they hurt each other, naturally in obedience to the same basic instinct. If we investigate the origin of Christianity in the Roman world, we find that co-operative unions for poverty, sickness and burial sprang up in the lowest stratum of contemporary society, and that in this stratum the chief antidote against depression, the little joy felt in mutual benefits, was deliberately fostered. Perhaps this was then a novelty, a real discovery? This calling up of the will to co-operation, to family organization, to communal life, to "Cœnacula," necessarily brought the Will for Power, already stimulated in the smallest degree, to a new and much fuller manifestation.
