The herd organization is a genuine advance and triumph in the fight with depression. As the community grows, a new interest matures even in the individual, and it often enough takes him out of the more personal side of his discontent, his aversion to himself, the "despectus sui" of Geulincx. All sick and diseased people instinctively strive after a herd organization, out of a desire to shake off their sense of oppressive discomfort and weakness; the ascetic priest divines this instinct and promotes it. Wherever there is a herd, it is the instinct of weakness that has wished for the herd, and the cleverness of the priests that has organized it. For mark this: by an equally natural necessity the strong strive as much for isolation as the weak for union. When the strong bind themselves together, it is only with a view to aggressive joint action and the joint satisfaction of their Will for Power, much against the wishes of their individual consciences. The weak, on the contrary, range themselves together with positive delight in such a gathering — their instincts are as much gratified by it as the instincts of the "born master" (that is, the solitary beast-of-prey species of man) are disturbed and wounded to the quick by organization. Beneath every oligarchy — such is the universal lesson of history — there is always lurking the desire for tyranny. Every oligarchy is continually quivering with the tension of the effort each individual must make to keep mastering this desire. (Such, for example, was the Greek oligarchy; Plato shows it in a hundred places, Plato, who knew his contemporaries — and himself.)

19. We have already come to know the ascetic priest's methods: stifling all vitality, mechanical activity, the little joy, and above all the "love your neighbour" herd organization, which awakens the communal consciousness of power to such a pitch that the individual's disgust with himself is eclipsed by his delight in the community's thriving. By modern standards these are the "innocent" methods of fighting depression. Let us turn now to the more interesting subject of the "guilty" methods. They all come down to one thing: producing emotional excess, which serves as the most effective anæsthetic against the depressing state of protracted pain. That is why priestly ingenuity has proved quite inexhaustible in working out one question: "By what means can you produce an emotional excess?" This sounds harsh. Obviously it would sound nicer, and grate less on the ear, if I said instead, if you please: "The ascetic priest always made use of the enthusiasm that lies in all strong emotions." But why go on soothing the delicate ears of our modern effeminates? Why should we budge a single inch before their verbal Pecksniffianism? For us psychologists that would be practical Pecksniffianism in its own right, quite apart from the nausea it gives us. Nowadays a psychologist's good taste (others might say his righteousness) lies, if anywhere, in fighting the shamefully moralized language that smears every modern judgment on men and things. For do not deceive yourself: the chief mark of modern souls and modern books is not lying, but the innocence that comes with their intellectual dishonesty. Meeting this "innocence" everywhere is the most distasteful part of the rather dangerous business a modern psychologist has to take on. It is part of our great danger; it is a road that perhaps leads us straight to the great nausea. I know quite well what all modern books will serve for, and can serve for (granted that they last, which I do not fear, and granted equally that some day there will be a generation with a more rigid, more severe and healthier taste). I know what all modernity will serve for in the eyes of posterity: as an emetic, — and this by reason of its moral sugariness and falsity, its ingrained feminism, which it is pleased to call "Idealism," and at any rate believes to be idealism. Our cultured men of today, our "good" men, do not lie — that is true; but it does them no honor! The real lie, the genuine, determined, "honest" lie (on whose value you can listen to Plato), would be far too tough and strong for them. It would require them to do what people have been forbidden to ask of them: to open their eyes to their own selves, and to learn to tell "true" from "false" in their own selves. Only the dishonest lie suits them. Whatever feels itself a good man can take no other attitude to anything than that of a dishonorable liar, an absolute liar, but none the less an innocent liar, a blue-eyed liar, a virtuous liar. These "good men" are all now tainted with morality through and through, and as far as honor goes they are disgraced and corrupted for all eternity. Which of them could stand one further truth "about man"? Or, to put it more tangibly, which of them could put up with a true biography? Take a few instances. Lord Byron wrote a most personal autobiography, but Thomas Moore was "too good" for it and burned his friend's papers. Dr. Gwinner, Schopenhauer's executor, is said to have done the same; for Schopenhauer also wrote much about himself, and perhaps also against himself: (εἰς ἑαντόν). The virtuous American Thayer, Beethoven's biographer, suddenly broke off his work: he had reached a certain point in that honorable and simple life and could stand it no longer. Moral: What sensible man nowadays writes one honest word about himself? He must already belong to the Order of Holy Foolhardiness. We are promised an autobiography of Richard Wagner; who doubts that it would be a clever autobiography? Think, if you please, of the grotesque horror the Catholic priest Janssen aroused in Germany with his inconceivably square and harmless pictures of the German Reformation. What would people not do if some real psychologist told us about a genuine Luther — told us not with the moralist simplicity of a country priest, or the sweet and cautious modesty of a Protestant historian, but, say, with the fearlessness of a Taine, which springs from strength of character and not from a prudent toleration of strength? (The Germans, by the bye, have already produced the classic specimen of this toleration, and they may well count him as one of their own: Leopold Ranke, that born classical advocate of every causa fortior, that cleverest of all the clever opportunists.)

20. But you will soon understand me. — In short, is there not reason enough for us psychologists never to get free of a certain mistrust of our own selves nowadays? Probably even we are still "too good" for our work. Whatever contempt we feel for this popular craze for morality, we are perhaps none the less its victims, its prey and its slaves; probably it infects even us. What was that diplomat warning us about, when he told his colleagues: "Let us especially mistrust our first impulses, gentlemen! they are almost always good"? This is how every psychologist should talk to his colleagues today. And so we return to our problem, which in fact demands a certain severity from us, a certain mistrust, especially of "first impulses." The ascetic ideal in the service of projected emotional excess: anyone who remembers the previous essay will already partly anticipate the essential meaning packed into these ten words. The thorough unhinging of the human soul, its plunge into terror, frost, ardor and rapture, so that it is freed, as by some lightning shock, from all the smallness and pettiness of unhappiness, depression and discomfort: what ways lead to this goal? And which of them leads there most safely?... At bottom all great emotions have this power, provided they find a sudden outlet — emotions such as rage, fear, lust, revenge, hope, triumph, despair, cruelty. And indeed the ascetic priest has had no scruples about enlisting the whole pack of hounds that rage in the human kennel, unleashing now these and now those. His aim is always the same: to wake man out of his protracted melancholy and chase away, at least for a time, his dull pain and shrinking misery, and always with a religious interpretation and justification to sanction it. Of course this emotional excess has to be paid for afterward — it makes the ill more ill — and so, by modern standards, this kind of remedy for pain is a "guilty" kind.

Fairness, however, demands that we stress all the more that this remedy is applied with a good conscience. The ascetic priest has prescribed it in the most implicit belief that it is useful and indispensable — often enough almost collapsing in the presence of the pain he created. Fairness also demands that we stress that the violent physiological revenges of such excesses, and perhaps even the mental disturbances, are not absolutely inconsistent with the general character of this remedy. As we showed previously, it is not meant to heal diseases but to fight the unhappiness of that depression, and its object was to ease and deaden that unhappiness. The object, then, was achieved. The keynote that let the ascetic priest make every kind of agonizing and ecstatic music play on the fibres of the human soul was, as everyone knows, the exploitation of the feeling of "guilt." I indicated the origin of this feeling in the previous essay — as a piece of animal psychology and nothing else: there we met the feeling of "guilt" in its crude state, as it were. Only in the hands of the priest, real artist that he was with the feeling of guilt, did it take shape — oh, what a shape! "Sin" — for that is the name of the new priestly version of the animal "bad-conscience" (the inverted cruelty) — has so far been the greatest event in the history of the diseased soul. In "sin" we find the most perilous and fatal masterpiece of religious interpretation. Imagine man, suffering from himself in some way or other, at any rate physiologically, perhaps like an animal shut up in a cage, unclear about the why and the wherefore! Imagine him in his desire for reasons (reasons bring relief), and again in his desire for remedies, for narcotics at last, as he consults one who knows even the occult — and see, lo and behold, his wizard, the ascetic priest, gives him a hint, the first hint about the "cause" of his trouble: he must search for it in himself, in his guiltiness, in a piece of the past, and he must understand his very suffering as a state of punishment. He has heard, he has understood, the unfortunate man: he is now in the plight of a hen with a line drawn round it. He never gets out of the circle of lines. The sick man has been turned into "the sinner" — and for a few thousand years now we have not been able to get away from the sight of this new invalid, "a sinner" — shall we ever get away from it? — wherever we look, there is the hypnotic gaze of the sinner, always moving in one direction (in the direction of guilt, the only cause of suffering); there is the evil conscience, this "greuliche thier," to use Luther's language; there is rumination over the past, a distorted view of action, the gaze of the "green-eyed monster" turned on all action; there is the wilful misunderstanding of suffering, its transvaluation into feelings of guilt and fear of retribution; there are the scourge, the hairy shirt, the starving body, contrition; there is the sinner breaking himself on the ghastly wheel of a restless and morbidly eager conscience; there are mute pain, extreme fear, the agony of a tortured heart, the spasms of an unknown happiness, the shriek for "redemption." In fact, with this system of procedure the old depression, dullness and fatigue were absolutely conquered, and life itself became very interesting again: awake, eternally awake, sleepless, glowing, burnt away, exhausted and yet not tired — such was the figure of man, "the sinner," once he was initiated into these mysteries. This grand old wizard of an ascetic priest, in his fight with depression, had clearly triumphed; his kingdom had come. Men no longer grumbled at pain, men panted after pain: "More pain! More pain!" So for centuries on end his acolytes and initiates shrieked their demand. Every emotional excess that hurt; everything that broke, overthrew, crushed, transported, ravished; the mystery of torture-chambers, the ingenuity of hell itself — all this was now discovered, divined and exploited, all this was put at the wizard's service, all this helped to bring about the triumph of his ideal, the ascetic ideal. "My kingdom is not of this world," he said, both at the beginning and at the end: had he still the right to talk like that? — Goethe has maintained that there are only thirty-six tragic situations: from that we would infer, if we did not know otherwise, that Goethe was no ascetic priest. He — knows more.

21. Where this kind of priestly medicine-mongering, the "guilty" kind, is concerned, every word of criticism is superfluous. As for the suggestion that emotional excess of this type, which in these cases the ascetic priest is eager to order for his sick patients (under the most sacred euphemism, as is obvious, and equally impregnated with the sanctity of his purpose), has ever really been of use to any sick man: who, if you please, would feel inclined to maintain such a proposition? At any rate, we should first come to an understanding about the expression "be of use." If you only mean that such a system of treatment has reformed man, I do not deny it. I merely add that to my mind "reformed" means as much as "tamed," "weakened," "discouraged," "refined," "daintified," "emasculated" (and so it means almost as much as injured). But when you are dealing mainly with sick, depressed and oppressed creatures, such a system, even granted that it makes the ill "better," always makes them more ill as well. Ask the mad-doctors what invariably results from a methodical application of penance-torture, contrition and salvation ecstasies. Ask history too. In every body politic where the ascetic priest has established this treatment of the sick, disease has each time spread with sinister speed through its whole length and breadth. What was always the "result"? A shattered nervous system on top of the existing malady, in the greatest as in the smallest, in individuals as in masses. The penance and redemption training gives us awful epileptic epidemics, the greatest known to history, such as the St. Vitus and St. John dances of the Middle Ages. Another phase of its after-effect is frightful mutilations and chronic depressions, which turn the temperament of a nation or a city (Geneva, Bale) once for all into its opposite. This training, again, is responsible for the witch-hysteria, a phenomenon analogous to somnambulism (eight great epidemic outbursts of this alone between 1564 and 1605). It also brings in its train those delirious death-cravings of large masses, whose awful "shriek," "evviva la morte!" was heard over the whole of Europe, interrupted now by voluptuous variations and now by a rage for destruction. Today the same emotional sequence, with the same intermittences and sudden changes, is observed universally wherever the ascetic doctrine of sin scores a great success once more (religious neurosis appears as a manifestation of the devil, there is no doubt of it. What is it? Quæritur). Speaking generally, the ascetic ideal and its sublime-moral cult, this most ingenious, reckless and perilous systematization of all methods of emotional excess, is written large in a dreadful and unforgettable fashion across the whole history of man, and unfortunately not only across history. I could scarcely name any other element that has done more destructive harm to the health and race efficiency of Europeans than this ideal. Without exaggeration, it can be called the real fatality in the history of the health of the European man. The most you can do is compare it with the specifically German influence: I mean the alcohol poisoning of Europe, which up to the present has kept pace exactly with the political and racial pre–dominance of the Germans (where they inoculated their blood, there too they inoculated their vice). Third in the series comes syphilis — magno sed proximo intervallo.

22. Wherever the ascetic priest has gained the mastery, he has corrupted the health of the soul, and so he has also corrupted taste in artibus et litteris — he corrupts it still. "So?" I hope I shall be granted this "so"; at any rate, I am not going to prove it first. Here is one solitary indication. It concerns the arch-book of Christian literature, their real model, their "book-in-itself." The Græco-Roman world was splendid, and its splendor included books. Right in the midst of it, face to face with an ancient world of writings not yet fallen into decay and ruin, at a time when certain books were still there to be read, books we would now give half our literature to possess, the simplicity and vanity of Christian agitators (they are generally called Fathers of the Church) dared to declare: "We too have our classical literature, we do not need that of the Greeks." And meanwhile they proudly pointed to their books of legends, their letters of apostles and their apologetic tractlets, just as the English "Salvation Army" today wages its fight against Shakespeare and other "heathens" with an analogous literature. You already guess it: I do not like the "New Testament." It almost upsets me to stand so isolated in my taste about this valued, this over-valued Scripture; the taste of two thousand years is against me; but what does it matter! "Here I stand! I cannot help myself" — I have the courage of my bad taste. The Old Testament is quite another matter; all honor to the Old Testament! In it I find great men, a heroic landscape, and one of the rarest phenomena in the world, the incomparable naïveté of the strong heart; further still, I find a people. In the New, on the contrary, I find just a hostel of petty sects, pure rococo of the soul, twisting angles and fancy touches, nothing but conventicle air, not to forget an occasional whiff of bucolic sweetness that belongs to the epoch (and the Roman province) and is less Jewish than Hellenistic. Meekness and braggadocio cheek by jowl; an emotional garrulousness that almost deafens; passionate hysteria, but no passion; painful pantomime; here manifestly everyone lacked good breeding. How dare anyone make as much fuss about their little failings as these pious little fellows do! No one cares a straw about it — let alone God. And finally they actually wish to have "the crown of eternal life," all these little provincials! In return for what, if you please? For what end? Insolence cannot be carried any further. An immortal Peter! Who could stand him! Their ambition makes one laugh: the creature serves up his most personal life, his melancholies and common-or-garden troubles, cut and dried, as though the Universe itself were obliged to bother about them, for he never tires of wrapping up God Himself in the petty misery in which his troubles are involved. And what about the atrocious form of this chronic hobnobbing with God? This Jewish, and not merely Jewish, slobbering and clawing importunacy towards God! — There are little despised "heathen nations" in East Asia from whom these first Christians could have learned something worth learning, a little tact in worshiping; these nations do not allow themselves to say aloud the name of their God. This seems to me delicate enough; it is certain that it is too delicate, and not only for primitive Christians. For a contrast, just recall Luther, the most "eloquent" and insolent peasant Germany has had, and think of the Lutheran tone in which he felt most in his element during his tête-à-têtes with God. Luther's opposition to the mediæval saints of the Church (in particular, to "that devil's hog, the Pope") was, there is no doubt, at bottom the opposition of a boor. He was offended at the good etiquette of the Church, that worship-etiquette of the sacerdotal code, which lets only the initiated and the silent into the holy of holies and shuts the door against boors. These were definitely not to be allowed a hearing on this planet — but Luther the peasant simply wished it otherwise; as it was, it was not German enough for him. He wished to talk directly, to talk personally, to talk "straight from the shoulder" with his God. Well, he has done it. The ascetic ideal, you will guess, was at no time and in no place a school of good taste, still less of good manners — at best it was a school for sacerdotal manners: that is, it contains in itself something that was a deadly enemy to all good manners. Lack of measure, opposition to measure, it is itself a "non plus ultra."

23. The ascetic ideal has corrupted more than health and taste. It has corrupted a third, a fourth, a fifth and a sixth thing as well — but I shall take care not to run through the whole catalogue (when would I ever reach the end?). My task here is not to expose what this ideal brought about. I want to expose only what it means, what it rests on, and what lies lurking behind it and beneath it: that of which it is the provisional expression, an obscure expression bristling with queries and misunderstandings. With only this in view I presumed "not to spare" my readers a glance at the awfulness of its results, a glance at its fatal results. I did so to prepare them for the final and most awful aspect that the question of this ideal's significance presents to me. What is the significance of the power of that ideal, the monstrousness of its power? Why is it given so much scope? Why is no better resistance offered against it? The ascetic ideal expresses one will: where is the opposing will, in which an opposing ideal expresses itself? The ascetic ideal has an aim. Put generally, this aim is that all the other interests of human life should, measured by its standard, look petty and narrow. It explains epochs, nations and men by reference to this one end. It forbids any other interpretation and any other end. It rejects, denies, affirms and confirms only in the sense of its own interpretation (and was there ever a more thoroughly worked-out system of interpretation?). It submits to no power; it believes instead in its own precedence over every power. It believes that nothing powerful exists in the world that has not first got to receive from "it" a meaning, a right to exist, a value, as an instrument in its work, a way and means to its end, to one end. Where is the counterpart of this complete system of will, end and interpretation? Why is the counterpart missing? Where is the other "one aim"? But I am told it is not missing. I am told that it has not only fought a long and successful fight with that ideal, but has already won the mastery over it in all essentials. Our whole modern science is supposed to attest this — that modern science which, like the genuine reality-philosophy it is, plainly believes in itself alone, plainly has the courage to be itself and the will to be itself, and has got on well enough without God, another world and negative virtues.

With all their noisy agitator-babble, however, they get nowhere with me. These trumpeters of reality are bad musicians; their voices do not rise from the depths audibly enough, they are not the mouthpiece of the abyss of scientific knowledge — for today scientific knowledge is an abyss — and the word "science" in such trumpeter-mouths is a prostitution, an abuse, an impertinence. The truth is just the opposite of what the ascetic theory maintains. Science today has absolutely no belief in itself, let alone in an ideal above itself. And wherever science is still made of passion, love, ardor and suffering, it is not the opposite of the ascetic ideal but rather the incarnation of that ideal's latest and noblest form. Does that sound strange? There are plenty of brave and decent working people, even among the learned men of today, who like their little corner. Just because they are pleased to be there, they sometimes become indecently loud in demanding that people today should be quite content, especially in science — for in science there is so much useful work to do. I do not deny it. There is nothing I should like less than to spoil these honest workers' delight in their handiwork, for I rejoice in their work. But the fact that science requires hard work, and that it has contented workers, is no proof at all that science as a whole has one end, one will, one ideal, one passion for a great faith today. The contrary, as I have said, is the case. When science is not the latest manifestation of the ascetic ideal — and such cases are so rare, so select and so exquisite that they cannot affect the general judgment — science is a hiding-place for every kind of cowardice, disbelief, remorse, despectio sui, bad conscience. It is the very anxiety that springs from having no ideal, the suffering from the lack of a great love, the discontent with an enforced moderation. Oh, what does science not cover today? How much, at any rate, does it not try to cover? The diligence of our best scholars, their senseless industry, their burning the candle of their brain at both ends, their very mastery in their handiwork: how often is the real meaning of all that to keep themselves from continuing to see a certain thing? Science as a self-anæsthetic: do you know that? You wound them — everyone who associates with scholars experiences this — you sometimes wound them to the quick with a perfectly harmless word. When you think you are paying them a compliment, you embitter them beyond all bounds, simply because you lacked the finesse to work out what kind of customers you had to deal with: the sufferer kind (who won't own up even to themselves what they really are), the dazed and unconscious kind who have only one fear — coming to consciousness.

24. And now look at the other side, at those rare cases of which I spoke, the most supreme idealists to be found among philosophers and scholars today. Have we, perhaps, found in them the sought-for opponents of the ascetic ideal, its anti-idealists? They themselves certainly think so, these "unbelievers" (for they are all of them that). The idea of being opponents of this ideal seems to be their last remnant of faith; they are so earnest about it, so passionate in word and gesture. But must what they believe therefore be true? We "knowers" have little by little come to distrust believers of every kind. Our suspicion has taught us, step by step, to draw the opposite conclusions from the ones people used to draw: wherever the strength of a belief stands out, we infer that what is believed is hard to prove, and even actually improbable. We do not deny again that "faith produces salvation," and for that very reason we do deny that faith proves anything. A strong faith that produces happiness arouses suspicion of the object of that faith. It does not establish its "truth"; it does establish a certain probability of — illusion. What is the position in these cases? These solitaries and deniers of today; these fanatics in one thing, in their claim to intellectual cleanness; these hard, stern, continent, heroic spirits who make up the glory of our time; all these pale atheists, anti-Christians, immoralists, Nihilists; these skeptics, "ephectics," and "hectics" of the intellect (in a certain sense they are the latter, both collectively and individually); these supreme idealists of knowledge, in whom alone the intellectual conscience dwells and is alive today — in fact they believe themselves as far away as possible from the ascetic ideal, these "free, very free spirits." And yet, if I may reveal what they cannot see themselves, since they stand too near themselves: this ideal is simply their ideal. They represent it today, and perhaps no one else does. They themselves are its most spiritualized product, its most advanced picket of skirmishers and scouts, its most insidious, delicate and elusive form of seduction. — If I am in any way a reader of riddles, I will be one with this sentence: for some time past there have been no free spirits, for they still believe in truth. When the Christian Crusaders in the East came into collision with that invincible order of assassins, that order of free spirits par excellence, whose lowest grade lives in a state of discipline such as no order of monks has ever attained, they somehow got an inkling of that symbol and tally-word reserved for the highest grade alone as their secretum: "Nothing is true, everything is allowed." Indeed, that was freedom of thought; with it they took leave of the very belief in truth. Has any European, any Christian freethinker, ever really strayed into this proposition and its labyrinthine consequences? Does he know the Minotauros of this den from experience? I doubt it — nay, I know otherwise. Freedom and unfettering in that sense are more foreign to these "mono-fanatics," these so-called "free spirits," than anything else. In no respect are they more tightly bound, and their fanatical belief in truth has no equal. I know all this from experience at close quarters, perhaps too well. I know that dignified philosophic abstinence to which a belief like that binds its adherents, that stoicism of the intellect which in the end forbids negation as rigidly as it forbids affirmation, that wish to stand still in front of the actual, the factum brutum, that fatalism in "petits faits" (ce petit faitalism, as I call it), in which French Science now attempts a kind of moral superiority over German. I know this renunciation of interpretation generally (that is, of forcing, doctoring, abridging, omitting, suppressing, inventing, falsifying, and all the other essential attributes of interpretation). All this, broadly considered, expresses the asceticism of virtue just as effectively as any repudiation of the senses does (it is at bottom only a modus of that repudiation). But what forces it into that unqualified will for truth is the faith in the ascetic ideal itself, even if it takes the form of unconscious imperatives. Make no mistake about it: it is the faith, I repeat, in a metaphysical value, an intrinsic value of truth, of a kind that is warranted and guaranteed only in this ideal (it stands and falls with that ideal). Judged strictly, a science without "hypotheses" does not exist; the very thought of one is inconceivable and illogical. A philosophy, a faith, must always exist first, to give science a direction, a meaning, a limit and a method, a right to exist. (Whoever holds the contrary opinion — whoever, for example, takes it upon himself to establish philosophy "upon a strictly scientific basis" — has first got to "turn upside down" not only philosophy but also truth itself. That is the gravest insult that could possibly be offered to two such respectable females!) Yes, there is no doubt about it — and here I quote my Joyful Wisdom, cp. Book V. Aph. 344: "The man who is truthful in that daring and extreme fashion which is the presupposition of the faith in science thereby asserts a different world from that of life, nature and history; and in so far as he asserts the existence of that different world, come, must he not similarly repudiate its counterpart, this world, our world? The belief on which our faith in science is based has remained to this day a metaphysical belief. Even we knowers of today, we godless foes of metaphysics, we too take our fire from that conflagration which was kindled by a thousand-year-old faith, from that Christian belief which was also Plato's belief, the belief that God is truth, that truth is divine.... But what if this belief becomes more and more incredible, what if nothing proves itself to be divine, unless it be error, blindness, lies — what if God himself proved himself to be our oldest lie?" — It is necessary to stop at this point and consider the situation carefully. Science itself now needs a justification (which is not for a minute to say that there is such a justification). Look in this context at the most ancient and the most modern philosophers: not one of them realizes how badly the Will for Truth needs a justification. Every philosophy has a gap here. What causes it? Until now the ascetic ideal dominated all philosophy; Truth was fixed as Being, as God, as the Supreme Court of Appeal, and Truth was not allowed to be a problem. Do you understand this "allowed"? From the moment that belief in the God of the ascetic ideal is repudiated, there exists a new problem: the problem of the value of truth. The Will for Truth needed a critique. Let us define our own task by these words: the value of truth is tentatively to be called in question.... (If this seems too laconically expressed, I recommend that the reader peruse again the passage from the Joyful Wisdom titled "How far we also are still pious," Aph. 344, and best of all the whole fifth book of that work, as well as the Preface to The Dawn of Day.)

25. No! You can't get round me with science, when I search for the natural antagonists of the ascetic ideal, when I put the question: "Where is the opposing will in which the opposing ideal expresses itself?" Science is not nearly independent enough to fill this role. In every department science needs an ideal value, a power that creates values, in whose service it can believe in itself — science itself never creates values. In itself, science does not stand against the ascetic ideal. Speaking roughly, it is rather the progressive force within that ideal's inner evolution. Tested more exactly, its opposition and antagonism are directed not at the ideal itself but only at that ideal's outworks, its outer garb, its masquerade, its temporary hardening, stiffening and dogmatizing. Science makes the life in the ideal free once more, while it repudiates the ideal's superficial elements. These two phenomena, science and the ascetic ideal, both rest on the same basis — I have already made this clear — the basis, I say, of the same overvaluation of truth (more accurately, the same belief in the impossibility of valuing and criticizing truth). Consequently they are necessarily allies, so that if they are attacked, they must always be attacked and called into question together. A valuation of the ascetic ideal inevitably entails a valuation of science as well. Lose no time in seeing this clearly, and be sharp to catch it! (Art — I am speaking provisionally, for I will treat it in greater detail on some other occasion — art, I repeat, in which lying is sanctified and the will for deception has good conscience on its side, is much more fundamentally opposed to the ascetic ideal than science is. Plato's instinct felt this — Plato, the greatest enemy of art that Europe has produced up to now. Plato versus Homer: that is the complete, the true antagonism. On the one side stands the whole-hearted "transcendental," the great defamer of life; on the other, its involuntary panegyrist, the golden nature. An artistic subservience to the ascetic ideal is therefore the most absolute artistic corruption there can be, though unfortunately it is one of the most frequent, for nothing is more corruptible than an artist.) Considered physiologically, moreover, science rests on the same basis as the ascetic ideal: a certain impoverishment of life is the presupposition of the one as of the other. Add to that frigidity of the emotions, a slackening of the tempo, the substitution of dialectic for instinct, and seriousness stamped on mien and gesture (seriousness, that most unmistakable sign of strenuous metabolism, of struggling, toiling life). Look at the periods in a nation's history when the learned man steps into the foreground. They are periods of exhaustion, often of sunset and decay; the effervescing strength is gone, and so are the confidence in life and the confidence in the future. The preponderance of the mandarins never signifies anything good, any more than the advent of democracy, or arbitration instead of war, equal rights for women, the religion of pity, and all the other symptoms of declining life. (Science handled as a problem! What is the meaning of science? On this point see the Preface to the Birth of Tragedy.) No! This "modern science" — mark this well — is at times the best ally of the ascetic ideal, and for the very reason that it is the most unconscious, most automatic, most secret and most subterranean ally! Up to now they have been playing into each other's hands, these "poor in spirit" and the scientific opponents of that ideal. (Take care, by the by, not to think that these opponents are the antithesis of this ideal, that they are the rich in spirit. They are not; I have called them the hectic in spirit.) These celebrated victories of science are certainly victories — but over what? Not one victory on their list ever defeated the ascetic ideal, even for a minute. On the contrary, it was made stronger, that is to say more elusive, more abstract, more insidious, by the fact that science from time to time ruthlessly destroyed and broke down a wall, an outwork, that had been built onto the main fortress and disfigured its appearance. Is anyone seriously suggesting that when theological astronomy fell, that ideal fell with it? — Has man, perhaps, grown less in need of a transcendental solution to his riddle of existence, because since then this existence has become more random, casual and superfluous in the visible order of the universe? Since Copernicus, has man not belittled himself ever further, and has his will to belittle himself not grown without a break? Alas, his belief in his dignity, his uniqueness, his irreplaceableness in the scheme of existence, is gone. He has become animal, literal, unqualified and unmitigated animal, he who in his earlier belief was almost God ("child of God," "demi-God"). Since Copernicus man seems to have fallen onto a steep slope. He rolls faster and faster away from the center — whither? Into nothingness? Into the "thrilling sensation of his own nothingness"? Well! Would this not be the straight way — to the old ideal? All science (and by no means only astronomy, about whose humiliating and deteriorating effect Kant has made a remarkable confession: "it annihilates my own importance"), all science, natural as much as unnatural — by unnatural I mean the self-critique of reason — sets out nowadays to talk man out of his present opinion of himself, as though that opinion had been nothing but a bizarre piece of conceit. You might go so far as to say that science finds its peculiar pride, its peculiar bitter form of stoical ataraxia, in preserving man's contempt for himself, that state which it took so much trouble to bring about, as man's final and most serious claim to self-appreciation (rightly so, in fact, for he who despises is always "one who has not forgotten how to appreciate"). But does all this involve any real effort to counteract the ascetic ideal? Does anyone really suggest, seriously, that Kant's victory over the theological dogmatism about "God," "Soul," "Freedom," "Immortality" has done that ideal any damage (as the theologians have long imagined)? — And in this connection it does not concern us for a single minute whether Kant himself intended any such result. It is certain that since Kant every type of transcendentalist is playing a winning game. They are emancipated from the theologians; what luck! He has revealed to them the secret art by which they can now pursue their "heart's desire" on their own responsibility, and with all the respectability of science. Similarly, who can grumble at the agnostics, reverers as they are of the unknown and the absolute mystery, if they now worship their very query as God? (Xaver Doudan talks somewhere of the ravages produced by l'habitude d'admirer l'inintelligible au lieu de rester tout simplement dans l'inconnu; the ancients, he thinks, must have been exempt from those ravages.) Suppose that everything "known" to man fails to satisfy his desires and on the contrary contradicts and horrifies them. What a divine way out, then, to be able to look for the responsibility not in the "desiring" but in the "knowing"! — "There is no knowledge. Consequently — there is a God": what a novel elegantia syllogismi! What a triumph for the ascetic ideal!

26. Or does the whole of modern history, perhaps, show more confidence in life and in its ideals? Its loftiest pretension today is to be a mirror. It rejects all teleology and wants no more "proving." It disdains to play the judge, and shows its good taste in that. It asserts as little as it denies; it fixes, it "describes." All this is ascetic to a high degree, yet nihilistic to a much higher degree; make no mistake about this! In the historian you see a gloomy, hard, but determined gaze, the eye of an isolated North Pole explorer (perhaps so as not to look within, so as not to look back?). There is snow; life is silenced here; the last crows that caw here are called "whither?", "Vanity," "Nada." Nothing more flourishes or grows here, except at most the metapolitics of St. Petersburg and the "pity" of Tolstoi. Then there is that other school of historians, a perhaps still more "modern" school, voluptuous and lascivious, which ogles life and the ascetic ideal with equal fervor, which wears the word "artist" like a glove, and has by now secured a "corner" for itself in all the praise of contemplation. Oh, what a thirst these sweet intellectuals arouse, even for ascetics and winter landscapes! Nay! The devil take these "contemplative" folk! I would much rather wander with those historical Nihilists through the gloomiest, grey, cold mist! Nay, I shall not mind listening (supposing I have to choose) to someone completely unhistorical and anti-historical (a man like Dühring, for instance, whose periods have intoxicated a hitherto shy and unavowed species of "beautiful souls" in contemporary Germany, the species anarchistica within the educated proletariate). The "contemplative" are a hundred times worse. Nothing has ever made me so intensely nauseous as one of those "objective" chairs, one of those scented mannikins-about-town of history, a thing half-priest, half-satyr (Renan parfum). The high, shrill falsetto of his applause betrays what he lacks and where he lacks it: it betrays where the Fates, in his case, have plied their ghastly shears, alas! in too surgeon-like a fashion! I find this distasteful, and it tries my patience. Let him stay patient at such sights who has nothing to lose by it. For me the sight is enraging; such spectators embitter me against the "play," even more than the play itself does (history itself, you understand). Anacreontic moods come over me imperceptibly. This Nature, who gave the steer its horn and the lion its χάσμ ὀδοντων: for what purpose did Nature give me my foot? — To kick, by St. Anacreon, and not merely to run away! To trample on all the worm-eaten "chairs," the cowardly contemplators, the lascivious eunuchs of history, the flirters with ascetic ideals, the righteous hypocrites of impotence! All reverence from me to the ascetic ideal, in so far as it is honorable! So long as it believes in itself and plays no pranks on us! But I do not like all these coquettish bugs, whose insatiable ambition is to smell of the infinite until at last the infinite smells of bugs. I do not like the whited sepulchres with their stagey imitation of life. I do not like the tired and the used up who wrap themselves in wisdom and look "objective." I do not like the agitators dressed up as heroes, who hide their dummy-heads behind the stalking-horse of an ideal. I do not like the ambitious artists who would fain play the ascetic and the priest, and are at bottom nothing but tragic clowns. I do not like, again, these newest speculators in idealism, the Anti-Semites, who roll their eyes in the patent Christian-Aryan-man-of-honor fashion today, and with moralist attitudes and agitation dodges so cheap that they exhaust any patience, try to rouse all the blockhead elements in the populace (the unfailing success of every kind of intellectual charlatanism in present-day Germany is tied to the almost indisputable and already quite palpable desolation of the German mind. I look for its cause in a too exclusive diet of papers, politics, beer and Wagnerian music, not forgetting the condition this diet presupposes: the national exclusiveness and vanity, the strong but narrow principle "Germany, Germany above everything," and finally the paralysis agitans of "modern ideas"). Europe today is above all wealthy and ingenious in means of excitement; it apparently has no more pressing need than stimulantia and alcohol. Hence the enormous counterfeiting of ideals, those most fiery spirits of the mind; hence also the repulsive, evil-smelling, perjured, pseudo-alcoholic air everywhere. I should like to know how many cargoes of imitation idealism, of hero-costumes and high-falutin' claptrap, how many casks of sweetened pity liqueur (Firm: la religion de la souffrance), how many crutches of righteous indignation to prop up these flat-footed intellects, how many comedians of the Christian moral ideal would have to be exported from Europe today before its air smelled pure again. It is obvious that this over-production opens up a new trade possibility, and obvious that a new business is to be done in little ideal idols and obedient "idealists" — don't pass over this tip! Who has the courage? We hold in our hands the possibility of idealizing the whole earth. But what am I saying, courage? Here we need only one thing — a hand, a free, a very free hand.

27. Enough! Enough! Let us leave these curiosities and complexities of the modern spirit, which provoke as much laughter as disgust. Our problem, the problem of the meaning of the ascetic ideal, can certainly do without them. What has it to do with yesterday or today? I shall deal with those matters more thoroughly and severely elsewhere (under the title "A Contribution to the History of European Nihilism"; I refer here to a work I am preparing: The Will to Power, an Attempt at a Transvaluation of All Values). I bring them up here for one reason only. Even in the most intellectual sphere, the ascetic ideal has at times just one real kind of enemies and damagers: the comedians of this ideal, because they awaken mistrust. Everywhere else the mind works seriously, powerfully and without counterfeiting, and there it dispenses altogether with an ideal (the popular name for this abstinence is "Atheism"), except for the will for truth. But this will, this remnant of an ideal, is, if you will believe me, that very ideal in its severest and cleverest formulation, esoteric through and through, stripped of all outworks; so it is not so much the ideal's remnant as its kernel. Unqualified honest atheism (and we, the most intellectual men of this age, breathe no other air) is not as opposed to that ideal as it seems. It is rather one of the last phases in the ideal's evolution, one of its syllogisms and pieces of inherent logic. It is the awe-inspiring catastrophe of a two-thousand-year training in truth, a training that finally forbids itself the lie of the belief in God. (India saw the same course of development, quite independently, and so with some demonstrative value: the same ideal driving to the same conclusion, with the decisive point reached five hundred years before the European era, or more precisely at the time of Buddha. It began in the Sankhyam philosophy, and Buddha then popularized it and made it into a religion.)

What has really triumphed over the Christian God? I ask the question with all strictness. The answer stands in my Joyful Wisdom, Aph. 357: "the Christian morality itself, the idea of truth taken with ever-increasing seriousness, the confessor-subtlety of the Christian conscience translated and sublimated into the scientific conscience, into intellectual cleanness at any price. To regard Nature as though it were a proof of the goodness and guardianship of God; to interpret history in honor of a divine reason, as a constant proof of a moral order of the world and a moral teleology; to explain our own personal experiences, as pious men have for long enough explained them, as though every arrangement, every nod, every single thing were invented and sent out of love for the salvation of the soul: all this is now done away with. The conscience is against it, and every subtler conscience regards it as disreputable, dishonorable, as lying, feminism, weakness, cowardice. By this severity, if by anything at all, we are good Europeans and heirs of Europe's longest and bravest self-mastery.". .. All great things bring about their own ruin by an act of self-dissolution: so wills the law of life, the law of necessary "self-mastery" even in the essence of life. The law-giver is always finally exposed to the cry, "patere legem quam ipse tulisti." So Christianity went to ruin as a dogma, through its own morality; and so Christianity must go to ruin again today as a morality. We are standing on the threshold of this event. Christian truthfulness draws one conclusion after another, and at last it draws its strongest conclusion, the one against itself. That happens when it puts the question: "what is the meaning of every will for truth?" And here I touch again on my problem, on our problem, my unknown friends (for as yet I know of no friends). What sense has our whole being, if not that in us that will for truth has become conscious of itself as a problem? — With this self-consciousness of the will for truth, morality from now on goes to pieces; there is no doubt about it. This is that great hundred-act play reserved for the next two centuries of Europe, the most terrible, the most mysterious, and perhaps also the most hopeful of all plays.

28. Without the ascetic ideal, man, the animal man, had no meaning. His existence on earth had no end. "What is man for, anyway?" was a question without an answer; the will for man and the world was lacking; behind every great human destiny rang a still greater "Vanity!" as a refrain. This is simply what the ascetic ideal means: something was lacking, a tremendous void encircled man. He did not know how to justify himself, to explain himself, to affirm himself; he suffered from the problem of what he meant. He suffered in other ways as well, since he was in the main a diseased animal. But suffering itself was not his problem. His problem was that the crying question "To what purpose do we suffer?" had no answer. Man is the bravest animal and the one most used to suffering, and he does not repudiate suffering in itself: he wills it, he even seeks it out, provided he is shown a meaning for it, a purpose of suffering. The curse that had until then lain over humanity was not suffering but the senselessness of suffering — and the ascetic ideal gave it a meaning! It was the only meaning until then; but any meaning is better than none, and in that connection the ascetic ideal was the "faute de mieux" par excellence of that time. In that ideal, suffering found an explanation; the tremendous gap seemed filled; the door to all suicidal Nihilism was shut. The explanation — there is no doubt about it — brought new suffering with it, deeper, more penetrating, more venomous, gnawing more brutally into life: it put all suffering under the perspective of guilt. But in spite of all that, man was saved by it. He now had a meaning, and from then on he was no longer a leaf in the wind, a shuttle-cock of chance and nonsense; he could "will" something, and it did not matter at all to what end, for what purpose or by what means he willed: the will itself was saved. What every complete will that takes its direction from the ascetic ideal makes plain cannot be disguised at all: this hate of the human, and even more of the animal, and more still of the material; this horror of the senses, of reason itself; this fear of happiness and beauty; this longing to get right away from all illusion, change, growth, death, wishing and even desiring. All this means — let us have the courage to grasp it — a will for Nothingness, a will opposed to life, a repudiation of the most fundamental conditions of life; but it is and remains a will! — And to say at the end what I said at the beginning: man will wish Nothingness rather than not wish at all.
